### Select Tenant Type

<table style="width:98%;">
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 98%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Choose first option as selected.</p>
<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image11.webp" style="width:4.69583in;height:1.99931in" /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>1. Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD)</p>
<p><strong>Purpose</strong>: Identity and access management for employees, partners, and apps.</p>
<p><strong>Use Case</strong>: Enterprise users sign in to Microsoft services (Azure, Microsoft 365, etc.) and custom apps.</p>
<p><strong>Features</strong>: Single sign-on (SSO), multi-factor authentication (MFA), conditional access, identity governance, and hybrid identity (integration with on-premises AD).</p>
<p>Example: A company (e.g., bringglobal.com) manages employee access to Microsoft 365 and internal applications using Entra ID.</p>
<p>2. Azure AD B2C (Business-to-Consumer)</p>
<p><strong>Purpose</strong>: Identity management for external users (customers) in B2C apps.</p>
<p><strong>Use Case</strong>: Public-facing applications where users can sign in with social accounts (Google, Facebook, etc.) or local accounts (email/password).</p>
<p><strong>Features</strong>: Customizable authentication flows, user registration, social logins, MFA, and branding customization.</p>
<p>Example: A retail website allows customers to create accounts and sign in using Google or Facebook via Azure AD B2C.</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Manage Identities

<table style="width:98%;">
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 98%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><ul>
<li><p>In this section, we learn about users and groups.</p></li>
<li><p>Users and groups are the basic building blocks for an identity solution.</p></li>
<li><p>In the previous section, we just created a ‘tenant’.</p></li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Lab scenario</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><p>Your organization is building a new lab environment for pre-production testing of apps and services.</p></li>
<li><p>A few engineers are being hired to manage the lab environment, including the virtual machines.</p></li>
<li><p>To allow the engineers to authenticate by using Microsoft Entra ID, you have been tasked with provisioning users and groups.</p></li>
<li><p>To minimize administrative overhead, membership of the groups should be updated automatically based on job titles.</p></li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Architecture diagram</strong></p>
<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image31.webp" style="width:4.67292in;height:2.42917in" alt="Diagram of the lab 01 architecture." /></p>
<p><strong>Job skills</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><p>Task 1: Create and configure user accounts.</p></li>
<li><p>Task 2: Create groups and add members.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Manage Groups

<table style="width:98%;">
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 98%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><ol type="1">
<li><p>In this task, you create a group account.</p></li>
<li><p>Group accounts can include user accounts or devices.</p></li>
<li><p>These are two basic ways members are assigned to groups: <strong>Statically</strong> and <strong>Dynamically</strong>.</p></li>
<li><p>Static groups require administrators to add and remove members manually.</p></li>
<li><p>Dynamic groups update automatically based on the properties of a user account or device. For example, job title.</p></li>
</ol></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

|  |
|:---|
| <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_12.webp" style="width:5.13889in;height:2.17083in" /> |

### Understand Expiration and Naming Policy

<table style="width:98%;">
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 98%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image74.webp" style="width:4.74236in;height:2.75764in" /></p>
<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_13.webp" style="width:5.26458in;height:2.81944in" /></p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>Expiration</strong> lets you configure a group lifetime in days. After that time the group must be renewed by the owner.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Naming policy</strong> lets you configure blocked words and add a prefix or suffix to group names.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

### Create new group – Select Group Type

<table style="width:98%;">
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 98%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image77.webp" style="width:3.84375in;height:2.31944in" /></p>
<p><strong>Security groups</strong>: Used to manage access to shared resources.</p>
<p>Members of a security group can include users, devices, and service principals.</p>
<p>Groups can be members of other groups, sometimes known as nested groups.</p>
<p>Users and service principals can be the owner of a security group.</p>
<p><strong>Microsoft 365 groups</strong>: Provide collaboration opportunities.</p>
<p>Members of a Microsoft 365 group can <strong>only</strong> include users.</p>
<p>Users and service principals can be the owner of a Microsoft 365 group.</p>
<p>People outside of your organization can be members of a group.</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

#  EntraID - Implment MFA for USER

<table style="width:87%;">
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 87%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image95.webp" style="width:6.53125in;height:0.88056in" alt="{D00DAC7A-980B-425D-901E-A0DCADD92823}" /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><ul>
<li><p>You are an Architect for Hexelo, an organization that needs to manage its Microsoft Entra tenant.</p></li>
<li><p>In this Challenge Lab, you will configure multi-factor authentication (MFA) by using Microsoft Entra ID.</p></li>
<li><p>First, you will modify the properties of a Microsoft Entra tenant, and then you will create a new user in the directory tenant by using Microsoft Entra ID.</p></li>
<li><p>Next, you will enable MFA for the new user.</p></li>
<li><p>Finally, you will test user access by using MFA and the Microsoft Authenticator mobile app.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><strong>Activities</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>Login</strong> with Temporary Access Pass (TAP): Credentials LabAdmin@hexelo45001364x2.onmicrosoft.com with password A2+H#3DL to authenticate via TAP, enabling secure access for <strong>initial setup</strong> without relying on standard admin credentials.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Update</strong> Technical Contact: Modify the technical contact field in Microsoft Entra ID properties to labadmin@hexelo.com, designating an email for MFA-related notifications and tenant authentication management.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Create</strong> Two Users: Set up two users, TestUser@hexelo45001364x2.onmicrosoft.com and MFAUser@hexelo45001364x2.onmicrosoft.com, using the TAP-authenticated LabAdmin account to simulate user management.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Enable</strong> MFA for MFAUser: Configure Multi-Factor Authentication for MFAUser, enforcing an additional layer of security for their sign-in process.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Test</strong> MFA Login: Logged in as MFAUser in a different browser, which prompted an Authenticator app verification, confirming MFA functionality and user experience.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Check</strong>Logs with LabAdmin: Sign back into the Azure portal as the LabAdmin and review audit logs (tracking administrative actions) and sign-in logs (monitoring authentication events) to verify MFA enforcement and user activity.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Note</strong>: Audit Logs track administrative actions and changes made within Microsoft Entra ID, such as user creation or MFA configuration.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Note</strong>: Sign-in Logs record user authentication events, including login attempts, successes, failures, and MFA verification details.</p></li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Achievements</strong>:</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Demonstrated secure admin access using TAP for initial configuration.</p></li>
<li><p>Successfully configured and tested MFA for a user, enhancing account security.</p></li>
<li><p>Gained practical experience in user management and monitoring through audit and sign-in logs.</p></li>
<li><p>Validated the MFA setup process and its impact on user authentication workflows.</p></li>
<li><p>Learned to manage tenant settings, such as updating technical contact details, for administrative notifications.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Enable MFA for MFAuser

<table style="width:87%;">
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 46%" />
<col style="width: 41%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td colspan="2"><ul>
<li><p>Enable per-user MFA for the MFAUser account in the hexelo45001364x2.onmicrosoft.com directory tenant.</p></li>
<li><p>You can use the Per-user method to require users to perform MFA each time they sign in unless they either sign in from a trusted IP address, or the remembered devices feature is turned on.</p></li>
<li><p>You can use a Conditional Access policy to require MFA under specific conditions that you define-this is the preferred method, unless your organizational licenses do not permit the use of Conditional Access.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>→On the users page, click ‘Per-user MFA’ gear icon on the top right</p>
<p>→In Old the navigation was different: on the directory tenant Users page, on the command bar, if needed, select the ellipsis (…) for More options, and then select Per-user MFA.</p>
<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image126.webp" /><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image127.webp" style="width:6.52778in;height:2.92083in" alt="{215338E3-2A71-4765-AF77-7AA5FBA59F01}" /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Select the user ‘MFAUser’ and click ‘Enable MFA’</p>
<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image128.webp" /><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image129.webp" /><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image130.webp" /><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image131.webp" style="width:2.81042in;height:2.34514in" alt="{D2533015-12A0-40E8-9662-4A70E04EECDA}" /></p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Enable</p>
<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image132.webp" /><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image133.webp" style="width:2.62917in;height:1.66875in" alt="{FB25B65D-79CB-41E8-8E8B-61A0B0E4EECF}" /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="2"><ul>
<li><p>There are two methods of enabling MFA for Azure users:</p></li>
<li><p>You can use the Per-user method to require users to perform MFA each time they sign in unless they either sign in from a trusted IP address, or the remembered devices feature is turned on.</p></li>
<li><p>You can use a Conditional Access policy to require MFA under specific conditions that you define-this is the preferred method, unless your organizational licenses do not permit the use of Conditional Access.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>

</table>

#  Management Groups and Subscriptions

<table style="width:98%;">
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 98%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><ul>
<li><p>It is about role-based access control.</p></li>
<li><p>The below sections show how to use permissions and scopes to control what actions identities can and cannot perform.</p></li>
<li><p>We can see how to make subscription management easier using management groups.</p></li>
<li><p>This lab requires an Azure subscription.</p></li>
<li><p>Your subscription type may affect the availability of features in this lab.</p></li>
<li><p>You may change the region, but the steps are written using <strong>East US</strong>.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>Task:</p>
<ul>
<li><p>To simplify management of Azure resources in your organization, the following tasks need to be implemented</p></li>
</ul>
<ul>
<li><p>Creating a management group that includes all your Azure subscriptions.</p></li>
<li><p>Granting permission to submit support requests for all subscriptions in the management group. The permissions should be limited only to:</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Create and manage virtual machines</p></li>
<li><p>Create support request tickets (do not include adding Azure providers)</p></li>
</ul></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>Lab Simulations</p>

#  RBAC: Role Assignments - \[Reader and Network Admin\] - Portal

<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image247.webp" style="width:7.67361in;height:1.10347in" alt="{DEA4D6B2-8BF3-4DD5-949B-740B339E9CA4}" />

→In this challenge, you will implement role-based access control (RBAC).

→First, you will assign the Reader role to an Azure user.

→Next, you will test the role assignment.

→Finally, you will assign the Network Contributor role to an Azure user, and then you will test the Network Contributor role assignment.

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><p>Understand the scenario</p>
<p>You are an Architect for Hexelo, an organization that needs to secure its Azure® environment.</p>
<ul>
<li><p>In this Challenge Lab, you will implement role-based access control (RBAC).</p></li>
<li><p>First, you will assign the Reader role to an Azure user.</p></li>
<li><p>Next, you will test the role assignment.</p></li>
<li><p>Finally, you will assign the Network Contributor role to an Azure user, and then you will test the Network Contributor role assignment.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><p><strong>→Display the existing Azure resource groups.</strong></p>
<p>→On the Azure portal home page, in Navigate, select Resource groups, and then review the existing resource groups.</p>
<p><strong>→Assign the Reader role to a user named TestUser-52746244@LODSPRODMCA.onmicrosoft.com in the AZ300-RG1 resource group by using Active Assignment type (Preview).</strong></p>
<p>→On the Resource groups blade, select AZ300-RG1.</p>
<p>→On the AZ300-RG1 service menu, select Access control (IAM).</p>
<p>→On the Access control (IAM) page, in the Grant access to this resource tile, select Add role assignment.</p>
<p>→On the Add role assignment blade, in Job function roles, select Reader, and then select Next.</p>
<p>→On the Members page, in Members, select +Select members.</p>
<p>→On the Select members blade, search for and select TestUser-52746244@LODSPRODMCA.onmicrosoft.com, and then select Select.</p>
<p>→On the Members page, select Next.</p>
<p>→On Assignment type (Preview) page, in Assignment type (Preview), select Active.</p>
<p>→In Assignment duration, ensure that Permanent is selected, and then select Review + assign twice to finalize the process.</p>
<p>→The Reader role will allow the user to view resources in the resource group.</p>
<p>→By default, a <strong>new Microsoft Entra user has no permissions to access Azure resources</strong>.</p>
<p>→You can use Azure role-based access control (RBAC) role assignments to grant access to</p>
<blockquote>
<p>→resources at a specific scope-subscription,</p>
<p>→resource group,</p>
<p>→resource-by assigning a role to a user,</p>
<p>→ group, service principal,</p>
<p>→managed identity.</p>
</blockquote>
<p>→There are two types of roles that you can use:</p>
<blockquote>
<p>→ built-in</p>
<p>→custom.</p>
</blockquote>
<p>→We can create a custom role by using the Azure portal, Azure PowerShell®, Azure command-line interface (CLI) 2.0, and the REST API.</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

#  RBAC: Custom Role \[VM Contributor Role\] - Powershell 

<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image360.webp" style="width:7.66597in;height:1.01806in" alt="{E176B047-F468-4F93-A4AB-3350D5BA6C8A}" />

→You are an Architect for Hexelo, an organization that needs to manage its Azure® environment.

→In this Challenge Lab, you will create custom role-based access control (RBAC) roles.

→ First, you will create a custom role by using Azure PowerShell®, and then you will create a custom role by using the Azure portal.

→Create Custom Role Using Cloud Shell

→Obtain the resource ID of the AZ300RG resource group by using the Get-AzResourceGroup Azure PowerShell cmdlet, and then record it in the following Resource ID text box:

→Run the following command to obtain the resource ID of the AZ300RG resource group:

> PowerShell
>
> Get-AzResourceGroup -Name AZ300RG
>
> The result should look like the following:
>
> <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image361.jpeg" style="width:4.60903in;height:1.46181in" alt="IMG_256" />

→Copy the resource ID, and then paste it into the Resource ID text box in the Challenge Lab instructions.

→Identify the operations associated with virtual machines by using the Get-AzProviderOperation cmdlet.

→Run the following command to identify the operations associated with virtual machines:

> PowerShell
>
> Get-AzProviderOperation "Microsoft.Compute/virtualmachines/\*" \| FT Operation, Description -AutoSize

→You can use the operations associated with an Azure resource as actions when you create an Azure role-based access control (RBAC) custom role.

→Retrieve the role definition for the Virtual Machine Contributor role, and then output it to \$home\clouddrive\VMOperatorRole.json by using the Get-AzRoleDefinition and the [ConvertTo-Json](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.utility/convertto-json?view=powershell-7) cmdlets.

→Run the following command to retrieve a role definition:

> PowerShell
>
> Get-AzRoleDefinition -Name "Virtual Machine Contributor" \| ConvertTo-Json \| Out-File \$home\clouddrive\VMOperatorRole.json

→Open the VMOperatorRole.json file in the Azure Cloud Shell code editor by using the code command in the \$home\clouddrive folder.

→If prompted, switch to Cloud Shell classic mode, and then run the commands again.

→Edit the VMOperatorRole.json file by changing the properties in the following table:

| **Property** | **Value** |
|:---|:---|
| Name | "Virtual Machine Operator52758007" |
| Id | Delete the entire line |
| IsCustom | true |
| Description | "Lets you view, start and stop virtual machines." |
| AssignableScopes | "/subscriptions/d4b09ad3-1fb7-452b-8d61-cfc641cdea02/resourceGroups/AZ300RG" |

<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image362.jpeg" style="width:6.31528in;height:1.15764in" alt="IMG_257" />

- 

- <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image363.jpeg" style="width:4.63472in;height:1.97986in" alt="IMG_258" />

  →Edit the VMOperatorRole.json file to contain only the "Microsoft.Compute/\*/read", "Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/start/action",  and "Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/deallocate/action" actions.

→Make sure that there is a comma at the end of each action, except for the final action in the list.

> <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image364.jpeg" style="width:4.79167in;height:2.51458in" alt="IMG_259" />

→Save the VMOperatorRole.json file.

→In the code editor window, in the upper-right corner, select the ellipsis (…) to display the More menu, select Save, enter VMOperatorRole.json as the file name, and then select Save.

<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image365.jpeg" style="width:1.86458in;height:2.03125in" alt="IMG_260" />

→On the More menu, select Close Editor.

→If the ellipsis does not appear, use the keyboard shortcut \[Ctrl+S\] to save the file, and \[Ctrl+Q\] to close the editor.

→Create a new custom role by using the Azure PowerShell [New-AzRoleDefinition](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/az.resources/new-azroledefinition?view=azps-3.8.0) cmdlet and the VMOperatorRole.json file.

→In the Cloud Shell window, run the following command to create a custom role:

> PowerShell
>
> New-AzRoleDefinition -InputFile "VMOperatorRole.json"
>
> <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image366.jpeg" style="width:5.64167in;height:0.82847in" alt="IMG_261" />

#  RBAC: Custom Role - \[Stg Acct Contributor\] - Portal 

→Retrieve the permissions granted to the Storage Account Contributor role by using the Azure portal.

- On the Azure portal home page, in Navigate, select Resource groups, and then select AZ300RG.

- On the AZ300RG service menu, select Access control (IAM).

- On the Access control (IAM) page, select the Roles tab.

  <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image383.jpeg" style="width:5.02083in;height:0.99931in" alt="IMG_256" />

- On the Roles page, in Name, search for and select Storage Account Contributor, and then on the Storage Account Contributor row, in the details column, select View.<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image384.jpeg" style="width:5.91528in;height:1.66181in" alt="IMG_257" />

- On the Storage Account Contributor blade, on the Permissions page, select each resource provider to view the corresponding permissions granted.

  <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image385.jpeg" style="width:5.58194in;height:4.91319in" alt="IMG_258" />

- Close the Storage Account Contributor blade.

<!-- -->

- Create a custom role named Storage Account Contributor (No Support) 52758007 that is based on the Storage Account Contributor role and that does not contain the Microsoft.Support provider.

<!-- -->

- On the Access control (IAM) page, select the Check access tab.

- <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image386.jpeg" style="width:5.525in;height:0.99583in" alt="IMG_259" />

- On the Check access page, in the Create a custom role tile, select Add.

  <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image387.jpeg" style="width:5.49028in;height:3.97917in" alt="IMG_260" />

- On the Create a custom role blade, in Custom role name, enter Storage Account Contributor (No Support) 52758007.

- In Baseline permissions, select Clone a role, in Role to clone, search for and Storage Account Contributor, and then select Next.

  <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image388.jpeg" style="width:3.49583in;height:2.95833in" alt="IMG_261" />

- On the Permissions page, review the permission list, and then select Next.

  <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image389.jpeg" style="width:4.82431in;height:2.39931in" alt="IMG_262" />

- On the Assignable scopes page, note that the custom role will be available only to the AZ300RG resource group, and then select Next.

  <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image390.jpeg" style="width:3.52222in;height:1.25278in" alt="IMG_263" />

- On the JSON page, select Edit.

  <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image391.jpeg" style="width:5.05208in;height:0.49931in" alt="IMG_264" />

- In the editor window, delete the line that contains Microsoft.Support, remove the comma at the end of the Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts line, and then select Save.

  <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image392.jpeg" style="width:4.82847in;height:2.27847in" alt="IMG_265" />

- On the JSON page, select Review + create, review the configuration, and then select Create.

- In the Create a custom role dialog, select OK.

  <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image393.jpeg" style="width:3.80347in;height:0.67431in" alt="IMG_266" />

<!-- -->

- Retrieve the role definition for the Storage Account Contributor (No Support) 52758007 custom role, and then verify that the role does not contain the Microsoft.Support provider.

> It may take a few minutes for the role to appear in the Azure portal. Periodically refresh the portal until the role appears.
>
> <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image394.jpeg" style="width:3.6in;height:0.46944in" alt="IMG_267" />

<td><ul>
<li><p>Implement your organization’s governance plans.</p></li>

<td style="text-align: left;"><p>Use Case</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Organization's cloud footprint has grown considerably in the last year.</p></li>
<li><p>During a recent audit, you discovered a substantial number of resources that do not have a defined owner, project, or cost center.</p></li>
<li><p>To improve management of Azure resources in your organization, you decide to implement the following functionality:</p>
<ul>
<li><p>apply <strong>resource tags</strong> to attach important metadata to Azure resources</p></li>
<li><p>enforce the use of resource tags for new resources by using Azure policy</p></li>
<li><p>update existing resources with resource tags</p></li>
<li><p>use resource locks to protect configured resources</p></li>
</ul></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>Interactive lab simulations, directly online that does not require any account etc.</p>
<ul>
<li><p><a href="https://mslearn.cloudguides.com/en-us/guides/AZ-900%20Exam%20Guide%20-%20Azure%20Fundamentals%20Exercise%2015">Manage resource locks</a>. Add a resource lock and test to confirm.</p></li>
<li><p><a href="https://mslearn.cloudguides.com/en-us/guides/AZ-900%20Exam%20Guide%20-%20Azure%20Fundamentals%20Exercise%2017">Create an Azure policy</a>. Create an Azure policy that restricts the location resources can be located. Create a new resource and ensure the policy is enforced.</p></li>
<li><p><a href="https://mslabs.cloudguides.com/guides/AZ-104%20Exam%20Guide%20-%20Microsoft%20Azure%20Administrator%20Exercise%203">Manage governance via Azure policy</a>. Create and assign tags via the Azure portal. Create an Azure policy that requires tagging. Remediate non-compliant resources.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>

<p>→when the remediation task is triggered, a non-compliant resource is automatically modified to align with the policy's defined configuration.</p>
<p>→A manual step is required to initiate a remediation task in Azure Policy, unless configured for automatic remediation during policy assignment.</p></td>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>→Scroll down and ensure it is ‘system assigned managed identity’</p>

<p>→Here, Type of Managed Identity specifies whether a system-assigned or user-assigned managed identity is used to authorize and execute the remediation task.</p>
<p>→A system-assigned identity is automatically created and tied to the policy assignment’s lifecycle, while a user-assigned identity is a standalone resource that can be reused across multiple assignments.</p>
<p>→ This setting ensures the remediation task has the necessary permissions to modify resources</p></td>

<table style="width:99%;">

<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_100.webp" style="width:3.6625in;height:1.90278in" alt="A computer screen with a white screen AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p>
<p>→Navigate to RG → Settings → Locks → +Add</p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_101.webp" style="width:3.65764in;height:1.97569in" alt="A computer screen shot of a computer AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p>
<p>→Provide a name and choose ‘delete’ option, so that any resource under the RG cannot be deleted, unless the lock is removed.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>→A non-admin user <mark>cannot</mark> unlock a resource locked by an admin in Azure unless they have been explicitly granted the Microsoft.Authorization/locks/* or Microsoft.Authorization/* permissions, typically assigned to the Owner or User Access Administrator roles.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image558.webp" style="width:2.59931in;height:1.41111in" alt="A computer screen with a white and blue screen AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_102.webp" style="width:5.04028in;height:1.9875in" alt="A computer screen with a white screen AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>→Notice the scope of locking, which is at RG level.</p>
<p>→If a resource lock (e.g., ReadOnly or Delete) is enabled on a resource group (RG) in Azure, you cannot delete the RG until the lock is removed, as the lock prevents deletion of the RG and its resources.</p>
<p>→Important: All Azure resources support the explicit application of <mark>resource locks</mark> (ReadOnly or Delete) at the resource, resource group, subscription, or management group level.</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<p>    "$schema": "https://schema.management.azure.com/schemas/2015-01-01/deploymentTemplate.json#",</p>
<p>    "contentVersion": "1.0.0.0",</p>
<p>    "parameters": {</p>
<p>      "storageAccountType": {</p>
<p>        "type": "string",</p>
<p>        "defaultValue": "Standard_LRS",</p>
<p>        "allowedValues": [</p>
<p>          "Standard_LRS",</p>
<p>          "Standard_GRS",</p>
<p>          "Standard_ZRS",</p>
<p>          "Premium_LRS"</p>
<p>        ],</p>

<p>          "description": "Storage Account type"</p>
<p>        }</p>
<p>      }</p>
<p>    },</p>
<p>    "variables": {</p>
<p>      "storageAccountName": "[concat(uniquestring(resourceGroup().id), 'standardsa')]",</p>
<p>      "count": 2</p>
<p>    },</p>
<p>    "resources": [</p>
<p>      {</p>
<p>        "type": "Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts",</p>
<p>        "name": "[variables('storageAccountName')]",</p>
<p>        "apiVersion": "2016-01-01",</p>
<p>        "location": "[resourceGroup().location]",</p>
<p>        "sku": {</p>
<p>            "name": "[parameters('storageAccountType')]"</p>
<p>        },</p>
<p>        "kind": "Storage",</p>
<p>        "properties": {</p>
<p>        }</p>
<p>      }</p>
<p>    ],</p>
<p>    "outputs": {</p>
<p>        "storageAccountName": {</p>
<p>            "type": "string",</p>
<p>            "value": "[variables('storageAccountName')]"</p>
<p>        }</p>
<p>    }</p>
<p>  }</p></td>

## Export the template – From existing disk

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 48%" />
<col style="width: 15%" />
<col style="width: 36%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_111.webp" style="width:4.66667in;height:2.68542in" alt="A screenshot of a computer AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>←Navigate to the ‘disk’</p>
<p>← Navigate to Automation → Export template → Click ‘Template’</p>
<p>←Note that this section has two sections viz., parameters and templates.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_112.webp" style="width:3.93056in;height:1.77986in" alt="A screenshot of a computer AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>←Navigate to Parameters for review</p>
<p>←Click ‘Download’ so that both Template and Parameters get downloaded as json.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="3" style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image628.webp" style="width:5.13125in;height:1.72292in" alt="A computer screen shot of a computer AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>Extract the zip and we get two files</p>
<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image629.webp" style="width:3.28958in;height:1.025in" alt="A screenshot of a computer AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p></td>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>←notice the json is exported, which is called ARM templates.</p>
<p>←Note: We can export ENTIRE-RESOURCE-GROUP or specific resources inside it.</p>
<p>→Below is a sample JSON file</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="3" style="text-align: left;"><p>{</p>
<p>    "$schema": "https://schema.management.azure.com/schemas/2019-04-01/deploymentTemplate.json#",</p>
<p>    "contentVersion": "1.0.0.0",</p>
<p>    "parameters": {</p>
<p>        "disk_name": {</p>
<p>            "defaultValue": "vm3-disk2",</p>
<p>            "type": "String"</p>
<p>        },</p>
<p>        "snapshot_externalid": {</p>

## Understanding IP Address

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 47%" />
<col style="width: 52%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Understanding IP Address Components.</p>
<p>→Example: IP address 192.168.1.1, where each number is an octet, first, second, third and fourth, respectively.</p>
<p>→Each octet can have a value between 0 and 255.</p>
<p>→Now, let's introduce the concept of CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing).</p>
<p>→CIDR is a way to represent the size of a network using a single number.</p>
<p>→For example, if we have <strong>192.168.1.1/24</strong> it means the IP address has CIDR of 24.</p>
<p>→The /24 means that the first 24 bits (or 3 octets) of the IP address are fixed.</p>
<p>→These fixed represent the ‘network’ that we are going to use it.</p>
<p>→The remaining 8 bits (or 1 octet) can be variable.</p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image740.webp" style="width:3.84444in;height:2.01597in" alt="{1B934307-FBFF-4570-BA4F-82C676623402}" /></p>
<p>→At machine level 185 is represented in binary as shown.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>→CIDR is a way to represent the size of a network using a single number.</p>
<p>→For example, in 192.168.1.1/24, the /24 indicates the <strong>first 24 bits</strong> of the IP address are <strong>fixed</strong></p>
<p>→They represent the network portion.</p>
<p>→The /24 means that the first 24 bits (or 3 octets) of the IP address are fixed.</p>
<p>→These fixed bits represent the network portion of the IP address. →The remaining 8 bits (or 1 octet) are variable and used for host addresses.</p>
<p>→The total number of usable host addresses in a /24 network is 254 (2^8 - 2, excluding the network and broadcast addresses).</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><table style="width:79%;">
<colgroup>

<col style="width: 19%" />

## Simplifying CIDR

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>Let's use a simple example to understand CIDR: Imagine you're at a university with many buildings, and each building has many rooms.</p>
<ul>
<li><p>The university is like the internet.</p></li>
<li><p>Each building is like a network.</p></li>
<li><p>Each room is like a device on the network.</p></li>
</ul>
<p>The IP address 192.168.1.1 can be thought of like a university address:</p>
<ul>
<li><p>192 is like the <strong>university</strong> name (fixed).</p></li>
<li><p>168 is like the <strong>building</strong> number (fixed).</p></li>
<li><p>1 is like the <strong>floor</strong> number (fixed).</p></li>
<li><p>1 is like the <strong>room</strong> number (variable).</p></li>
</ul>
<p>The CIDR /24 means that the first 3 parts (192.168.1) are fixed, like the university, building, and floor. The last part (1) can be any number from 1 to 254, like the room number. Think of it like a big apartment complex:</p>
<ul>
<li><p>/24 means you have 256 rooms (addresses) on the same floor ( subnet).</p></li>
<li><p>/16 would mean you have 256 floors (subnets) with 256 rooms each.</p></li>
<li><p>/8 would mean you have 256 buildings (subnets) with 256 floors (subnets) and 256 rooms each.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><ul>
<li><p>Having a /8 CIDR means you have a large subnet that can accommodate approximately 16,777,216 devices.</p></li>
<li><p>This is because a /8 CIDR has more available IP addresses than a /16 or /24.</p></li>
<li><p>/8 allows the highest number of devices to be connected.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Subnet masks

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><ul>
<li><p>Above we touched CIDR.</p></li>
<li><p>A subnet mask is a 32-bit number that helps determine the scope of a subnet.</p></li>
<li><p>It's usually written in a format like 255.255.255.0.</p></li>
<li><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image744.webp" /><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image745.webp" />The subnet mask is used to determine which part of the IP address is the network ID and which part is the host ID.</p></li>
<li><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image746.webp" />For example,</p>
<ul>
<li><p>if we have an IP address <strong>192.168.1.1</strong> with a subnet mask <strong>255.255.255.0</strong>, (8 bits, 8 bits, 8 bits, zero bits)</p></li>
<li><p>the subnet mask would indicate that the first 24 bits (192.168.1) are the network ID. 8x3 = 24</p></li>
<li><p>and the last 8 bits (1) are the host ID.</p></li>
</ul></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Subnet

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>Subnet and subnet mask are related but different topics.</p>
<ul>
<li><p>A <strong>subnet</strong> refers to a smaller network within a larger network.</p></li>
<li><p>This is created by dividing the larger network into smaller segments.</p></li>
<li><p>A <strong>subnet mask</strong> is a 32-bit (8x4) number that helps determine the scope of a subnet.</p></li>
<li><p>Helps in identifying which part of the IP address is the network ID and which part is the host ID.</p></li>
</ul>
<p>Think of it like a city:</p>
<ul>
<li><p>The subnet is like a neighborhood (a smaller area within the city).</p></li>
<li><p>The subnet mask is like a map that shows the boundaries of the neighborhood (which streets are part of the neighborhood and which are not).</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

### Criteria to chose correct range

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Based on Size, if we need more IPs in its TOTAL NETWORK, we pick appropriately.</p>
<p>→Once we pick appropriate one, then we need to ‘subnet’ them.</p>
<table style="width:60%;">
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 15%" />
<col style="width: 18%" />
<col style="width: 26%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th style="text-align: center;"><strong>Range</strong></th>
<th style="text-align: center;"><strong>Total Usable IPs</strong></th>
<th style="text-align: center;"><strong>Typical Use</strong></th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;">10.0.0.0/8</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">16,777,214</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Large orgs, ISPs, clouds</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;">172.16.0.0/12</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">1,048,574</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Medium/large networks</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;">192.168.0.0/16</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">65,534</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Home, small office, labs</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Based on Org Policy</p>
<p>Enterprises often standardize on one range (e.g., all internal services in 10.0.0.0/8)</p>
<p>Some use:</p>
<p>10.x.x.x → core networks</p>
<p>172.16.x.x → region/site specific</p>
<p>192.168.x.x → local/dev/test</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Avoiding Conflicts</p>
<p>Internal VPNs</p>
<p>Peered VPCs/VNETs</p>
<p>Remote clients/home routers (most use 192.168.x.x)</p>
<p>Choose less common ranges like 172.30.x.x or 10.100.x.x to reduce conflict risk</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Based on Cloud recommendations</p>
<p>AWS: defaults to 172.31.0.0/16</p>
<p>Azure: often uses 10.0.0.0/8 ranges for VNETs</p>
<p>GCP: prefers 10.128.0.0/9 and 172.16.0.0/12 for shared VPCs</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Based on Security Segmentation</p>
<p>10.0.0.0/8 → production</p>
<p>172.16.0.0/12 → staging</p>
<p>192.168.0.0/16 → dev/test</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Private IP Address

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><ul>
<li><p>These are those IP addresses that are <strong>not routable</strong> on the internet.</p></li>
<li><p>They are used for devices on a local network, such as a home network or a office network.</p></li>
<li><p>Private IP addresses are typically assigned from the following ranges:</p>
<ul>
<li><p>10.0.0.0 to 10.255.255.255</p></li>
<li><p>172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255</p></li>
<li><p>192.168.0.0 to 192.168.255.255</p></li>
</ul></li>
<li><p>These private IP addresses can be used by multiple devices on different networks, because they are not unique on the internet.</p></li>
<li><p>For example, you can have a device with the IP address 192.168.1.1 on your home network, and another device with the same IP address 192.168.1.1 on a different network, without any conflicts</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Public IP Address

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><ul>
<li><p>These are the IP addresses that are routable on the internet.</p></li>
<li><p>They are unique and can be used to identify a device on the internet.</p></li>
<li><p>Public IP addresses are typically assigned by an Internet Service Provider (ISP) or a network administrator.</p></li>
<li><p>They can be used to access a device from anywhere on the internet.</p></li>
<li><p>For example, a website might have a public IP address like 203.0.113.1, which can be accessed from anywhere on the internet.</p></li>
<li><p>Here's a key difference between public and private IP addresses:</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Private IP addresses are used for devices on a local network and are not routable on the internet.</p></li>
<li><p>Public IP addresses are used for devices that need to be accessed from the internet and are routable on the internet.</p></li>
</ul></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Network Address Translation (NAT)

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>NAT is a technique used to allow devices with private IP addresses to access the internet. Here's how it works:</p>
<ul>
<li><p>A device on a local network with a private IP address (e.g. 192.168.1.1) wants to access a website on the internet.</p></li>
<li><p>The router on the local network translates the private IP address to a public IP address (e.g. 203.0.113.1) using NAT.</p></li>
<li><p>The request is then sent to the website on the internet using the public IP address.</p></li>
<li><p>When the website responds, the router translates the public IP address back to the private IP address, so the device on the local network can receive the response.</p></li>
</ul>
<p>NAT allows multiple devices on a local network to share a single public IP address, which helps conserve IP addresses and improves network security.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Ports

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><ul>
<li><p>Port numbers are used to identify a specific process or service running on a device.</p></li>
<li><p>They are like extensions on a phone number, allowing multiple conversations to happen simultaneously.</p></li>
<li><p>Port numbers range from 0 to 65535, but some ports are reserved for specific services:</p>
<ul>
<li><p>HTTP (web) typically uses port 80</p></li>
<li><p>HTTPS (secure web) typically uses port 443</p></li>
<li><p>FTP (file transfer) typically uses port 21</p></li>
<li><p>SSH (secure shell) typically uses port 22</p></li>
</ul></li>
<li><p>When a device sends data to a server, it includes the destination IP address and port number.</p></li>
<li><p>The server then uses the port number to direct the data to the correct process or service. For example, if you visit a website at http://example.com, your device sends a request to the server at IP address 203.0.113.1 on port 80.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Firewall

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><ul>
<li><p>A firewall is a network security system that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing network traffic.</p></li>
<li><p>It's like a gatekeeper that decides what traffic is allowed to pass through and what traffic is blocked.</p></li>
<li><p>Firewalls can be hardware-based (e.g. a router) or software-based (e.g. a program on your computer).</p></li>
<li><p>A firewall typically has a set of rules that determine what traffic is allowed or blocked.</p></li>
<li><p>These rules can be based on factors such as:</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Source IP address: Where the traffic is coming from</p></li>
<li><p>Destination IP address: Where the traffic is going to</p></li>
<li><p>Port number: What service or process the traffic is intended for</p></li>
<li><p>Protocol: What type of traffic it is (e.g. TCP, UDP, ICMP)</p></li>
</ul></li>
<li><p>For example, a firewall might have a rule that allows incoming traffic on port 80 (HTTP) from any source IP address, but blocks all incoming traffic on port 22 (SSH) from unknown IP addresses.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Azure VNET

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><ul>
<li><p>In Azure, a VNET (Virtual Network) is a virtual representation of a network.</p></li>
<li><p>You can think of it as a logical isolation of your network resources.</p></li>
<li><p>A VNET can have one or more subnets, which are smaller segments of the VNET.</p></li>
<li><p>For example, you might create a VNET called "MyNetwork" and then create two subnets within it:</p></li>
</ul>
<ul>
<li><p>Subnet "FrontEnd" with IP address range 10.0.1.0/24</p></li>
<li><p>Subnet "BackEnd" with IP address range 10.0.2.0/24</p></li>
<li><p>Each subnet can have its own set of security rules and routing tables, allowing you to control traffic flow between subnets.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Azure VNET – Address Space

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><ul>
<li><p>The address space of a VNET is the range of IP addresses that are available for use within the VNET.</p></li>
<li><p>When we create a VNET, we specify the <strong>address space</strong> for the VNET.</p></li>
<li><p>This can be a private IP address range, such as 10.0.0.0/16.</p></li>
<li><p>The address space further gets divided into subnets, which are smaller segments of the address space.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Each subnet</strong> has its own <strong>subnet address range</strong>, which is a subset of the VNET's address space.</p></li>
<li><p>For example, if we create a VNET with an address space of <strong>10.0.0.0/16</strong>, we might create two subnets with the following address ranges:</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Subnet "FrontEnd" with address range 10.0.1.0/24</p></li>
<li><p>Subnet "BackEnd" with address range 10.0.2.0/24</p></li>
</ul></li>
<li><p>The subnet mask for each subnet determines the number of available IP addresses within the subnet.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Azure Subnet configuration

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>When you create a subnet in Azure, you need to specify the subnet address range and the subnet name.</p>
<p>You can also configure other settings, such as:</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Subnet mask: Determines the number of available IP addresses in the subnet.</p></li>
<li><p>Default gateway: Specifies the IP address of the default gateway for the subnet.</p></li>
<li><p>DNS servers: Specifies the IP addresses of the DNS servers for the subnet.</p></li>
</ul>
<p>→An example of how you might configure a subnet in Azure:</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Subnet name: FrontEnd</p></li>
<li><p>Subnet address range: 10.0.1.0/24</p></li>
<li><p>Subnet mask: 255.255.255.0</p></li>
<li><p>Default gateway: 10.0.1.1</p></li>
<li><p>DNS servers: 10.0.1.2, 10.0.1.3</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>Here are some default settings that Azure will use:</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>Subnet mask</strong>: Azure will automatically assign a subnet mask based on the subnet address range specified.</p></li>
<li><p>For example, if address range is <strong>10.0.1.0/24</strong>, a subnet mask of <strong>255.255.255.0</strong> is auto-assigned.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Default gateway</strong>: Azure will automatically assign a default gateway IP address for the subnet.</p></li>
<li><p>It is usually the <strong>first IP address in the subnet range</strong>.</p></li>
<li><p>For example, if your subnet address range is <strong>10.0.1.0/24</strong>, the default gateway IP address would be <strong>10.0.1.1</strong>.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>DNS servers</strong>: Azure will automatically assign DNS servers for the subnet, which are usually the <strong>Azure-provided DNS servers</strong>.</p></li>
</ul>
<p>Here are some specific default settings that Azure will use:</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Subnet mask: <strong>255.255.255.0</strong> for /24 subnets, <strong>255.255.0.0</strong> for /16 subnets, etc.</p></li>
<li><p>Default gateway: First IP address in the subnet range (e.g. <strong>10.0.1.1</strong> for a <strong>10.0.1.0/24</strong> subnet)</p></li>
<li><p>DNS servers: Azure-provided DNS servers (e.g. <strong>168.63.129.16</strong>)</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Azure Network Security Groups (NSG)

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→NSGs are a way to control and filter incoming and outgoing network traffic to and from Azure resources, such as virtual machines and subnets.</p>
<p>→An NSG is simply a <strong>firewall</strong> that allows you to define security rules to <strong><u>permit or deny</u></strong> traffic based on factors such as:</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Source IP address</p></li>
<li><p>Destination IP address</p></li>
<li><p>Port number</p></li>
<li><p>Protocol (e.g. TCP, UDP, ICMP)</p></li>
</ul>
<p>→We can associate an NSG with a [<strong>subnet</strong>] or [<strong>network interface card</strong>]</p>
<p>→Examples of NSG rules:</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Allow incoming traffic on port 80 (HTTP) from any source IP address</p></li>
<li><p>Deny incoming traffic on port 22 (SSH) from any source IP address except for a specific IP address (e.g. 192.168.1.100)</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→There are two main types of NSG rules:</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>Inbound rules</strong>: Control incoming traffic to a subnet or NIC.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Outbound rules</strong>: Control outgoing traffic from a subnet or NIC.</p></li>
</ul>
<p>→Each rule type has several components:</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>Priority</strong>: A unique number that determines the order in which rules are applied.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Source</strong>: The source IP address or range of IP addresses.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Destination</strong>: The destination IP address or range of IP addresses.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Protocol</strong>: The protocol (e.g. TCP, UDP, ICMP) and port number.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Action</strong>: Allow or Deny.</p></li>
</ul>
<p>→For example, you might create an inbound rule with the following settings:</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Priority: 100</p></li>
<li><p>Source: Any</p></li>
<li><p>Destination: 10.0.1.0/24</p></li>
<li><p>Protocol: TCP</p></li>
<li><p>Port: 80</p></li>
<li><p>Action: Allow</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→The <strong>priority</strong> of an Azure NSG rule determines the order in which the rule is applied.</p>
<p>→Lower numbers having higher priority.</p>
<p>→Rules are evaluated in order of priority, and the first rule that matches the traffic is applied.</p>
<p>→If multiple rules have the same priority, the rule with the most specific match (e.g. specific IP address vs. any IP address) is applied first.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→There are default rules for NSG</p>
<p>These default rules include:</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>Allow incoming traffic from the internet on ports 80 (HTTP) and 443 (HTTPS)</strong>: This allows incoming traffic from the internet to reach your Azure resources on these common ports.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Allow outgoing traffic to the internet on any port</strong>: This allows your Azure resources to send outgoing traffic to the internet on any port.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Deny all incoming traffic from the internet by default</strong>: This is a catch-all rule that denies any incoming traffic from the internet that doesn't match one of the above rules.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## NSG Association with Subnet

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 60%" />
<col style="width: 39%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>→To apply the rules to a subnet or NIC, we must first <strong>associate</strong> the NSG with that subnet or NIC.</p>
<p>→There are <strong>two types</strong> of associations:</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Subnet association: Associate an NSG with a subnet to apply the rules to all NICs in that subnet.</p></li>
<li><p>NIC association: Associate an NSG with a NIC to apply the rules only to that specific NIC.</p></li>
</ul>
<p>When you associate an NSG with a subnet or NIC, the rules in the NSG are applied to all incoming and outgoing traffic to and from the subnet or NIC.</p>
<p>You can associate an NSG with a subnet or NIC during creation or after creation, and you can also change the association later if needed.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>While NSGs are a powerful tool for controlling traffic to and from Azure resources, there are some limitations to be aware of:</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>100 rules per NSG</strong>: You can have a maximum of 100 rules per NSG.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>1000 NSGs per subscription</strong>: You can have a maximum of 1000 NSGs per subscription.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Only one NSG per subnet or NIC</strong>: You can associate only one NSG with a subnet or NIC.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>No support for Layer 7 rules</strong>: NSGs only support Layer 3 and Layer 4 rules, and do not support Layer 7 rules.</p></li>
</ul>
<p>Additionally, NSGs are <strong>stateful</strong>, which means that they track the state of connections and can allow return traffic on a connection that was initiated from within the subnet or NIC.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image754.webp" style="width:4.31458in;height:2.96806in" /></p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>←Here we can see there are to possibilities pictured.</p>
<p>←<strong>First</strong> subnet has two VMs with their NICs.</p>
<p>←Those two VMs have their own NSGs attached to NICs.</p>
<p>←<strong>Second</strong> subnet has two VMs with their NICs.</p>
<p>←However, the NSG is applied at subnet level thereby automatically getting attached to NIC of all VM, by default.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image755.webp" style="width:4.28333in;height:2.31736in" alt="{A8CD1351-9E93-465C-AADC-8E4690F906BD}" /></p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Azure Application Security Groups (ASG)

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→ASGs are a way to group virtual machines and apply network security rules to them.</p>
<p>→This is regardless of their subnet or NIC.</p>
<p>→ASGs are similar to NSGs, but they are more flexible and allow for more granular control over network security.</p>
<p>→With ASGs, we can:</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Group virtual machines by application or workload</p></li>
<li><p>Apply network security rules to such groups rather than individual VMs.</p></li>
<li><p>This simplifies network security management by reducing the number of rules and groups to manage.</p>
<p>→ASGs are particularly useful in scenarios where wehave multiple VMs that need to communicate with each other, but also need to be isolated from other networks or subnets.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><ul>
<li><p><strong>NSG (Network Security Group)</strong> is primarily used to control traffic at the <strong>subnet level</strong>.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>ASG (Application Security Group)</strong> is primarily used to control traffic at the <strong>virtual machine (VM) level</strong>.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→ASG as mentioned is grouping of related VMs and then putting rules to them.</p>
<p>→Below we have 3 layers wherein they can be grouped together.</p>
<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image756.webp" style="width:7.525in;height:3.85139in" alt="{C62071D1-C468-48EA-9485-EFA87A39821E}" /></p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Azure VNET Peering

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→VNET peering allows us to connect two or more VNETs</p>
<blockquote>
<p>→The VNETs can be in same subscription</p>
<p>→The VNETs can be across different subscriptions,</p>
<p>→The VNETs can be even across different Azure Active Directory (AAD) tenants.</p>
</blockquote>
<p>There are two types of VNET peering:</p>
<ul>
<li><p>VNET peering: Allows you to peer two VNETs in the same region.</p></li>
<li><p>Global VNET peering: Allows you to peer two VNETs in different regions.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

#  Vnet - Creation with Portal - NSG - ASG 

## Introduction

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><ul>
<li><p>This lab is the first of three labs that focuses on virtual networking.</p></li>
<li><p>In this lab, you learn the basics of virtual networking and subnetting.</p></li>
<li><p>You learn how to protect your network with network security groups (NSG) and application security groups (ASG).</p></li>
<li><p>You also learn about DNS zones and records.</p></li>
</ul>
<p>Implementation will be driven with below two networks</p>
<ul>
<li><p>The <strong>CoreServicesVnet</strong> virtual network has the largest number of resources. A large amount of growth is anticipated, so a large address space is necessary for this virtual network.</p></li>
<li><p>The <strong>ManufacturingVnet</strong> virtual network contains systems for the operations of the manufacturing facilities. The organization is anticipating a large number of internal connected devices for their systems to retrieve data from.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

### Architecture

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image757.webp" style="width:5.72986in;height:2.92917in" alt="Network layout" /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→These virtual networks and subnets are structured in a way that accommodates existing resources yet allows for the projected growth. Let's create these virtual networks and subnets to lay the foundation for our networking infrastructure.</p>
<p><strong>Did you know?</strong> It is a good practice to avoid overlapping IP address ranges to reduce issues and simplify troubleshooting. Overlapping is a concern across the entire network, whether in the cloud or on-premises. Many organizations design an enterprise-wide IP addressing scheme to avoid overlapping and plan for future growth.</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

#  Vnet - Creation with Portal - Powershell - AZ 

<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image936.webp" style="width:7.66597in;height:1.04375in" alt="{D682984F-9726-4F1B-B9A2-EBEE329D3DE7}" />

→You are an Administrator for Hexelo, an organization that needs to implement virtual networking in Azure®.

→In this Challenge Lab, you will implement Azure virtual networking.

→ First, you will create an Azure virtual network by using the Azure portal.

→Next, you will create an Azure virtual network by using Azure PowerShell® commands.

→Finally, you will create an Azure virtual network by using an Azure CLI 2.0 command.

## VNET Creation Details 

→ Create an Azure virtual network (VNet) by using the values in the following table. For any property that is not specified, use the default value.

| **Property**         | **Value**           |
|:---------------------|:--------------------|
| Resource group       | AZ300-RGlod52764907 |
| Virtual network name | VNet1               |
| Region               | (US) East US 2      |
| IPv4 address space   | 10.1.0.0/16         |
| Subnet name          | Production          |
| Subnet address range | 10.1.0.0/24         |

- **Steps on Portal**

<!-- -->

- On the Azure portal home page, in Azure services, select Create a resource.

- In the Azure marketplace, search for and select Virtual Network, and then select the Virtual network tile.

- On the Virtual Network blade, review the information, and then select Create.

- On the Create virtual network blade, on the Basics page, in Project details, in Resource group, select AZ300-RGlod52764907.

- In Instance details, in Virtual network name, enter VNet1.

- In Region, select (US) East US 2, and then select IP addresses tab.

- In the existing address space tile, change the address prefix to 10.1.0.0, and then in the Address space size, ensure that /16 is selected.

- Delete the default subnet.

- Select Add a subnet.

- On the Add a subnet blade, in Name, enter Production.

- In IPv4, in Starting address, ensure that 10.1.0.0 is selected, and then in Size, ensure that /24 is selected.

- Select Add.

- On the Create virtual network blade, select Review + create.

- Review the configuration, and then select Create.

> There are three main components of a VNet that you must plan and implement:

- A *virtual network* is a container that holds other networking components and configurations.

- A *virtual address space* is a block of IP addresses that can be further divided into subnets. A VNet requires at least one virtual address space. The address spaces inside a VNet do not have to be contiguous.

- A *subnet* is a block of IP addresses that are part of an address space. A VNet requires at least one subnet. The subnet must be part or all the virtual address space in which it is created.

→Wait until VNet1 has been fully deployed before moving on to the next step in the Challenge Lab.

- **Add the 172.16.0.0/16 Subnet address range to VNet1.**

<!-- -->

- On the Deployment blade, select Go to resource.

- On the VNet1 service menu, in Settings, select Address space.

- In Add additional Subnet address range, enter 172.16.0.0/16, and then select Save.

<!-- -->

- **Add a subnet named Development to the VNet1 VNet that has a Subnet address range of 172.16.1.0/24.**

<!-- -->

- On the VNet1 service menu, in Settings, select Subnets.

- On the Subnets page, on the Command bar, select +Subnet.<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image937.jpeg" style="width:3.88542in;height:0.5625in" alt="IMG_256" />

- On the Add a subnet blade, in Name, enter Development.

- In IPv4Subnet address range, select 172.16.0.0 - 172.16.255.255.

- In Starting address, enter 172.16.1.0, ensure that Size is set to /24 (256 addresses), and then select Add.

→When creating a new subnet, you must enter a Subnet address range that falls within one of the address spaces you have defined for the VNet.

→When you design the Subnet address ranges of your subnets, remember that the **first three** IP addresses in each subnet are reserved by Azure for internal use.

## Create VNET using Powershell 

- Open an Azure Cloud Shell PowerShell® session without mounting a storage account-use the existing subscription.

<!-- -->

- On the Azure portal toolbar, in the global controls, select the Cloud Shell icon.

- In the Welcome to Azure Cloud Shell dialog, select PowerShell.

- In the Getting started dialog, select No storage account required, in Subscription, select the existing Challenge Labs option, and then select Apply.

<!-- -->

- Create a VNet named VNet2 in the AZ300-RGlod52764907 resource group by using the New-AzVirtualNetwork cmdlet, the EastUS2 region, and the address prefix 10.0.0.0/16.

<!-- -->

- Run the following command to create a VNet:

> PowerShell
>
> \$virtualNetwork = New-AzVirtualNetwork -ResourceGroupName AZ300-RGlod52764907 -Location EastUS2 -Name VNet2 -AddressPrefix 10.0.0.0/16

- Your output should look like the following screenshot:

> <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image965.jpeg" style="width:4.85069in;height:0.26319in" alt="IMG_256" />

- Retrieve the value of the VNet2 VNet in the AZ300-RGlod52764907 resource group by using the Get-AzVirtualNetwork cmdlet, and then store the value in a variable named \$Vnet.

<!-- -->

- Run the following command to define a variable that holds the value of the VNet2 VNet:

> PowerShell
>
> \$Vnet = Get-AzVirtualNetwork -Name "VNet2" -ResourceGroupName "AZ300-RGlod52764907"

- Add a subnet named Production in VNet2 by using the Add-AzVirtualNetworkSubnetConfig cmdlet and the \$Vnet variable, assign an address prefix of 10.0.0.0/24, and then store the value in a variable named \$subnetConfig.

<!-- -->

- Run the following command to add a subnet named Production to VNet2 and store the value in a variable named \$subnetConfig:

> PowerShell
>
> \$subnetConfig = Add-AzVirtualNetworkSubnetConfig -Name Production -VirtualNetwork \$VNet -AddressPrefix 10.0.0.0/24

- Write the subnet configuration to VNet2 by using the Set-AzVirtualNetwork cmdlet and the \$Vnet variable.

<!-- -->

- Run the following command to write the subnet configuration to the virtual network:

> PowerShell
>
> \$Vnet \| Set-AzVirtualNetwork

<ul>
<li><p>Create VNet for below scenario.</p></li>
<li><p>We have 2 Departments. Currently each has 200 hosts and in future they will need additional 20 per department. Design a network as per the requirement.</p></li>
<li><p>Solution:</p></li>
<li><p>First, what will be overall IP count🡪 2 x (200+20) = 440, will be the Ips needed, where 2 is total departments, 200 is current hosts and 20 is each department’s future expansion requirements. Hence the total is 440.</p></li>
<li><p>Then to cater for 440, we need an ADDRESS SPACE bigger than this.</p></li>
<li><p>We can start with /23 that gives 🡪 512 Ips for ADDRESS SPACE.</p></li>
<li><p>This Address space when divided into two (because of 2 dept), we will get 256 hosts.</p></li>
<li><p>Meaning we will need 2 subnets each with 256 hosts.</p></li>
<li><p>We can give Subnet1 the CIDR block as /24 which gives 256 Ips.</p></li>
<li><p>We can give Subnet2 same.</p></li>
</ul></td>

#  Vnet peering - Route Tables - UDR 

## Introduction 

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><ul>
<li><p>In this lab you explore communication between virtual networks.</p></li>
<li><p>You implement virtual network peering and test connections. You will also create a custom route.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><ul>
<li><p>Your organization segments core IT apps and services (such as DNS and security services) from other parts of the business, including your manufacturing department.</p></li>
<li><p>However, in some scenarios, apps and services in the core area need to communicate with apps and services in the manufacturing area.</p></li>
<li><p>In this lab, you configure connectivity between the segmented areas.</p></li>
<li><p>This is a common scenario for separating production from development or separating one subsidiary from another.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

### Architecture

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_194.webp" style="width:6.5in;height:2.69931in" alt="Lab 05 architecture diagram" /></p>
<p>→Route table</p>
<p>→Subnet</p>
<p>→Network Watcher</p>
<p>→Peering</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Here the Perimeter indicated, mean it is a ‘route-table’ in azure.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→This architecture can be described as below.</p>
<p>→There will be two VNETs defined viz., CoreServicesVnet and ManufacturingVnet</p>
<p>→Each VNet has own subnet viz., Core for first and Manufacturing for second.</p>
<p>→There will be a VNet Peering done to connect between both of them.</p>
<p>→After Peering, we will be able to ping each of them.</p>
<p>→As a last step, we will define a Route Table with a User Defined Route (UDR) for connection to internet vis-a-vis CoreServices VM.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→IMPORTANT TO UNDERSTAND PERIMETER</p>
<p>→We are configuring VNet peering between CoreServicesVNet (10.0.0.0/24) and ManufacturingVNet (172.16.0.0/24).</p>
<p>→ Further, we are adding a new 'Perimeter' subnet (10.0.1.0/24) to CoreServicesVNet.</p>
<p>→This is to enhance network segmentation.</p>
<p>→This setup allows secure communication between the VNets and isolates the Perimeter subnet for specific tasks, such as hosting the Perimeter VM.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→FLOW</p>
<p>→<strong>Perimeter VM</strong>?: The Perimeter VM is a virtual machine deployed in the 'Perimeter' subnet (10.0.1.0/24) within the CoreServicesVNet, designed to act as a security boundary or gateway for incoming and outgoing traffic.</p>
<p>→<strong>Purpose</strong>?: It typically serves as a firewall, proxy, or VPN endpoint, controlling and inspecting traffic between the external internet and the internal network, enhancing security by isolating external access points.</p>
<p>→<strong>Traffic Flow Start</strong>: Traffic originates from an external source (e.g., the internet) and enters through Task 6, reaching the Perimeter VM, which applies security rules and filters.</p>
<p>→<strong>Traffic Flow End-to-End</strong>: The Perimeter VM forwards filtered traffic to the CoreServicesVM (10.0.0.0/24) within the same VNet, which then communicates with the ManufacturingVM (172.16.0.0/24) via VNet peering, completing the flow.</p>
<p>→<strong>Traffic Flow End</strong>: The traffic ends at the ManufacturingVM or returns to the external source after processing, depending on the request, with the Perimeter VM ensuring secure egress.</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

#  Vnet peering - with VM testing

<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1120.webp" style="width:7.67431in;height:1.14306in" alt="{B0D2C1F4-FA5D-48C7-A8D3-2252859AACDC}" />

→You are an Administrator for Hexelo, an organization that needs to configure network peering between two Azure® virtual networks.

→In this Challenge Lab, you will configure Azure virtual networking peering. First, you will review the existing environment. Next, you will configure Azure virtual network peering. Finally, you will create two virtual machines by using Azure PowerShell®, and then you will use the virtual machines to test the virtual network peering connections.

## Review Existing Objects

- Review the address space and subnet configurations of the VNET1 virtual network in the AZ300-RGlod52767134 resource group.

<!-- -->

- On the Azure portal home page, in Navigate, select Resource groups.

- On the Resource groups blade, select AZ300-RGlod52767134.

- On the AZ300-RGlod52767134 blade, select VNET1.

- On the Overview page, verify that the virtual network is in the East US region and that the address space for the virtual network is 10.11.0.0/16.

  <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1121.jpeg" style="width:4.95833in;height:0.57222in" alt="IMG_256" />

- On the VNET1 service menu, in Settings, select Subnets, and then verify that there is a subnet named FrontEnd that is associated to an address range of 10.11.0.0/24.

  <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1122.jpeg" style="width:4.04514in;height:2.33264in" alt="IMG_257" />

→VNET1 is in the East US region and is associated to an address space of 10.11.0.0/16. VNET1 contains a subnet named FrontEnd that is associated to an address range of 10.11.0.0/24.

→Review the configuration of the VNET2 virtual network in the AZ300-RGlod52767134 resource group.

→VNET2 is in the East US 2 region and is associated to an address space of 10.41.0.0/16. VNET2 contains a subnet named FrontEnd that is associated to an address range of 10.41.0.0/24.

## Configure Peering

- Add two virtual network peerings named VNET2-to-VNET1 and VNET1-to-VNET2 that will allow traffic to flow in both directions between the VNET1 and VNET2 virtual networks.

<!-- -->

- On the VNET2 service menu, in Settings, select Peerings.

- On the Peerings page, on the command bar, select +Add.

- On the Add peering blade, in Remote virtual network summary, in Peering link name, enter VNET1-to-VNET2.

- In Virtual network, select VNET1 (AZ300-RGlod52767134).

- In Local virtual network summary, in Peering link name, enter VNET2-to-VNET1, and then select Add.

→You can use *virtual network peering* to connect virtual networks together.

→For connectivity purposes, Azure will view the connected networks as if they are one network, and traffic will be routed between the peered virtual networks across the Microsoft backbone, rather than through a gateway.

→For this reason, traffic between peered virtual networks will ***<u>never traverse the public internet</u>***.

→You can choose between two types of peering:

- *Virtual network peering* connects virtual networks in the **same region**.

- *Global virtual network peering* connects virtual networks in **different regions**.

→You can use *user-defined routes* to implement service chaining by configuring a virtual machine in the peered virtual network as the next hop IP address.

→You can also configure a gateway in a peered virtual network as a transit point to an on-premises network. This is referred to as *gateway transit*.

→Verify that the peering status of VNET2-to-VNET1 is Connected.

- On the VNET2 Peerings page, in the Peering state column, ensure that the status is Connected.

  →Verify that the peering status of VNET1-to-VNET2 is Connected.

<!-- -->

- On the VNET2 Peerings page, in the Remote virtual network name column, select the VNET1 name link.

- On the VNET1 service menu, in Settings, select Peerings.

- On the VNET1 Peerings page, in the Peering state column, ensure that the status is Connected.

## Create Azure VM using PowerShell

Create an Azure virtual machine by using the New-AzVM cmdlet and the values in the following table. For any property that is not specified, use the default value.

| **Property**                    | **Value**           |
|:--------------------------------|:--------------------|
| ResourceGroupName               | AZ300-RGlod52767134 |
| Name                            | VM1                 |
| Location                        | East US             |
| VirtualNetworkName              | VNET1               |
| SubnetName                      | FrontEnd            |
| Size                            | Standard_DS3_v2     |
| SecurityGroupName               | VM1SG-52767134      |
| PublicIpAddressName             | VM1PIP-52767134     |
| OpenPorts                       | 80,3389             |
| User                            | AZ300-VMAdmin       |
| Password for user AZ300-VMAdmin | AZ300-VMPassw0rd!   |

In this Challenge Lab, you MUST specify the exact attribute values or the deployment will fail.

- Run the following command to create an Azure virtual machine:

> PowerShell
>
> New-AzVm -ResourceGroupName "AZ300-RGlod52767134" -Name "VM1" -Location "East US" -VirtualNetworkName "VNET1" -SubnetName "FrontEnd" -Size "Standard_DS3_v2" -SecurityGroupName "VM1SG-52767134" -PublicIpAddressName "VM1PIP-52767134" -OpenPorts 80,3389

- When prompted for the User, enter AZ300-VMAdmin, and then press Enter to set the administrator account name for the new virtual machine.

- When prompted for the Password for user AZ300-VMAdmin, enter AZ300-VMPassw0rd!, and then press Enter to set the administrator account password for the new virtual machine.

> Want to learn more? Review the documentation on the [New-AzVM](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/az.compute/new-azvm).
>
> You can use the New-AzVM cmdlet to create both Windows® and Linux virtual machines. To create a Linux virtual machine, use the -Linux parameter, otherwise the virtual machine will use Windows.

→Create a second Azure virtual machine by using the New-AzVM cmdlet and the values in the following table:

| **Property**                    | **Value**           |
|:--------------------------------|:--------------------|
| ResourceGroupName               | AZ300-RGlod52767134 |
| Name                            | VM2                 |
| Location                        | East US 2           |
| VirtualNetworkName              | VNET2               |
| SubnetName                      | FrontEnd            |
| Size                            | Standard_DS3_v2     |
| SecurityGroupName               | VM2SG-52767134      |
| PublicIpAddressName             | VM2PIP-52767134     |
| OpenPorts                       | 80,3389             |
| User                            | AZ300-VMAdmin       |
| Password for user AZ300-VMAdmin | AZ300-VMPassw0rd!   |

→Run the following command to create an Azure virtual machine:

> PowerShell
>
> New-AzVM -ResourceGroupName "AZ300-RGlod52767134" -Name "VM2" -Location "East US 2" -VirtualNetworkName "VNET2" -SubnetName "FrontEnd" -Size "Standard_DS3_v2" -SecurityGroupName "VM2SG-52767134" -PublicIpAddressName "VM2PIP-52767134" -OpenPorts 80,3389

- When prompted for the User, enter AZ300-VMAdmin, and then press Enter to set the administrator account name for the new virtual machine.

- When prompted for the Password for user AZ300-Admin, enter AZ300-VMPassw0rd!, and then press Enter to set the administrator account password for the new virtual machine.

> After creating the two VMs, you can minimize the Cloud Shell window for upcoming tasks.
