## Test Peering

- Open a remote desktop connection to the VM1 virtual machine by using the Public IP address

<!-- -->

- On the Virtual machines blade, select VM1.

- On the command bar, select Connect, and then select Connect.

- On the Connect blade, in Most common, in Native RDP, select Download RDP File.

- If prompted VM1.rdp could harm your device. Do you want to keep it anyway?, select Keep.

- Open the downloaded file, and then select Connect.

- When prompted, sign in as AZ300-VMAdmin by using AZ300-VMPassw0rd! as the password.

- When prompted, select Yes.

> You can dismiss any prompts, and when displayed, you can minimize Server Manager.
>
> Want to learn more? Review the documentation on [connecting to an Azure virtual machine](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/windows/connect-rdp).

- Configure a firewall rule named Allow ICMPv4-In on VM1 that allows incoming ICMPv4 traffic through the Windows firewall on VM1 by using the New-NetFirewallRule cmdlet in Windows PowerShell.

<!-- -->

- In VM1, on the Start menu, open Windows PowerShell.

- Run the following command to create a new firewall rule:

> PowerShell
>
> New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "Allow ICMPv4-In" -Protocol ICMPv4
>
> This firewall rule will allow you to use the Ping command to test the Azure virtual network peering connection. You should not allow incoming Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) traffic in a production environment.
>
> Want to learn more? Review the documentation on the [New-NetFirewallRule](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/netsecurity/new-netfirewallrule?view=win10-ps) cmdlet.
>
> Minimize the VM1 remote desktop connection, but do not close it.

→Open a remote desktop connection to the VM2 virtual machine by using the Public IP address, and then complete the connection as AZ300-VMAdmin by using AZ300-VMPassw0rd! as the password.

→Configure a firewall rule named Allow ICMPv4-In that allows incoming ICMPv4 traffic through the Windows firewall on VM2 by using the New-NetFirewallRule cmdlet in Windows PowerShell.

- Test the VNET2-to-VNET1 peering connection by using Ping from the VM2 virtual machine to 10.11.0.4 - the private IP address of VM1.

> Ping 10.11.0.4

> <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1153.jpeg" style="width:4.01597in;height:2.00833in" alt="IMG_256" />
>

#  Vnet peering - Routes - UDR - NVA - Traffic forwarding 

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>You are a Security Engineer with Hexelo, an organization that needs to manage an Azure virtual network.</p>
<p>In this Challenge Lab, you will ensure that all traffic between the front-end and back-end subnets of the virtual network are routed through a firewall virtual appliance. First, you will create the route tables and routes, and then you will then associate them to the subnets. Next, you will enable IP forwarding on the virtual appliance. Finally, you will verify that traffic is being routed through the virtual appliance.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Here we are configuring a network setup to route all traffic.</p>
<p>→Traffic will be between the <strong>front-end</strong> and <strong>back-end</strong> subnets of a virtual network.</p>
<p>→This will be channeld through a <strong>firewall virtual appliance</strong> for enhanced security and control.</p>
<p>→This involves creating route tables and routes</p>
<p>→Then associating them with the subnets</p>
<p>→Then enabling IP forwarding on the virtual appliance to ensure proper traffic flow.</p>
<p>→This setup is required to protect the network by filtering and monitoring traffic, preventing unauthorized access, and ensuring compliance with security policies.</p>
<p>→Finally, verification confirms the routing is functioning as intended through the appliance.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→<strong>Create a Route table named app-frontend-rt by using the RG1lod52744319 resource group and the East US region, and then disable gateway route propagation.</strong></p>
<blockquote>
<p>→On the Azure portal toolbar, search for and select Route tables.</p>
</blockquote>
<ul>
<li><blockquote>
<p>→On the Route tables blade, on the command bar, select Create.</p>
</blockquote></li>
<li><blockquote>
<p>→On the Create Route table blade, in Resource group, select RG1lod52744319.</p>
</blockquote></li>
<li><blockquote>
<p>→In Region, ensure that East US is selected.</p>
</blockquote>
<blockquote>
<p>→In Name, enter app-frontend-rt.</p>
</blockquote></li>
<li><blockquote>
<p>→In Propagate gateway routes, select No, and then select Review + create.</p>
</blockquote></li>
<li><blockquote>
<p>→Review the configuration, and then select Create.</p>
</blockquote>
<p>→<strong>Add a route named to-backend to the app-frontend-rt route table, and then configure the route by using an address prefix of 10.1.1.0/24 and a Virtual appliance next hop address of 10.1.255.4.</strong></p></li>
</ul>
<ul>
<li><blockquote>
<p>→On the Deployment page, select Go to resource.</p>
</blockquote></li>
<li><blockquote>
<p>→On the app-frontend-rt service menu, in Settings, select Routes, and then on the command bar, select Add.</p>
</blockquote>
<blockquote>
<p>→On the Add route blade, in Route name, enter to-backend.</p>
</blockquote></li>
<li><blockquote>
<p>→In the Destination type, select IP Addresses.</p>
</blockquote>
<blockquote>
<p>→In Destination IP addresses/CIDR ranges, enter 10.1.1.0/24.</p>
</blockquote></li>
<li><blockquote>
<p>→In Next hop type, select Virtual appliance.</p>
</blockquote>
<blockquote>
<p>→In Next hop address, enter 10.1.255.4, and then select Add.</p>
</blockquote>
<blockquote>
<p>→ <strong>Associate the app-frontend-rt route table to the frontend subnet in the app-vnet virtual network.</strong></p>
</blockquote></li>
</ul>
<ul>
<li><blockquote>
<p>→On the app-frontend-rt service menu, in Settings, select Subnets.</p>
</blockquote></li>
<li><blockquote>
<p>→On the Subnets command bar, select Associate.</p>
</blockquote></li>
<li><blockquote>
<p>→On the Associate subnet blade, in Virtual network, select app-vnet, in Subnet, select frontend, and then select OK.</p>
</blockquote></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1173.webp" style="width:6.44167in;height:1.90972in" alt="{E4A860E3-A486-4564-9A36-EEEDA603A937}" /></p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<td style="text-align: left;"><p>←This configuration shows the creation of a User Defined Route (UDR) named "to-backend" in Azure, which overrides the default system routes to direct traffic.</p>
<p>←It specifies a destination IP address range of 10.1.10.24, routing traffic through a virtual appliance with the IP address 10.1.255.4 as the next hop.</p>
<p>←IP forwarding must be enabled on the virtual appliance's network interface to ensure proper traffic flow, enhancing network security and control by channeling traffic through the appliance.</p>
<p>←The next hop address (10.1.255.4) is chosen as it likely corresponds to the IP address of the firewall virtual appliance's network interface within the subnet (e.g., 10.1.255.0/24), ensuring traffic is routed to the appliance for processing.</p>
<p>←This value is selected based on the virtual network's IP addressing scheme and the appliance's configuration, aligning with the lab's goal of routing traffic through the firewall.</p></td>

<td style="text-align: left;"><p>←Here we are configuring bidirectional traffic routing between the front-end (10.1.0.0/24) and back-end (10.1.10.24) subnets through a firewall virtual appliance (10.1.255.4) using UDRs named "to-backend" and "to-frontend".</p>
<p>←This ensures all traffic, in both directions, is filtered and secured by the appliance, which is critical for comprehensive network protection.</p>

<p>←Both routes are required to enforce consistent security policies across the entire communication flow.</p></td>

## Enable IP Forwarding

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><p><strong>→Open an Azure Cloud Shell Bash session without mounting a storage account.</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><blockquote>
<p>→On the Azure portal toolbar, in the global controls, select the Cloud Shell icon.</p>
</blockquote></li>
<li><blockquote>
<p>→In the Welcome to Azure Cloud Shell window, select Bash.</p>
</blockquote></li>
<li><blockquote>
<p>→In the Getting started window, select No storage account required, in Subscription, select the existing Challenge Labs option, and then select Apply.</p>
</blockquote>
<p><strong>→Create a secure shell (SSH) connection to VM3 by using azureuser@172.191.137.194, and then when prompted, enter AzurePwd52744319 as the password.</strong></p>
<blockquote>
<p>→In Cloud Shell, run the following command to connect to the Linux virtual machine:</p>
</blockquote>
<blockquote>
<p>ssh azureuser@172.191.137.194</p>
</blockquote>
<blockquote>
<p>→When prompted, enter yes, and then press Enter.</p>
</blockquote>
<blockquote>
<p>→In azureuser@172.191.137.194's password, enter AzurePwd52744319, and then press Enter.</p>
</blockquote></li>
</ul>
<blockquote>
<p><strong>→Enable IP forwarding by using the sudo user and the sysctl command, and then exit the SSH connection.</strong></p>
</blockquote>
<ul>
<li><blockquote>
<p>→Run the following command to enable IP forwarding:</p>
</blockquote></li>
</ul>
<blockquote>
<p>bash</p>
<p>sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1</p>
</blockquote>
<blockquote>
<p>→Enter exit, and then press Enter to close the SSH connection.</p>
</blockquote>
<ul>
<li><blockquote>
<p><a href="http://manpages.ubuntu.com/manpages/focal/en/man8/sudo.8.html">sudo</a></p>
</blockquote></li>
<li><blockquote>
<p><a href="http://manpages.ubuntu.com/manpages/focal/en/man8/sysctl.8.html">sysctl</a></p>
</blockquote></li>
<li><blockquote>
<p><a href="http://manpages.ubuntu.com/manpages/focal/en/man1/exit.1posix.html">exit</a></p>
</blockquote>
<blockquote>
<p>→Leave Cloud Shell open for the next task.</p>
</blockquote></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1231.webp" style="width:5.67708in;height:1.54167in" alt="{197D1BA8-40BD-43BB-B5BB-25FBAA5F74C7}" /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1232.webp" style="width:5.1875in;height:1.80208in" alt="{C5FC0EB2-7725-4FD3-A12E-01C5EE8414EE}" /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1233.webp" style="width:6.59375in;height:2.66667in" alt="{666CE186-BE64-4C47-BAA8-F5EEDF0FA657}" /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1234.webp" style="width:7.52431in;height:4.36181in" alt="{C8261C0E-1BF8-46A5-80F5-D83556F801F6}" /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1235.webp" style="width:4.83333in;height:1.07292in" alt="{0110B079-7082-4074-9A45-BECE9138E51D}" /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→What we have done is configured a secure network setup in this Challenge Lab by routing all traffic between the front-end and back-end subnets through a firewall virtual appliance.</p>
<p>→We created User Defined Routes (UDRs) named "to-backend" and "to-frontend" with specific IP ranges (10.1.10.24 and 10.1.0.0/24) and directed traffic to the virtual appliance at 10.1.255.4.</p>
<p>→We associated these routes with the respective subnets and enabled IP forwarding on VM3 using an SSH connection via Azure Cloud Shell, ensuring the appliance can process and forward traffic.</p>
<p>→This bidirectional routing enhances security by filtering traffic in both directions, with VM3 acting as the key intermediary, while VM1 and VM2 likely represent the front-end and back-end resources.</p>
<p>→Finally, we verified the setup to confirm proper traffic flow through the appliance.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"></td>

<table>

<td><p><strong>→In Cloud Shell, create an ssh connection to VM2 by using azureuser@52.170.193.83, and then when prompted, enter AzurePwd52744319 as the password.</strong></p>
<blockquote>
<p>→In Cloud Shell, run the following command to connect to the Linux virtual machine:</p>
</blockquote>

<p>ssh azureuser@52.170.193.83</p>
</blockquote>
<blockquote>
<p>→When prompted, enter yes, and then press Enter.</p>
</blockquote>
<blockquote>
<p>→In azureuser@52.170.193.83's password, enter AzurePwd52744319, and then press Enter.</p>
</blockquote>
<p><strong>→In the SSH session, update the virtual machine by using sudo and apt-get.</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><blockquote>
<p>→Run the following command to update the Linux virtual machine:</p>
</blockquote></li>
</ul>
<blockquote>
<p>bash</p>
<p>sudo apt-get update</p>
</blockquote>
<p><strong>→Install the traceroute tool by using sudo and apt.</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><blockquote>
<p>→Run the following command to install the traceroute tool:</p>
</blockquote></li>
</ul>
<blockquote>
<p>bash</p>
<p>sudo apt install traceroute</p>
</blockquote>
<p><strong>→Verify that traffic sent to VM1 is routed through the virtual appliance VM3 by using the traceroute tool, and then exit the SSH connection.</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><blockquote>
<p>→Run the following command to use the traceroute tool:</p>
</blockquote></li>
</ul>
<blockquote>
<p>bash</p>
<p>traceroute VM1</p>
</blockquote></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1236.webp" style="width:6.17708in;height:1.61458in" alt="{D07F38EA-0BB1-43A2-A769-904288F8CA40}" /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1237.webp" style="width:6in;height:1.72917in" alt="{E6471C06-355A-47B2-BAEF-BA4D535B9E5A}" /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1238.webp" style="width:4.61458in;height:1.39583in" alt="{8F3E903D-FFDB-4A6C-9D62-F34B852CB610}" /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1239.webp" style="width:5.89583in;height:1.875in" alt="{A7475574-C134-4359-A446-B96022CD656A}" /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→What we have done is established an SSH connection to VM2 (52.170.193.83) via Azure Cloud Shell, updated the Linux virtual machine using sudo apt-get update, and installed the traceroute tool with sudo apt install traceroute.</p>
<p>→We then used the traceroute command (traceroute VM1) to verify that traffic from VM2 to VM1 is correctly routed through the firewall virtual appliance VM3, confirming the UDR and IP forwarding configurations.</p>
<p>→Finally, we exited the SSH session, ensuring the network setup's effectiveness is validated.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>IMPORTANT:</p>
<p>→we can now safely say that any traffic between VM1 and VM2 will be channeled via VM3, given the UDRs ("to-backend" and "to-frontend") and IP forwarding configuration on VM3.</p>
<p>→The network appliance (VM3) serves as a firewall virtual appliance here to filter, monitor, and secure the traffic between the two subnets, ensuring all communication passes through it for enhanced control and protection.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→If <strong><u>VM3 is not present</u></strong>, the UDRs ("to-backend" and "to-frontend") would fail to route traffic through a firewall virtual appliance, falling back to Azure’s default system routes.</p>
<p>→Traffic between VM1 and VM2 would then follow the standard VNet routing, potentially going directly between subnets without filtering or security checks.</p>
<p>→This could lead to vulnerabilities, as unmonitored or unfiltered traffic might expose the network to unauthorized access or attacks, undermining the lab’s security objectives.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Further, what was already there is Network Security Groups (NSGs)</p>
<p>→This was acting as a firewall layer to filter traffic at the subnet or VM level based on defined rules</p>
<p>→This was working alongside VM3, which routes and inspects traffic using UDRs and IP forwarding.</p>
<p>→NSGs enhance security by allowing or denying traffic based on source, destination, and port, providing a foundational protective layer on VM1 and VM2 subnets.</p>
<p>→VM3 complements this by adding <strong>advanced routing</strong> and deep packet inspection, ensuring a robust security framework.</p>
<p>→This combined approach strengthens network protection, mitigating risks of unauthorized access or attacks.</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Start Peering – VNET1

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1263.webp" style="width:5.94236in;height:4.01389in" /></p>

</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>🡪Configure details as below. Note that we are configuring on VNET1, however adding a ‘remote’ VNET.</p>
<p>🡪Notice the name as well viz., vnet2-vnet1</p>
<p>🡪Further down we can see a local configuration as well where we are configuring vnet1-vnet2.</p>
<p>🡪Once done, this becomes two way sync.</p>
<p>🡪Notice the screenshots for the sync part as well.</p>
<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1264.webp" style="width:7.43194in;height:3.84861in" /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1265.webp" style="width:7.6875in;height:3.37986in" /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1266.webp" style="width:7.07361in;height:4.21875in" /></p>
<p>Examples for each case</p>
<ol type="1">
<li><p><strong>Allow 'VNET1' to access 'VNET2'</strong><br />
<strong>Use case:</strong> A web app in <strong>App Service (VNET1)</strong> needs to connect to a <strong>SQL Database in a VM (VNET2)</strong> for data access.<br />
<strong>Example:</strong> Web frontend hosted in App Service connects to backend API or database in another VNet.</p></li>
</ol>
<ol start="2" type="1">
<li><p><strong>Allow 'VNET1' to receive forwarded traffic from 'VNET2'</strong><br />
<strong>Use case:</strong> <strong>VNET2</strong> receives traffic from a third-party service and needs to route it to <strong>VNET1</strong> for processing.<br />
<strong>Example:</strong> A firewall in VNET2 filters internet traffic and then forwards safe requests to apps in VNET1.</p></li>
</ol>
<ol start="3" type="1">
<li><p><strong>Allow gateway or route server in 'VNET1' to forward traffic to 'VNET2'</strong><br />
<strong>Use case:</strong> You have a <strong>VPN Gateway in VNET1</strong> connected to your on-premises network, and you want on-premises users to access resources in <strong>VNET2</strong>.<br />
<strong>Example:</strong> On-prem users connect via VPN to VNET1 and reach VMs or services in VNET2.</p></li>
</ol>
<ol start="4" type="1">
<li><p><strong>Enable 'VNET1' to use 'VNET2’s' remote gateway or route server</strong><br />
<strong>Use case:</strong> Instead of creating another VPN Gateway in VNET1, you let it use the <strong>VPN Gateway in VNET2</strong> to access on-prem resources.<br />
<strong>Example:</strong> Cost-saving design where multiple VNets share a central VPN Gateway hosted in one VNet.</p></li>
</ol></td>
</tr>
<tr>

## What is needed on both sides (Azure and On-Prem)

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>Azure Side:</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Virtual Network (VNet)</p></li>
<li><p>Virtual Network Gateway</p></li>
<li><p>Public IP address for the Virtual Network Gateway</p></li>
<li><p>Local Network Gateway</p></li>
<li><p>VPN Connection</p></li>
<li><p>Azure VPN Gateway policy (IKE/IPsec parameters)</p></li>
</ul>
<p>On-Premises Side:</p>
<ul>
<li><p>VPN device (router/firewall)</p></li>
<li><p>Public IP address for the VPN device</p></li>
<li><p>Private IP address range (non-overlapping with Azure VNet)</p></li>
<li><p>IKE/IPsec configuration (matching Azure VPN Gateway policy)</p></li>
<li><p>Routing configuration (for traffic to Azure VNet)</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Encryption 

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>Encryption for Azure VPN Gateway (Site-to-Site VPN):</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Azure Side:</p>
<ul>
<li><p>IKE (Internet Key Exchange): IKEv1 or IKEv2 for key negotiation</p></li>
<li><p>IPsec: ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) for data encryption</p></li>
<li><p>Encryption Algorithms: AES-256, AES-192, AES-128, or 3DES</p></li>
<li><p>Integrity Algorithms: SHA-256, SHA-1, or MD5</p></li>
<li><p>Diffie-Hellman (DH) Groups: DH Group 2, 14, 24, ECP256, ECP384, or others</p></li>
<li><p>Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS): Optional, using DH groups</p></li>
</ul></li>
<li><p>On-Premises Side:</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Matching IKE version (IKEv1 or IKEv2)</p></li>
<li><p>Matching IPsec configuration (ESP)</p></li>
<li><p>Compatible Encryption Algorithms: AES-256, AES-192, AES-128, or 3DES</p></li>
<li><p>Compatible Integrity Algorithms: SHA-256, SHA-1, or MD5</p></li>
<li><p>Compatible DH Groups for key exchange</p></li>
<li><p>PFS configuration (if enabled on Azure)</p></li>
</ul></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<td><p><strong>P2S (Point-to-Site) Connection</strong><br />
A Point-to-Site connection is established between a VPN Gateway and a VPN client (e.g., a user working remotely from home) to securely connect to the Azure virtual network and access resources (like VMs) using their private IP.</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Establishes an IPSec tunnel between the client and the Azure network</p></li>
<li><p>Supports protocols like IKEv2, SSTP, and OpenVPN</p></li>
</ul>
<p>You need a certificate from a provider or a self-signed certificate to authenticate the connection.</p>
<p><strong>Note:</strong> P2S is ideal for individual client devices needing secure, temporary, or low-scale remote access to Azure.</p></td>

## Architecture

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><strong>Load balancer</strong></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1337.webp" style="width:4.52222in;height:2.10278in" alt="Diagram of the lab tasks." /></p>
<p>→Here we will be defining one Vnet that contains two subnets.</p>
<p>→Each subnet contains one VM.</p>
<p>→These two VMs are considered as one backend pool.</p>
<p>→Ontop of both of the VMs there will be a Loadbalancer configured to route the incoming traffic.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>Application Gateway → Very important that app gateway must be in own subnet.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1338.webp" style="width:6.5in;height:3.04375in" alt="Diagram of the lab tasks." /></p>
<p>→In this case the concept is same.</p>
<p>→However, here an adidtional implementation is done viz., one VM has images hosted and other Videos Hosted</p>
<p>→Unlike previously a typical LB is used, however, in this case there will be an Azure Application Gateway will be used.</p>
<p>→This AAG will distribute the traffic as per the URL.</p>
<p>→Eg. If the incoming request URL has ‘images’ it gets redirected to first one.</p>
<p>→If the incoming request URL has ‘videos’ it gets redirected to second one.</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

#  Traffic Management - Load Balancer 

<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1530.webp" style="width:7.67917in;height:1.15347in" alt="{EB0B1E7D-8F22-44E2-977D-8BA8387A3EE4}" />

→Understand the scenario

→You are an Administrator for Hexelo, an organization in need of implementing an Azure® load balancer.

→In this Challenge Lab, you will implement an Azure load balancer.

→ 1<sup>st:</sup> Create an Azure load balancer.

→2<sup>nd</sup> Configure a backend pool for the load balancer

→3<sup>rd</sup> Configure an HTTP health probe.

→4<sup>th</sup> Finally, create a load balancing rule.

→Create a Load Balancer named MyLoadBalancer by using the values in the following table. For any property not specified, use the default value.

| **Property**                          | **Value**           |
|:--------------------------------------|:--------------------|
| Resource group                        | AZ300-RGlod52771577 |
| Name                                  | MyLoadBalancer      |
| Region                                | East US             |
| SKU                                   | Standard            |
| Type                                  | Public              |
| Frontend IP configuration - Name      | LB-FIP52771577      |
| Public IP address                     | Create new          |
| Public IP address - Name              | LB-PIP52771577      |
| Public IP address - Availability zone | Zone-redundant      |

- On the Azure portal home page, in Azure services, select Create a resource.

- In the Azure Marketplace, search for and select Load Balancer, and then select the Load Balancer tile.

- On the Load Balancer blade, select Create.

- On the Create load balancer blade, on the Basics page, in Project details, in Resource group, select AZ300-RGlod52771577.

- In Instance details, in Name, enter MyLoadBalancer.

- In Region, select East US.

- In SKU, select Standard (Recommended), and then in Type, select Public.

- Select Next : Fronted IP configuration, and then select Add a frontend IP configuration.

- On the Add frontend IP address blade, in Name, enter LB-FIP52771577, and then in Public IP address, select Create new.

- In the Add a public IP address tile, in Name, enter LB-PIP52771577, in Availability zone, select Zone-redundant, and then select Save.

- On the Add frontend IP configuration blade, select Save to add the frontend IP address.

- On the Create load balancer blade, select Review + create.

- Review the configuration, and then select Create.

→An Azure load balancer evenly distributes incoming traffic to multiple virtual machines to provide a higher level of scale and availability.

→Wait for the deployment of the VM1, VM2, and VM3 virtual machines to finish before moving on to the next task.

> <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1531.jpeg" style="width:3.75069in;height:1.46528in" alt="IMG_256" />

## Existing Infra as part of Lab - Review 

→We have 3 VMs already created as part of the lab and they will be load balanced

<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1555.webp" style="width:7.67222in;height:2.49444in" alt="{E4A1C47F-63EE-4B7E-9CF8-CCC2ABBE6B85}" />

### Steps as per the Lab instructions

- Create a backend pool named MyBackendPool in the MyLoadBalancer load balancer, configure the backend pool to use the MyVNet virtual network and contain VM1, VM2, and VM3, and then ensure that each virtual machine is configured to use the IP address to which it is dynamically assigned.

<!-- -->

- On the Deployment blade, select Go to resource.

- On the MyLoadBalancer service menu, in Settings, select Backend pools.

- On the Backend pools command bar, select +Add.

- On the Add backend pool blade, in Name, enter MyBackendPool.

- In Virtual network, select MyVNet (AZ300-RGlod52771577).

- In IP configurations, select Add.

- On the Add IP configurations to backend pool blade, select the VM1, VM2, and VM3 checkboxes, and then select Add.

- On the Add backend pool blade, review the configuration, and then select Save.

  <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1556.jpeg" style="width:4.79931in;height:3.80556in" alt="IMG_256" />

→When you add virtual machines to the backend pool of a load balancer, traffic will be distributed to the virtual machines according to a load balancing rule.

- Create an HTTP health probe named MyHealthProbe in MyLoadBalancer by using port 80, and an interval of 15.

<!-- -->

- On the MyLoadBalancer service menu, in Settings, select Health probes.

- On the Health probes command bar, select Add.

- On the Add health probe blade, in Name, enter MyHealthProbe.

- In Protocol, select HTTP.

- In Port, ensure that the value is set to 80.

- In Interval, enter 15, and then select Save.

→You can configure a health probe to dynamically add and remove a virtual machine from the backend pool of a load balancer when the virtual machine fails a health check.

→The interval value defines the number of seconds between probe attempts.

→The unhealthy threshold value defines the number of unhealthy threshold or consecutive probe failures that must occur before a virtual machine is considered unhealthy.

→ Create a load balancing rule named MyHTTPRule using the values in the following table. For any property not specified, use the default value.

| **Property**        | **Value**               |
|:--------------------|:------------------------|
| Name                | MyHTTPRule              |
| Frontend IP address | LB-FIP52771577          |
| Backend pool        | MyBackendPool           |
| Port                | 80                      |
| Backend port        | 80                      |
| Health probe        | MyHealthProbe (HTTP:80) |

- On the MyLoadBalancer service menu, select Load balancing rules.

- On the Load balancing rules page, on the command bar, select +Add.

- On the Add load balancing rule blade, in Name, enter MyHTTPRule.

- In Frontend IP address, select LB-FIP52771577.

- In Backend pool, select MyBackendPool.

- In Port, enter 80, and then in Backend port, enter 80.

- In Health probe, select MyHealthProbe (HTTP:80)-the health probe may take a few minutes to become fully available. If it does not appear, wait a few minutes and refresh the page.

- Review all remaining default values, and then select Save.

> The health probe may take a few minutes to become fully available. If it does not appear, wait a few minutes and refresh the page.
>
> You can create a load balancing rule to define how traffic will be distributed to the virtual machines that are in the backend pool.

## Configure Backend Pools 

→Navigate to the LB that is created → Settings → Backend pools

<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_277.webp" style="width:4.71667in;height:3.36042in" alt="{A85C42CD-A043-45C9-AD5A-BC2E0E3B1B09}" />

→Provide name and VNET details and then click ‘+Add’ to add IP configurations

<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_278.webp" style="width:5.93472in;height:3.175in" alt="{968175D5-38E8-4D11-8DB5-125DABE67C8E}" />

→In Azure Load Balancer, the Backend Pool Configuration determines how backend resources are identified:

- NIC (Network Interface Card): Associates the backend pool with virtual machines (VMs) via their network interfaces. This links the VMs directly to the load balancer based on their NICs.

- IP Address: Associates the backend pool with specific IP addresses of VMs or other resources, offering more granular control.

If you choose NIC, the load balancer uses the VMs' NICs to distribute traffic. However, in the IP Configurations section, you still need to explicitly add VMs because this step specifies which VMs' IP configurations (tied to their NICs) are included in the pool. This ensures the load balancer knows exactly which VMs to balance traffic across, even when using NIC-based configuration.

→Select all the VMs and click Add

<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_279.webp" style="width:4.57569in;height:2.73056in" alt="{D0FA7DD7-AB3B-459B-A23D-512D83F1149A}" />

→We can see they are added

<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1568.webp" style="width:4.26667in;height:2.22917in" alt="{2F1A163C-611D-49BB-AEBA-C8DD9747CDA7}" />

→Continue with clicking ‘save’ button

→Naviage back and check on the LB

<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_280.webp" style="width:5.80347in;height:2.98611in" alt="{BE441A50-89D1-445E-A28D-D5751A51B0EB}" />

## Create LB Rule

→Navigae to LB Rules

<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_283.webp" style="width:5.04861in;height:3.39653in" alt="{5299943B-87E6-49D5-9F17-512C82CC41E6}" />

→Fillout details as shown and save

<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_284.webp" style="width:4.09861in;height:5.50417in" alt="{C8E8C89C-F325-4C93-92F3-F3B007ECD716}" />

→This Azure Load Balancer rule, named "MyIPv4Rule," distributes incoming traffic across a group of backend pool instances using a hash-based method for load balancing.

→It operates on IPv4 traffic, using port 80 for both frontend and backend, with TCP as the protocol and a session persistence of 4 minutes.

→The rule includes health probes to ensure backend health and uses an outbound source network address translation (SNAT) for communication.

→If this rule is **not created**, the Azure Load Balancer will not distribute traffic as specified, and the load balancing functionality for that specific configuration (e.g., port 80, IPv4, TCP) will not work.

→Existing traffic may still pass through other rules or default settings, but the intended load balancing behavior will be absent.

→Post saving

<p>🡪Navigate to the VM and click on the Run command and click the ‘RunPowerShellScript’.</p>
<p>🡪Use below script, installs the IIS web server with management tools, deletes the default iisstart.htm file, and creates a new one displaying "Hello World from [computer name]". Running it in a Windows VM via the 'run command' option will set up a basic web server with a custom welcome page.</p>
<p>Install-WindowsFeature -name web-Server -IncludeManagementTools</p>
<p>remove-item 'C:\inetpub\wwwroot\iisstart.htm'</p>
<p>Add-Content -Path 'C:\inetpub\wwwroot\iisstart.htm' -Value $("Hello World from " + $env:computername)</p></td>

#  Azure Storage - Blob - File Share 

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><ul>
<li><p>In this lab you learn to create storage accounts for Azure blobs and Azure files.</p></li>
<li><p>You learn to configure and secure blob containers. You also learn to use Storage Browser to configure and secure Azure file shares.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><ul>
<li><p>Your organization is currently storing data in on-premises data stores.</p></li>
<li><p>Most of these files are not accessed frequently.</p></li>
<li><p>You would like to minimize the cost of storage by placing infrequently accessed files in lower-priced storage tiers. You also plan to explore different protection mechanisms that Azure Storage offers, including network access, authentication, authorization, and replication.</p></li>
<li><p>Finally, you want to determine to what extent Azure Files is suitable for hosting your on-premises file shares.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

### Create containers and apply retention policy

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 47%" />
<col style="width: 52%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>→An access policy on a container blob defines shared access permissions and constraints like start time, expiry time, and access type.<br />
It can include retention policies to prevent data deletion/modification for a specified period (immutability).<br />
Useful for compliance, audit, or secure data sharing via SAS tokens.</p>
<p>→A container in Azure Storage is a logical unit used to organize blobs within a storage account.</p>
<p>→This is similar to a folder in a traditional file system.</p>
<p>→It serves as the top-level namespace for storing blob data such as images, videos, and documents.</p>
<p>→Containers also enable access control by allowing permissions to be set at the container level, making them essential for managing and securing blob storage.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_300.webp" style="width:3.08194in;height:1.96389in" alt="A screenshot of a computer AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p>
<p>Navigate to Data storage 🡪 Containers 🡪 + Container</p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_301.webp" style="width:1.73403in;height:2.41111in" alt="A computer screen with a white screen AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p>
<p>→Provide a proper name and ensure the access level is ‘private’.</p>
<p>→Continue by clicking ‘create’</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_302.webp" style="width:5.10486in;height:2.12917in" alt="A screenshot of a computer AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p>
<p>→Select the container that we created and use the elipses(3 dots) and click ‘Access policy’</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_303.webp" style="width:2.09375in;height:2.01111in" alt="A screenshot of a computer AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p>
<p>→Click +Add policy under immutable blob storage</p>
<p>→Next configuration means blobs in the container cannot be modified or deleted for 180 days from the time they're created or last updated,<br />
enforcing a time-based write-once, read-many (WORM) policy for compliance or regulatory needs.</p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_304.webp" style="width:2.17569in;height:2.25278in" alt="A computer screen shot of a computer AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p>
<p>→Configure for 180 days and click ‘save’</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

### Create Fileshares

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 46%" />
<col style="width: 53%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>→File Shares in Azure Storage provide a fully managed, cloud-based file system.</p>
<p>→This file system can be accessed via the SMB protocol.</p>
<p>→This allows seamless integration with on-premises and cloud environments.</p>
<p>→They are used to store and share files across multiple virtual machines or users, supporting scenarios like lift-and-shift migrations and application storage.</p>
<p>→File Shares offer scalable, durable, and secure file storage with easy access and management in the cloud.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1909.webp" style="width:2.79931in;height:1.31736in" alt="A screenshot of a computer AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p>
<p>→Navigate to storage accounts and click the configured account</p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_317.webp" style="width:3.54028in;height:1.51111in" alt="A screenshot of a computer AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p>
<p>Navigate to Data storage 🡪 File shares 🡪 click + File share</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_318.webp" style="width:2.77014in;height:2.47014in" alt="A screenshot of a computer AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p>
<p>→Provide ‘basic’ details</p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1917.webp" style="width:2.75833in;height:2.40556in" alt="A screenshot of a computer AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p>
<p>→Navigate to Backup and ensure ‘Enable Backup’ is removed.</p>
<p>→By default it is enabled</p>
<p>→The Backup setting for a new file share enables automated backups to protect data against accidental deletion or corruption.</p>
<p>→When enabled, the file share data is backed up to Azure Backup, a separate, secure backup service.</p>
<p>→This service provides point-in-time recovery of files and folders, ensuring data durability and protection.</p>
<p>→Azure Backup manages the backup storage and retention policies automatically.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_319.webp" style="width:2.10486in;height:2.42847in" alt="A computer screen with a white screen AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p>
<p>→Once the check is removed, click ‘Review + create’ + create</p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1919.webp" style="width:3.64653in;height:1.65278in" alt="A computer screen shot of a computer AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p>
<p>→Notice the file share is created.</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

### Create Service Endpoint 

<table>

<tbody>
<tr>
<td colspan="2"><p>→Service endpoints extend your VNet's private IP address space to Azure services</p>
<p>→They allow secure access over the Azure backbone.<br />
→They improve security by enabling traffic to specific services like Azure Storage or SQL to stay within the VNet.<br />
→Service endpoints are configured per subnet and can be restricted using network security groups.</p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1936.webp" /><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1937.webp" /><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1938.webp" /><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1939.webp" /><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1940.webp" style="width:1.99375in;height:2.35208in" alt="A screenshot of a computer AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p>
<p>→Navigate to Settings 🡪 Service endpoints and click +Add</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_324.webp" style="width:1.58194in;height:2.34097in" alt="A computer screen shot of a computer screen AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p>
<p>→There are various options under ‘service’ where we are choosing Storage.</p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1945.webp" /><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1946.webp" /></p>
<p>Option under Service, where we can select various services for endpoints. for info only</p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_325.webp" style="width:2.71667in;height:1.42292in" alt="A screenshot of a computer AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p>
<p>→Notice the endpoint is added</p>
<p>→Note: With service endpoints, the source IP address for service traffic from this subnet(eg. Default here) will switch from using public IPv4 addresses to using private IPv4 address.</p>
<p>→Existing IP firewall rules using Azure public IP addresses will stop working with this switch.</p>
<p>→Please ensure IP firewall rules allow for this switch before setting up service endpoints. You may also experience temporary interruption to service traffic from this subnet while configuring service endpoints.</p></td>

<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1970.webp" style="width:2.48542in;height:1.76806in" alt="{92ABD79E-4FA2-4630-A2FF-C094B4A8516B}" /></p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>←Understand this typical usecase.</p>
<p>←We typically have a store (Eg. Azure Storage Accounts), where we store some data (Eg. Files/images/etc).</p>
<p>←These needs to be accessed by some Webapplication running on a VM, which is again inside the Azure.</p>
<p>←Given both VM (web app inside it) and Storage Account are residing on Azure, we may think that any connection from VM to SA will go directly via VNIC→VNET→SA on https.</p>
<p>←This is NOT the case.</p>
<p>←These accesses are on https and must ‘by default’ exit the azure bubble and hit the internet and comeback to SA to access the files.</p>
<p>←This is normal as there could be other apps interested which are outside of the azure wanting to access the store.</p>
<p>←However, this is not secure</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1971.webp" style="width:2.90556in;height:1.4in" /></p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>←To achieve the security we will need to use few Azure Services viz.,</p>
<p>→<strong>Service Endpoint on VNet</strong></p>
<p>→<strong>Private Link on the Azure Storage Account</strong></p>
<p>←This way an internal Azure App can communicate directly using its own Vnet infrastructure.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image1972.webp" style="width:2.86181in;height:1.83056in" /></p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>←Once enabled, the Azure private Link will have its own VNIC, meaning with an ‘internal ip’ address</p>
<p>←This way Azure VM can talk on internal infra, while we can keep the external access as needed or disable it.</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Vnet - Add Service Endpoint and Link to subnet

<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→When adding a Service Endpoint to a VNet subnet, you're enabling secure, direct connectivity to a specific Azure service (e.g., Azure Storage) over the Azure backbone network.</p>

## Storage Account - Add Private Endpoint

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→When adding a Private Link to an Azure service like a Storage Account, you're creating a <strong>private endpoint</strong></p>
<p><strong>→</strong>This endpoint is with a private IP address within your VNet.</p>
<p>→This will connect securely to that specific service instance.</p>
<p>→This routes traffic directly to the service(Eg. Storage Account) over the Azure backbone, avoiding public internet exposure.</p>
<p>→It ensures enhanced security and low-latency access to the targeted service.</p></td>
</tr>

#  Azure Storage - Customer Managed Key on AKV

<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2067.webp" style="width:7.66944in;height:1.33056in" alt="{3B69F7B4-2EC7-432B-8171-1248948ABC0A}" />

→Understand the scenario

→You are an Architect with Hexelo and responsible for your organization's Azure environment.

→You need to secure an Azure storage account.

→ First, you will configure a storage account to use a customer-managed storage service encryption key, and then you will configure the storage account to use secure transfer.

→ Next, you will configure firewall rules to restrict storage account access to a specific IP address, and then you will generate a shared access signature to be used to grant time-limited, delegated access to a storage account.

→Finally, you will test the access to the storage account by using Microsoft Azure Storage Explorer.

## Lab Steps

- **Create a customer-managed key named SAKey-52778588 in the KeyVault52778588 key vault.**

<!-- -->

- In the Azure portal, on the portal menu, select Resource groups.

- <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2068.jpeg" style="width:2.09375in;height:2.75in" alt="IMG_256" />

- Select AZ300-RGlod52778588.

- On the Overview page, select KeyVault52778588.

- <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2069.jpeg" style="width:3.23958in;height:1.57292in" alt="IMG_257" />

- On the KeyVault52778588 resource menu, in Objects, select Keys.

- Select Generate/Import.

- In Name, enter SAKey-52778588, and then select Create.

> To save time, a key vault was configured as part of this challenge setup.

- **Enable the Azure Disk Encryption for volume encryption access configuration for the KeyVault52778588 key vault.**

<!-- -->

- On the KeyVault52778588 resource menu, in Settings, select Access configuration.

- Select the Azure Disk Encryption for volume encryption check box, and then select Apply.

- Close the KeyVault52778588 page, and then close the Resource groups page.

<!-- -->

- **Configure an existing storage account named sa52778588 to use the storage service encryption key named SAKey-52778588 that is stored in the KeyVault52778588 key vault.**

<!-- -->

- In the upper-left corner, select Home to return to the Azure portal home page.

- On the home page, select Storage accounts.

- <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2070.jpeg" style="width:3.29375in;height:1.38472in" alt="IMG_258" />

- Select sa52778588.

- On the sa52778588 resource menu, in Security + networking, select Encryption.

- Select Customer-managed Keys.

- In Encryption key, select Select from key vault.

- <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2071.jpeg" style="width:3.97917in;height:0.89583in" alt="IMG_259" />

- Select Select a key vault and key.

- On the Select key from Azure Key Vault blade, in Key Vault, select KeyVault52778588.

- In Key, select SAKey-52778588, and then select Select.

- <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2072.jpeg" style="width:5.59375in;height:2.36458in" alt="IMG_260" />

- On the Encryption page, select Save.

→By default, the data in a storage account is encrypted by using Microsoft-managed encryption keys.

→When encrypting Azure blobs and files, you can choose to use your own key rather than the Microsoft-managed key; however, tables and queues are always encrypted by using Microsoft-managed keys.

→[Azure Key Vault](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-ca/azure/key-vault/key-vault-overview) protects cryptographic keys and other secrets and is a prerequisite for using your own keys to encrypt Azure blobs and files.

→This configuration is crucial for organizations needing robust data protection for their Azure deployments.

## Generate SAS for Account 

- Configure a shared access signature (SAS) for the sa52778588 storage account by using a start time that matches the current time displayed in the W10-Admin system tray and an end time that is eight hours later than the start time.

<!-- -->

- On the sa52778588 resource menu, in Settings, select Shared access signature.

- In Allowed resource types, select the Service, Container, and Object check boxes.<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2120.webp" style="width:3.05208in;height:1.30208in" alt="IMG_256" />

- In Start, enter the current time displayed in the W10-Admin system tray.

- In End, ensure that the time value is eight hours later than the start time.<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2121.jpeg" style="width:4.65625in;height:1.57292in" alt="IMG_257" />

- In Shared access signature, review the settings, and then select Generate SAS and connection string.

→A [SAS](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-dotnet-shared-access-signature-part-1?toc=/azure/storage/blobs/toc.json) is generated by the owner of a storage account.

→It can be used to grant access to specific services (Blob, File, Queue, or Table) and resource types (Service, Container, or Blob) by using specific permissions (Read, Write, Delete, and others) for a specific amount of time.

→Using a SAS, you can also restrict access to requests from HTTPS and specific IP addresses.

→As a best practice, you should follow the security principle of least privilege, granting the fewest permissions necessary to the minimum number of services and resource types.

→ Copy the Connection String and save it to ConnectionString.txt on the Desktop of W10-Admin.

→Search for Shared Access Signature --\> Under Security + Networking, click the same.

## Configure Security for Storage Account 

- Enable the Azure Disk Encryption for volume encryption access policy for the KeyVault52791505 key vault.

<!-- -->

- Review the documentation on [securing access to a key vault](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/key-vault/key-vault-secure-your-key-vault).

<!-- -->

- Create a key named SAKey-52791505 in the KeyVault52791505 key vault.

<!-- -->

- Configure an existing storage account named saa52791505 to use a customer-managed encryption key named SAKey-52791505 that is stored in the KeyVault52791505 key vault.

<!-- -->

- Review the documentation on [storage service encryption](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-service-encryption).

→ To save time, a key vault was configured as part of this challenge setup. For this challenge, you do not need to [configure access to the key vault](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/key-vault/general/security-features), but in your own environment, you must create policies that will allow your storage accounts and applications to access the key vault.

→ You can use a variety of [security mechanisms](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/security-recommendations) to help protect your Azure data while it is at rest or in transit. These mechanisms include role-based access control (RBAC) and Microsoft Entra ID, storage encryption keys, secure HTTPS and SMB 3.0 connections, and shared access signatures. You can configure storage account security either when you create the storage account or after you create the storage account.

- Enable secure transfer for the saa52791505 storage account to allow requests from secure (encrypted) connections only.

→You can enable and disable secure transfer by using the Azure portal, the REST API, Azure PowerShell, CLI 2.0, NodeJS, the .NET software development kit (SDK), Python SDK, or the Ruby SDK.

- Configure the saa52791505 storage account firewall to allow access from the IP address of your lab virtual machine only.

> By default, the data in a storage account is encrypted using Microsoft-managed encryption keys. When encrypting Azure blobs and files, you can choose to use your own key rather than the Microsoft-managed key; however, tables and queues are always encrypted using Microsoft-managed keys.

- Configure a user delegation shared access signature (SAS) for the saa52791505 storage account by using a start time that matches the current time displayed in the W10-Admin system tray and an end time that is eight hours later than the start time.

A SAS is generated by the owner of a storage account. It can be used to grant access to specific services (Blob, File, Queue, or Table) and resource types (Service, Container, or Blob) by using specific permissions (Read, Write, Delete, and others) for a specific amount of time. Using a SAS, you can also restrict access to HTTPS and specific IP addresses.

As a best practice, you should follow the security principle of least privilege, granting access only to the minimum number of services and resource types with the fewest permissions necessary.

## Configure Monitoring for Storage Account

→Modify classic diagnostic settings for the blob properties of the sab52791505 storage account to enable minute metrics, and then set Logging version 2.0 to Read.

→There are [two versions of Azure storage metrics](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-metrics-migration?toc=/azure/storage/blobs/toc.json) available in the Azure portal.

→The old version is referred to as *old metrics* in Microsoft documentation, but it is labeled as *classic* in the Azure portal.

→ Old metrics can collect capacity metrics for blob storage and transaction metrics for all storage services.

→Data for old metrics is stored in \$Metric tables in the storage account being monitored. 

→[Data for new metrics](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/monitor-blob-storage?tabs=azure-portal) is automatically enabled, and it can be accessed by using Azure Monitor, Event Hubs, and Azure Monitor APIs (.NET and REST).

→You can store new metrics data in a storage account if you need it for more than 93 days.

- Begin configuring an alert rule for the sab52791505 storage account that contains a condition that uses the Regenerate Storage Account Keys signal, and then trigger the alert when the status changes to Failed.

<!-- -->

- Create an action group named Storage Admins in the AZ300-RG resource group, configure a display name of SA Admins, and then configure an Email/SMS message/Push/Voice notification named Email storage admins that sends an email to your personal email address.

- Assign the alert rule name Storage account key generation failed, and then ensure that the alert is saved in the AZ300-RG resource group.

An Action Group in Azure is a collection of notification and action preferences used by alert rules. When an alert is triggered, the action group defines how and where notifications are sent—such as email, SMS, push, or calling webhooks. It can also trigger automation like Azure Functions, Logic Apps, or ITSM tools. Action Groups help ensure prompt responses to critical conditions.

#  Azure Storage - Explorer - Create Snapshot

<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2237.webp" style="width:7.67222in;height:1.09097in" alt="{28FC6B9C-7F28-4F63-995B-56C583732B3B}" />

You are an Architect for Hexelo, an organization that is migrating its primary web app from its on-premises datacenter to Azure.

In this Challenge Lab, you will use Azure Storage Explorer. First, you will create an Azure Storage Account, and then you will upload blob data to a container. Next, you will install Azure Storage Explorer. Finally, you will create a snapshot as a proof of concept.

## Create Storage Account

- **Create a StorageV2 (general purpose v2) Azure Storage Account named sa52830606 in the East US region that is configured to use Locally-redundant storage (LRS) for replication and the Hot access tier and Secure transfer required options.**

<!-- -->

- On the Microsoft Azure portal home page, in Azure services, select Storage accounts.

- On the Storage accounts blade, select Create storage account.

- On the Create a storage account blade, in Instance details, in Storage account name, enter sa52830606.

- In Region, ensure that (US) East US is selected.

- In Redundancy, select Locally-redundant storage (LRS), and then select Next

- On the Advanced page, in Security, ensure that the Require secure transfer for REST API operations checkbox is selected.

- In Blob storage, in Access tier, ensure that Hot: Optimized for frequently accessed data and everyday usage scenarios is selected.

- Select Review, and then select Create.

<!-- -->

- **Create a blob container named images that has a Public access level of Private (no anonymous access) and then upload the C:\Windows\blue-gray.jpg file to the blob container.**

<!-- -->

- On the Deployment blade, select Go to resource.

- On the sa52830606 service menu, in Data storage, select Containers.

- On the Containers page, on the command bar, select + Container.

- On the New container blade, in Name, enter images, and then select Create.

- On the Containers page, select images.

- On the images blade, select Upload.

- On the Upload blob blade, select Browse for files.

- In the Open dialog, browse to the C:\Windows folder.

- Select blue-gray.jpg, and then select Open.

- On the Upload blob blade, select Upload.

## Install Azure Explorer

- Open a new Microsoft Edge browser tab, go to https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/features/storage-explorer/, and then download and install Azure Storage Explorer for Windows x64 using the default options.

Start Storage Explorer.

Verify that Storage Explorer has used the current user account to connect to the subscription-if prompted for credentials, sign in as admin1-52830606@cloudslice.onmicrosoft.com using rM8mUj+S6+@K as the password.

- In the Microsoft Azure Storage Explorer, select Sign in with Azure, and then sign in to Azure as admin1-52830606@cloudslice.onmicrosoft.com using rM8mUj+S6+@K as the password.

- On the Select Azure Environment page, in Which Azure environment will you use to sign in?, select Azure, and then select Next.

- In the new browser tab, sign in as admin1-52830606@cloudslice.onmicrosoft.com using rM8mUj+S6+@K as the password.

- Close the Authentication Complete browser tab and return to the Microsoft Azure Storage Explorer window.

- In the left pane, select Open Explorer.

### Create Snapshot

- Create a snapshot of the blob file and display it using the Manage snapshots option.

<!-- -->

- In Microsoft Azure Storage Explorer, in the files container, right-click on the file that you uploaded, and then on the command bar, select Create Snapshot.

- Right-click the file again, and then in Manage History, select Manage Snapshots.

<!-- -->

- Use the option Promote snapshot to overwrite the original blob file to emulate a revert operation.

<!-- -->

- In Snapshot Manager, right click the snapshot of the image file, and then select Promote Snapshot.

- In the confirmation dialog, select Yes.

<!-- -->

- Obtain the Shared Access Signature for the original image you uploaded to the files folder, and then confirm that you can access it by pasting the shared access signature url in a new Microsoft Edge browser tab.

<!-- -->

- In the files folder, right-click the original image file, and then select Get Shared Access Signature.

- In the Share Access Signature dialog, select Create.

- Copy the URL field and paste it into a new Microsoft Edge browser tab.

- Confirm the image that you uploaded opens in the browser.

> Want to learn more? Review the documentation on [Shared Access Signatures](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-sas-overview).

→ On the file that is uploaded, right-click and click ‘Create Snapshot (from bottom 6).

<td style="text-align: left;"><p>🡪SINGLE REGION</p>
<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2302.webp" style="width:1.59236in;height:2.65972in" /></p></td>

<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>🡪Does not guarantee DC Failures.</p>
<p>🡪Locally Redundant Storage</p>
<p>🡪It has 9 nines of availability.</p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>🡪This protects even a DC failure.</p>
<p>🡪It is a single region.</p>
<p>🡪Does not guarantee Region Failure</p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>🡪Gives 16 nines of availability.</p>
<p>🡪Protects against regional failure.</p>
<p>🡪Notice here secondary copy gets replicated ‘async’</p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>🡪Same as MULTI REGION, however, the secondary region enables ‘READ-ACESS’ guaranteed.</p></td>
</tr>

<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2325.webp" /><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2326.webp" style="width:3.58333in;height:2.39583in" alt="A screenshot of a computer AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p>
<p>Click Upload.</p></td>

<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2327.webp" style="width:3.76042in;height:3.95833in" alt="A screenshot of a computer AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p>
<p>🡪Using the browse option we can upload.</p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2328.webp" style="width:3.45208in;height:3.125in" alt="A screenshot of a computer AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p>
<p>🡪We have uploaded a file and check the ‘advanced’ option what it provides.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2329.webp" style="width:3.85417in;height:3.9375in" alt="A screenshot of a computer AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>🡨<strong>Blob type</strong>:<br />
Determines the type of blob — e.g.,</p>
<p><strong>Block blob</strong> (for most files like images),</p>
<p><strong>Page blob</strong> (for VHDs),</p>
<p><strong>Append blob</strong> (for logs).</p>
<p>🡨<strong>Upload .vhd files as page blobs (recommended)</strong>:<br />
If checked, .vhd files (virtual hard disks) will be uploaded as <strong>Page blobs</strong> for better performance and compatibility.</p>
<p>🡨<strong>Block size</strong>:<br />
Sets the size of each block in a Block blob upload — larger files are split into blocks of this size (default is usually fine).</p>
<p>🡨<strong>Access tier</strong>:<br />
Defines how frequently the blob is accessed — <strong>Hot</strong> (frequent), <strong>Cool</strong> (infrequent), or <strong>Archive</strong> (rarely accessed, long-term storage).</p></td>
</tr>

## Rehydration 

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>WHAT IS IT?</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>Definition</strong>: Rehydration is moving data from Azure Blob Storage's archive tier to an online tier (hot or cool) to make it accessible.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Why Needed</strong>: Archive tier data is offline, unreadable, and unmodifiable until rehydrated to hot or cool tier.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>What Leads</strong> to It: Data stored in archive tier for long-term, low-cost storage needs rehydration for access or modification.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Benefits</strong>: Enables access to archived data for reading or editing while optimizing costs with tiered storage.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Methods</strong>: Rehydrate by copying the blob to a new blob in hot/cool tier or changing its tier using Set Blob Tier.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Tools</strong>: Use Azure Portal, PowerShell, Azure CLI, or AzCopy to initiate rehydration.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Priority</strong> Options: Standard priority (up to 15 hours) or high priority (faster, under 1 hour for small blobs).</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Costs</strong>: Involves data read/write transaction fees; high-priority rehydration is costlier.</p></li>
<li><p>Early <strong>Deletion</strong> Fee: Copying avoids fees for moving blobs before 180-day archive minimum; Set Blob Tier may incur fees.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Automation</strong>: Use scripts (e.g., PowerShell) or Azure Logic Apps for bulk rehydration, not lifecycle management.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>WHEN DOES IT GO TO ARCHIVAL</p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>Manual</strong> Archiving: User explicitly sets blob tier to archive via Azure Portal, CLI, PowerShell, or SDKs.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Lifecycle Management Policy</strong>: Automated rules move blobs to archive tier based on age or last access time.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Infrequent</strong> Access: Data not accessed for a long period (e.g., 30+ days) is archived to reduce storage costs.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Cost Optimization</strong>: User chooses archive for long-term, rarely accessed data like backups or compliance records.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Application Design</strong>: Apps or workflows store data in archive tier for regulatory or retention requirements.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Cold Storage Transition</strong>: Data in cool tier moved to archive after a set period via lifecycle rules.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Large-Scale Backups</strong>: Bulk data like logs or historical records archived to minimize storage expenses.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p><strong><u>Real world Use Cases</u></strong></p>
<p><strong>1. Enterprise App Hosting (Lift &amp; Shift)</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>Scenario</strong>: Legacy apps moved to Azure still need file system access.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Usage</strong>: Azure VMs mount the file share as a network drive.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Example</strong>: A .NET app reads/writes files to \\&lt;storageaccount&gt;.file.core.windows.net\shared.</p></li>
</ul>
<p><strong>2. Shared Storage Across VMs</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>Scenario</strong>: Multiple Azure virtual machines need to share files.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Usage</strong>: All VMs mount the same Azure File Share.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Example</strong>: Web servers write logs to a common location.</p></li>
</ul>
<p><strong>3. Hybrid Cloud File Access</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>Scenario</strong>: On-prem servers or systems need access to cloud storage.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Usage</strong>: On-prem machines mount the file share using VPN or ExpressRoute.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Example</strong>: Backups from on-prem to Azure.</p></li>
</ul>
<p><strong>4. Containerized Workloads</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>Scenario</strong>: Containers running on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) or App Services need persistent shared storage.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Usage</strong>: Azure File Share mounted as a volume.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Example</strong>: Shared configuration files or media.</p></li>
</ul>
<p><strong>5. Developer/Test Environments</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>Scenario</strong>: Developers or test VMs need access to centralized files.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Usage</strong>: Dev/test VMs mount file shares during their session.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Example</strong>: Sharing large test datasets or logs.</p></li>
</ul>
<p><strong>6. File-based Integration Between Services</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><p><strong>Scenario</strong>: One process writes files, another reads them.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Usage</strong>: Both access the same Azure File Share.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Example</strong>: A batch job uploads files that a reporting job processes later.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

However, if you wish to manage the encryption keys yourself, you can apply <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/windows/disk-encryption-overview">Azure Disk Encryption</a>, and then manage the encryption keys by using Azure Key Vault. Azure Disk Encryption uses BitLocker encryption for Windows virtual machines and DM-Crypt encryption for Linux virtual machines.</p></td>

#  Azure Storage - Cosmos DB with HA

<table style="width:87%;">
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 87%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2424.webp" style="width:6.52431in;height:0.91944in" alt="{7C361714-6F39-49CE-89AE-3396254C9A51}" /></p>
<p>You are a Data Engineer at Hexelo. You need to provision a new Azure® Cosmos DB account that is designed for high availability. First, you will deploy an Azure Cosmos DB account. Next, you will create a container in a new database, and then you will add items to the container. Finally, you will enable high availability, and then you will test the configuration.</p></td>
</tr>

</table>

## Create Container 

<table style="width:87%;">
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 42%" />
<col style="width: 44%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>→A Cosmos DB container is a scalable storage unit within a Cosmos DB database.</p>
<p>→This inturn holds items (documents, rows, or nodes) and their associated data.</p>
<p>→ It supports partitioning for distributing data and enables efficient querying and management.</p>
<p>→To achieve this it uses APIs like SQL, MongoDB, or Gremlin.</p>
<p>→Containers are highly flexible, allowing customization of indexing, partitioning, and throughput settings.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Click Data Explorer</p>
<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_413.webp" style="width:3.08611in;height:2.12778in" alt="{2F3F8590-C967-45CE-A3D0-1C2BECDF13F0}" /></p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Click +New Container</p>
<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_414.webp" style="width:3.27639in;height:1.24236in" alt="{937944C1-D003-4B81-AB51-82762734A377}" /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Provide details like database id (create new option), container id, partition key and ‘container through put (choose manual)</p>
<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_415.webp" style="width:3.09514in;height:4.56458in" alt="{7453ED85-B103-4344-B0EA-5664F4A3EEC6}" /></p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Followed by these leaving as is and click ok</p>
<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_416.webp" style="width:3.28264in;height:3.30833in" alt="{D194E50D-A03F-4614-B0B0-14F75D72E11F}" /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>→You create a container in a database. The Azure portal allows you to create the database at the same time as the first container.</p>
<p>→The <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/partitioning-overview">partition key</a> is used to automatically distribute data across multiple servers for high scalability.</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Perform a manual failover

<colgroup>

<col style="width: 47%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><p>→Perform a manual failover to the West US region for the Azure Cosmos DB account, and then verify that the read region has become the new write region.</p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Navigate back to Settings →Replicate Globally configuration and click ‘Change write region’</p>
<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_425.webp" style="width:3.48333in;height:1.24236in" alt="{44A1C255-1E8C-4DAF-B37E-80AB1D0496D1}" /></p></td>

<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Select as shown below</p>

<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_426.webp" style="width:2.88681in;height:3.35417in" alt="{8CF99CAC-06B1-4065-9B5A-470A1586D1FD}" /></p></td>

<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_427.webp" style="width:3.4875in;height:1.29931in" alt="{C1980C3B-B7AD-4EC2-9F3A-C743B8200EA4}" /></p></td>

<p>You are a Data Engineer with Hexelo.</p>
<p>→You need to provision a new Azure® SQL Database that is enabled for automatic failover to support disaster recovery.</p>
<p>→First, you will deploy an Azure SQL Database as the primary replica.</p>

<p>→Finally, you will test a failover operation.</p></td>

<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>→ A <a href="https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-sql/database/auto-failover-group-overview?tabs=azure-powershell#terminology-and-capabilities">failover group</a> is a group of databases that can fail over automatically to another region during a disaster recovery situation.</p>
<p>→A failover group is a logical container that groups multiple databases so they can fail over together to a secondary region, ensuring high availability and easier disaster recovery. It provides a single failover policy and read/write/read-only endpoints to keep apps connected during region outages</p></td>

## Create VNET RULE (Service Endpoint) 

<table style="width:87%;">
<colgroup>

<col style="width: 44%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>→Here we are configuring a virtual network (VNet) rule to control access to SQL Server.</p>
<p>→This will help in limiting connections to specific networks.</p>
<p>→This enhances security by restricting public access to only the designated VNet, such as <strong>SQVM1-vnet-default</strong> in below case.</p>
<p>→The rule ensures that only resources <strong>within</strong> this VNet can communicate with the SQL Server.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Click All resources</p>
<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2714.webp" /><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2715.webp" style="width:2.45833in;height:3.23958in" alt="{CDF92C8B-357E-4164-9E86-132DE4716E0F}" /></p></td>

<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2716.webp" /><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2717.webp" style="width:3.26875in;height:3.51389in" alt="{7AC26810-47A0-4747-B346-06D9571DEFF3}" /></p></td>
</tr>
