#  Compute - VMSS - HA - Sacling - LB 

<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2944.webp" style="width:7.67847in;height:1.29931in" alt="{77D3E992-7333-4ABD-AF7D-7022964D926E}" />

→ You are an Administrator for Hexelo, an organization that needs to implement high availability and scalability in Azure®.

→In this Challenge Lab, you will deploy multiple Azure virtual machine scale sets acting as web server and app server tiers. →First, you will create a virtual machine scale set (VMSS) for the web server tier.

→Next, you will use an Azure Resource Manager (ARM) template to create a virtual machine scale set for the app server tier.

→Finally, you will allow connectivity to the virtual machine scale set for the web server tier.

→ Create an Azure virtual machine scale set by using the values in the following table. For any property that is not specified, use the default value.

| **Property**                   | **Value**                                 |
|:-------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|
| Resource group                 | corp-datalod52838879                      |
| Virtual machine scale set name | vmfe52838879                              |
| Region                         | (US) East US                              |
| Orchestration mode             | Uniform                                   |
| Security type                  | Standard                                  |
| Instance count                 | 2                                         |
| Image                          | Windows Server 2019 Datacenter - x64 Gen2 |
| Size                           | Standard_B2s - 2 vcpus, 4 GiB memory      |
| Username                       | Student                                   |
| Password                       | Azure!JGa51\*p#hBn3                       |
| OS disk type                   | Standard HDD                              |
| Virtual network                | (new) vnet-eastus (corp-datalod52838879)  |
| Load balancing options         | Azure load balancer                       |
| Load balancer name (new)       | vmfe52838879-lb                           |

- On the Azure portal home page, in Azure services, select Create a resource.

- In the Azure Marketplace, search for and select Virtual machine scale set and then select Create.

> <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2945.jpeg" style="width:2.08264in;height:1.03264in" alt="IMG_256" />

- On the Create a virtual machine scale set blade, on the Basics page, in Project details, in Resource group, select corp-datalod52838879.

- In Scale set details, in Virtual machine scale set name, enter vmfe52838879, in Region, ensure that (US) East US is selected.

- In Orchestration, in Orchestration mode, select Uniform, and then in Security type, select Standard.

- In Scaling, in Instance count, ensure that 2 is entered.

- In Instance details, in Image, select Windows Server 2019 Datacenter - x64 Gen2, and then in Size, select See all sizes.

- On the Select a VM size blade, in Search by VM size, search for and select B2s, and then select Select.

> <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2946.jpeg" style="width:3.10139in;height:2.91736in" alt="IMG_257" />

- In Administrator account, in Username, enter Student, in Password and Confirm password, enter Azure!JGa51\*p#hBn3.

- On the Create a virtual machine scale set blade, advance to the Disks page.

- On the Disks page, in OS disk, in OS disk type, select Standard HDD, and then select Next: Networking.

- On the Networking page, in Virtual network configuration, in Virtual network, ensure that (new) vnet-eastus (corp-datalod52838879) is selected.

- In Load balancing, in Load balancing options, select Azure load balancer, and then in Select a load balancer, select Create a load balancer.

- On the Create a load balancer blade, in Load balancer name, enter vmfe52838879-lb, and then select Create.

- Select Review + create, and then select Create.

> If you see an error message The virtual machine scale set with Flexible orchestration mode does not have outbound connectivity. Please use an Azure load balancer or configure a NAT gateway or user-defined routes (UDR) on the subnet, make sure you have selected Uniform Orchestration mode on the Basics page.
>
> <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2947.jpeg" style="width:4.13056in;height:0.45278in" alt="IMG_258" />
>
> The deployment will take approximately 3-5 minutes.

→Configure the vmfe52838879 scale set to use a Custom autoscale policy by using the values in the following table. For any property that is not specified, use the default value.

| **Property**                | **Value**               |
|:----------------------------|:------------------------|
| How to scale your resource  | Custom autoscale        |
| Scale mode                  | Scale based on a metric |
| Metric name                 | Percentage CPU          |
| Scale out CPU threshold (%) | 80                      |
| Scale out Operation         | Increase count by 1     |
| Scale in CPU threshold (%)  | 25                      |
| Scale in Operation          | Decrease count by 1     |
| Minimum number of instances | 2                       |
| Maximum number of instances | 4                       |
| Default number of instances | 2                       |

- <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2948.jpeg" style="width:4.04306in;height:0.9625in" alt="IMG_259" />

- 

- <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2949.jpeg" style="width:5.04931in;height:0.39583in" alt="IMG_260" />

> Make sure you save the Custom Autoscale policy once configured.
>
> Want to learn more? Review the documentation on [autoscale with Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machine-scale-sets/virtual-machine-scale-sets-autoscale-overview).

→ Note:

Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets (VMSS) allow you to deploy and manage a group of identical, load-balanced VMs automatically.\
They provide high availability, automatic scaling, and simplified management compared to managing individual VMs.\
VMSS integrates with Azure Load Balancer and Autoscale to handle traffic spikes efficiently and reduce operational overhead.

#### Configure Scale-Out Rule

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 42%" />
<col style="width: 57%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><p>→ Adding a rule, with below key configurations</p>
<p>→ Metric name == percentage cpu</p>
<p>→ operator = greater than</p>
<p>→ operation = increase county by</p>
<p>→ instance count = 1</p>
<p>→ Click Add after configuring</p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→This rule enables auto-scaling by monitoring the percentage CPU usage. When the CPU exceeds a specified threshold (greater than), it triggers an increase in instance count by 1. This adds a new virtual machine to handle the load, ensuring the system scales out to maintain performance. The process continues as needed based on the metric.</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

![](subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2982.webp)![](subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2984.webp)<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_535.webp" style="width:3.75417in;height:6.68264in" alt="{58483048-455C-461E-A755-CD6549E01CC7}" />

#### Configure Scale-IN Rule

→ Now that we have added scale-out rule, we also need to have ‘**scale-in**’ rule

→ Click +Add a rule again

<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_536.webp" style="width:4.85694in;height:2.31319in" alt="{77CCC72C-97A6-42C3-ACF7-1092F8A31678}" />

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 36%" />
<col style="width: 63%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><p>→ Scale-in Rule</p>
<p>→ metric name=percentage cpu</p>
<p>→ operator = less than</p>
<p>→ metric threshold=25</p>
<p>→ operation=decrease county by</p>
<p>→ instance count=1</p>
<p>→ contiune by ‘add’</p></td>
<td><p>This scale-in rule monitors the percentage CPU usage. When the CPU falls below 25%, it triggers a decrease in instance count by 1. This removes a virtual machine to optimize resources, with the process continuing by adding more conditions if specified.</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

![](subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2989.webp)![](subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2990.webp)<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_537.webp" style="width:3.46319in;height:6.15in" alt="{9DE7A8D8-7F3E-422F-881A-2A82C9CEC6F3}" />

##  CreateVMSS - APP TIER 

→Create an Azure virtual machine scale set by using the https://github.com/LODSContent/ChallengeLabs_ArmResources/tree/master/ARMTemplates/201-vmss-internal-loadbalancer ARM template and the values in the following table. For any property that is not specified, use the default value.

| **Property**          | **Value**            |
|:----------------------|:---------------------|
| Resource group        | corp-datalod52838879 |
| Vm Sku                | Standard_A1_v2       |
| Ubuntu OS Version     | 16.04-LTS            |
| Vmss Name             | vm52838879           |
| Instance Count        | 2                    |
| Admin Username        | Student              |
| Authentication Type   | Password             |
| Admin Password Or Key | Azure!JGa51\*p#hBn3  |

→In a new browser window, view the https://github.com/LODSContent/ChallengeLabs_ArmResources/tree/master/ARMTemplates/201-vmss-internal-loadbalancer sample template on GitHub, and then select Deploy to Azure to deploy the template to Azure.

> <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2996.jpeg" style="width:2.06528in;height:0.83681in" alt="IMG_256" />

- On the Custom deployment blade, on the Basics page, in Project details, in Resource group, select corp-datalod52838879.

- In Instance details, in Vm Sku, ensure that Standard_A1_v2 is selected, in Ubuntu OS Version, ensure that 16.04-LTS is selected, in Vmss Name, enter vm52838879, and then in Instance Count, ensure that 2 is entered.

- In Admin Username, enter Student, in Authentication Type, ensure that Password is selected, and then in Admin Password Or Key, enter Azure!JGa51\*p#hBn3.

- On the Custom deployment blade, select Review + create, and then select Create to deploy the virtual machine scale set.

→The deployment will take approximately 3-5 minutes. This template will deploy a virtual machine scale set of Linux virtual machines behind a load balancer with NAT rules.

→ Configure the vm52838879 scale set to use a Custom autoscale policy by using the values in the following table. For any property that is not specified, use the default value.

| **Property**                | **Value**               |
|:----------------------------|:------------------------|
| How to scale your resource  | Custom autoscale        |
| Scale mode                  | Scale based on a metric |
| Metric name                 | Percentage CPU          |
| Scale out CPU threshold (%) | 80                      |
| Scale out Operation         | Increase count by 1     |
| Scale in CPU threshold (%)  | 25                      |
| Scale in Operation          | Decrease count by 1     |
| Minimum number of instances | 2                       |
| Maximum number of instances | 4                       |
| Default number of instances | 2                       |

- On the Azure portal menu, select All resources, and then select vm52838879 virtual machine scale set.

- On the vm52838879 service menu, in Availability + scale, select Scaling.

- On the Scaling page, in Choose how to scale your resource, select Custom autoscale.

> <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2997.jpeg" style="width:1.73819in;height:0.98542in" alt="IMG_257" />

- In Default, in Scale mode, select Scale based on a metric, and then in Rules, select the Add a rule link to add a scale out rule.

> <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2998.jpeg" style="width:3.24375in;height:0.79583in" alt="IMG_258" />

- On the Scale rule blade, in Metric name, ensure that Percentage CPU is selected, scroll down, in Operator, ensure that Greater than is selected, in Metric threshold to trigger scale action, enter 80, in Operation, ensure that Increase count by is selected, in instance count, ensure that 1 is entered, and then select Add.

> <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image2999.jpeg" style="width:3.34722in;height:1.96597in" alt="IMG_259" />

- In Rules, select the Add a rule link again to add a scale in rule.

- On the Scale rule blade, in Metric name, ensure that Percentage CPU is selected, scroll down, in Operator, select Less than, in Metric threshold to trigger scale action, enter 25, in Operation, ensure that Decrease count by is selected, in instance count, ensure that 1 is entered, and then select Add.

> <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3000.jpeg" style="width:2.35208in;height:1.42292in" alt="IMG_260" />

- In Instance limits, in Minimum, ensure that 2 is entered, in Maximum, enter 4, and then in Default ensure that 2 is entered.

> <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3001.jpeg" style="width:3.52431in;height:0.60903in" alt="IMG_261" />

- On the Scaling page, on the command bar, select Save to update the autoscale configuration.

> Want to learn more? Review the documentation on [autoscale with Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machine-scale-sets/virtual-machine-scale-sets-autoscale-overview).
>
> If you opened a new browser window for the template, you can close it now, and then return to the Azure portal in the original browser window.

## Configure NSG on FE VMSS

→ Enter the IP address for the vmfe52838879-lb-publicip Public IP address in the following text box, without leading or trailing spaces:

> vmfe52838879-lb-publicip Public IP address

- On the Azure portal menu, select All resources, and then select the vmfe52838879-lb-publicip Public IP address.

- On the Overview page, in Essentials, in IP address, locate the IP address, and then copy the value to the text box above without leading or trailing spaces.

<!-- -->

- For the vmfe52838879 virtual machine scale set, add a network security group (NSG) inbound port rule named Allow_RDP_HTTP_HTTPS to allow RDP, HTTP, and HTTPS traffic for the front-end web server tier.

<!-- -->

- On the Azure portal menu, select All resources, and then select the vmfe52838879 virtual machine scale set.

- On the vmfe52838879 service menu, in Networking, select Network settings.

- On the Network settings page, select Create port rule, and then select Inbound port rule.

- On the Add inbound security rule pane, in Destination port ranges, enter 3389,80,443, in Name, enter Allow_RDP_HTTP_HTTPS, and then select Add to add the rule.

> <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3014.jpeg" style="width:2.04514in;height:2.45972in" alt="IMG_256" />
>
> Want to learn more? Review the documentation on [Network security groups](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/network-security-groups-overview).

###  Configure NSG 

→ navigate to networking … add NSG along with Inbound Port rules

<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_542.webp" style="width:6.40764in;height:3.74514in" alt="{4AAF4CEC-450A-4B54-9472-A715DE729D1C}" />

→ Click inbound port rule

<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_543.webp" style="width:5.25in;height:1.80208in" alt="{A747E609-6026-487E-A7ED-3E84F5C2041B}" />

→ Enter details as below.

<table style="width:99%;">
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 54%" />
<col style="width: 45%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3024.webp" style="width:3.37569in;height:5.84722in" alt="{BE5DB6F9-B304-4040-B51D-32170D098574}" /></p></td>
<td><p><strong>Source</strong>: Who is allowed to initiate the traffic (set to Any, meaning from anywhere).</p>
<p><strong>Source port ranges</strong>: The port(s) on the source side (usually left as *, meaning any).</p>
<p><strong>Destination</strong>: The target resource (set to Any, meaning applies to any target in this NSG).</p>
<p><strong>Service</strong>: Predefined service (set to Custom, so ports are manually specified).</p>
<p><strong>Destination port ranges</strong>: The ports being opened —</p>
<p>3389 (RDP),</p>
<p>80 (HTTP),</p>
<p>443 (HTTPS).</p>
<p><strong>Protocol</strong>: Type of traffic (set to Any, allows both TCP and UDP).</p>
<p><strong>Action</strong>: What to do with the traffic (set to Allow).</p>
<p><strong>Priority</strong>: Rule priority (lower number = higher priority; 310 in this case).</p>
<p><strong>Name</strong>: Rule name — Allow_RDP_HTTP_HTTPS, describes purpose.</p>
<p><strong>Description</strong>: Optional note (left blank).</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

→ Notice it is added

#  Compute - VMSS - Enable HA - Scalabilty

<table style="width:87%;">

<p>You are an Administrator for Hexelo, an organization that needs to implement high availability and scalability in Azure®.</p>
<p>In this Challenge Lab, you will deploy multiple Azure virtual machine scale sets acting as web server and app server tiers. First, you will create a virtual machine scale set (VMSS) for the web server tier. Next, you will use an Azure Resource Manager (ARM) template to create a virtual machine scale set for the app server tier. Finally, you will allow connectivity to the virtual machine scale set for the web server tier.</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>→Navigate to VMSS→Availability + scale → Scaling → Custom autoscale</p>

</tr>

</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><ul>
<li><p>→On the Scale rule blade, in Metric name, ensure that Percentage CPU is selected, scroll down, in Operator, select Less than, in Metric threshold to trigger scale action, enter 25, in Operation, ensure that Decrease count by is selected, in instance count, ensure that 1 is entered, and then select Add.</p></li>

<p>🡪Before we create the availability sets, let us understand this picture.</p>
<p>🡪We can start with a topmost layer called Region.</p>
<p>🡪Each region has multiple zones.</p>
<p>🡪Each zone has multiple Datacenters, physically separated.</p>
<p>🡪Each datacenter has multiple racks, where each rack has its own power and network link.</p>
<p>🡪Each rack has multiple blade servers (or physical servers).</p>
<p>🡪Each physical server has multiple virtualized VMs.</p></td>
</tr>

#  Compute - VM using Powershell and install WebServer (First Attempt)

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>Understand the scenario</p>
<ul>
<li><p>You are an Administrator for Hexelo, an organization that is migrating virtual machines to Azure.</p></li>
<li><p>In this Challenge Lab, you will be using Azure Cloud-Shell to manage the virtual machines with PowerShell. First, you will configure Azure Cloud Shell for use with PowerShell. Next, you will install Windows Web Server. Finally, you will test connection to the web service.</p></li>
</ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3245.webp" style="width:7.6875in;height:1.95208in" /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>Sign in to the Azure portal as Connor-52871925@cloudslice.onmicrosoft.com using RSf82+r!aJ!q as the password.</p>
<p>Configure an Azure Cloud Shell PowerShell session by using the existing PSRGlod52871925 resource group, the existing storage account, and a new file share named shell.</p>
<ul>
<li><p>In the Azure Portal, in the global controls, select the Cloud Shell icon.</p></li>
<li><p>In the Welcome to Azure Cloud Shell dialog box, select PowerShell.</p></li>
<li><p>In the Getting started window, select Mount storage account, in Storage account subscription, select the existing Challenge Labs option, and then select Apply.</p></li>
<li><p>In the Mount storage account window, ensure that Select existing storage account is selected, and then select Next.</p></li>
<li><p>In the Select storage account window, in Resource group, select PSRGlod52871925.</p></li>
<li><p>In Storage account name, select the existing storage account.</p></li>
<li><p>In File share, select Create a file share, in Name, enter shell, select Ok, and then in the Select storage account window, select Select.</p></li>
</ul>
<blockquote>
<p>Want to learn more? Review the documentation on <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cloud-shell/get-started/ephemeral?tabs=azurecli">Azure Cloud Shell</a>.</p>
</blockquote></td>
</tr>

## Install Webserver and test 

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><ul>
<li><p>On DevSystem1, install the Web Server role.</p></li>
</ul>
<blockquote>
<p>Expand this hint for guidance on installing the Web Server role.</p>
</blockquote>
<ul>
<li><p>In the Cloud Shell window, run the following command:</p></li>
</ul>
<blockquote>
<p>Invoke-AzVMRunCommand -ResourceGroupName PSRGlod52871925 -VMName DevSystem1 -CommandID RunPowerShellScript -ScriptString {Install-WindowsFeature web-server}</p>
<p>This command is being sent to the DevSystem1 virtual machine. The installation of the Web Server role will take several minutes to complete. Wait until the command is finished before continuing.</p>
</blockquote>
<ul>
<li><p>After the installation is complete, display the default website on DevSystem1, and then, if it is not running, start it.</p></li>
</ul>
<blockquote>
<p>Expand this hint for guidance on displaying the default website.</p>
</blockquote>
<ul>
<li><p>Run the following PowerShell cmdlet to display the default web site:</p></li>
</ul>
<blockquote>
<p>Invoke-AzVMRunCommand -ResourceGroupName PSRGlod52871925 -VMName DevSystem1 -CommandID RunPowerShellScript -ScriptString {Get-Website}</p>
<p>This command is being sent to the DevSystem1 virtual machine. The command could take up to one minute to complete. Wait until the results are returned from the command before continuing.</p>
</blockquote>
<ul>
<li><p>Create a new HTTP Allow rule on the devsystem1-nsg1 network to allow access to the new web site.</p></li>
</ul>
<blockquote>
<p>Expand this hint for guidance on creating an allow rule.</p>
<p>powershell</p>
<p>Get-AzNetworkSecurityGroup -Name devsystem1-nsg1 -ResourceGroupName PSRGlod52871925 | Add-AzNetworkSecurityRuleConfig -Name http-rule -Description "Allow HTTP" -Access Allow -Protocol Tcp -Direction Inbound -Priority 100 -SourceAddressPrefix Internet -SourcePortRange * -DestinationAddressPrefix * -DestinationPortRange 80 |</p>
<p>Set-AzNetworkSecurityGroup</p>
<p>Want to learn more? Review the documentation on <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/network-security-groups-overview">Azure Network Security Groups</a>.</p>
</blockquote></td>
</tr>
<tr>

## Configure VNET

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><p>→Create a new subnet configuration stored in a variable named $subnetConfig with a subnet name FrontEnd, and an address prefix 192.168.1.0/24 by using the New-AzVirtualNetworkSubnetConfig PowerShell cmdlet.</p>
<p>Expand this hint for guidance on creating a subnet configuration.</p>
<p>→Run the following command to configure the subnet:</p>
<p>$subnetConfig = New-AzVirtualNetworkSubnetConfig -Name FrontEnd -AddressPrefix 192.168.1.0/24</p>
<p>Want to learn more? Review the documentation on <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/az.network/new-azvirtualnetworksubnetconfig">New-AzVirtualNetworkSubnetConfig</a>.</p>
<p>→Create a new Virtual Network named ChallengeVnet in a variable named $vnet with an address prefix of 192.168.0.0/16, and the subnet configuration you created in the previous step by using the New-AzVirtualNetwork PowerShell cmdlet.</p>
<p>→Run the following command to create a virtual network:</p>
<p>$vnet = New-AzVirtualNetwork -ResourceGroupName $resourceGroup -Location $location -Name ChallengeVnet -AddressPrefix 192.168.0.0/16 -Subnet $subnetConfig</p>
<p>Want to learn more? Review the documentation on <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/az.network/new-azvirtualnetwork">New-AzVirtualNetwork</a>.</p>
<p>→Create a new Static Public IP Address named challengepubdns52738772 in a variable named $pip with an idle timeout set to 5 minutes by using the New-AzPublicIpAddress PowerShell cmdlet.</p>
<p>→Run the following command to create a public IP address and specify a DNS name:</p>
<p>$pip = New-AzPublicIpAddress -ResourceGroupName $resourceGroup -Location $location -Name "challengepubdns52738772" -AllocationMethod Static -IdleTimeoutInMinutes 5</p>
<p>Want to learn more? Review the documentation on <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/az.network/new-azpublicipaddress">New-AzPublicIpAddress</a>.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3306.webp" style="width:7.6875in;height:4.80486in" /></p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Configure Network Interface / NSG

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><p>→<strong>Create a network security group Inbound rule</strong> named ChallengeRDP in a variable named $nsgRuleRDP that allows RDP access on TCP port 3389 with a priority of 500 by using the New-AzNetworkSecurityRuleConfig PowerShell cmdlet.</p>
<p>→Run the following command to create an inbound network security group rule for port 3389:</p>
<p>$nsgRuleRDP = New-AzNetworkSecurityRuleConfig -Name ChallengeRDP -Protocol TCP -Direction Inbound -Priority 500 -SourceAddressPrefix * -SourcePortRange * -DestinationAddressPrefix * -DestinationPortRange 3389 -Access Allow</p>
<p>Want to learn more? Review the documentation on <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/az.network/new-aznetworksecurityruleconfig">New-AzNetworkSecurityRuleConfig</a>.</p>
<p>→<strong>Create a new network security group</strong> named ChallengeNSG in a variable named $nsg and associate the network security group rule that you created in the previous step by using the New-AzNetworkSecurityGroup PowerShell cmdlet.</p>
<p>Expand this hint for guidance on creating a network security group.</p>
<p>→Run the following command to create a network security group named ChallengeNSG:</p>
<p>$nsg = New-AzNetworkSecurityGroup -ResourceGroupName $resourceGroup -Location $location -Name ChallengeNSG -SecurityRules $nsgRuleRDP</p>
<p>Want to learn more? Review the documentation on <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/az.network/new-aznetworksecurityruleconfig">New-AzNetworkSecurityGroup</a>.</p>
<p>→<strong>Create a new network interface</strong> named ChallengeNIC in a variable named $nic associated to the FrontEnd subnet, public IP address, and network security group you created in earlier steps by using the New-AzNetworkInterface PowerShell cmdlet.</p>
<p>Expand this hint for guidance on creating a network interface.</p>
<p>→Run the following command to create a virtual network interface:</p>
<p>$nic = New-AzNetworkInterface -Name ChallengeNIC -ResourceGroupName $resourceGroup -Location $location -SubnetId $vnet.Subnets[0].Id -PublicIpAddressId $pip.Id -NetworkSecurityGroupId $nsg.Id</p>
<p>Want to learn more? Review the documentation on <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/az.network/new-aznetworkinterface">New-AzNetworkInterface</a>.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3307.webp" style="width:7.6875in;height:3.32639in" /></p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Create VM - Command Line 

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><p>→Create a new VM configuration in a variable named $vmConfig setting the VMName to $vmName, the Standard SecurityType, the Standard_B2ms size, the latest 2022-datacenter-azure-edition-core Windows image, the credential variable $cred and the network interface you created earler by using the New-AzVMConfig PowerShell cmdlet.</p>
<p>Expand this hint for guidance on creating a virtual machine configuration.</p>
<p>→Run the following command to create a virtual machine configuration:</p>
<p>$vmConfig = New-AzVMConfig -VMName $vmName -VMSize Standard_B2ms | Set-AzVMOperatingSystem -Windows -ComputerName $vmName -Credential $cred | Set-AzVMSourceImage -PublisherName MicrosoftWindowsServer -Offer WindowsServer -Skus 2022-datacenter-azure-edition-core -Version latest | Add-AzVMNetworkInterface -Id $nic.Id</p>
<p>Want to learn more? Review the documentation on <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/az.compute/new-azvmconfig">New-AzVMConfig</a>.</p>
<p>→Deploy a virtual machine by using your $vmConfig virtual machine configuration by using the New-AzVM PowerShell cmdlet.</p>
<p>→Run the following command to deploy a virtual machine:</p>
<p>New-AzVM -ResourceGroupName $resourceGroup -Location $location -VM $vmConfig</p>

<p>Want to learn more? Review the documentation on <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/az.compute/new-azvm">New-AzVM</a>.</p>
<p>Want to learn more? Review the documentation on using PowerShell to create an <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/windows/quick-create-powershell">Azure Virtual Machine</a>.</p></td>

## Configure VNET

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><p>→Create a new subnet configuration stored in a variable named $subnetConfig with a subnet name FrontEnd, and an address prefix 192.168.1.0/24 by using the New-AzVirtualNetworkSubnetConfig PowerShell cmdlet.</p>
<p>→Run the following command to configure the subnet:</p>
<p>$subnetConfig = New-AzVirtualNetworkSubnetConfig -Name FrontEnd -AddressPrefix 192.168.1.0/24</p>
<p>→Want to learn more? Review the documentation on <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/az.network/new-azvirtualnetworksubnetconfig">New-AzVirtualNetworkSubnetConfig</a>.</p>
<p>→Create a new Virtual Network named ChallengeVnet in a variable named $vnet with an address prefix of 192.168.0.0/16, and the subnet configuration you created in the previous step by using the New-AzVirtualNetwork PowerShell cmdlet.</p>
<p>→Run the following command to create a virtual network:</p>
<p>$vnet = New-AzVirtualNetwork -ResourceGroupName $resourceGroup -Location $location -Name ChallengeVnet -AddressPrefix 192.168.0.0/16 -Subnet $subnetConfig</p>
<p>Want to learn more? Review the documentation on <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/az.network/new-azvirtualnetwork">New-AzVirtualNetwork</a>.</p>
<p>→Create a new Static Public IP Address named challengepubdns52738772 in a variable named $pip with an idle timeout set to 5 minutes by using the New-AzPublicIpAddress PowerShell cmdlet.</p>
<p>Expand this hint for guidance on creating a static public IP address.</p>
<p>→Run the following command to create a public IP address and specify a DNS name:</p>
<p>$pip = New-AzPublicIpAddress -ResourceGroupName $resourceGroup -Location $location -Name "challengepubdns52738772" -AllocationMethod Static -IdleTimeoutInMinutes 5</p>
<p>Want to learn more? Review the documentation on <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/az.network/new-azpublicipaddress">New-AzPublicIpAddress</a>.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Creates a subnet configuration object named "FrontEnd" with the address range 192.168.1.0/24.</p>
<p>→Creates a virtual network named "ChallengeVnet" with the address range 192.168.0.0/16 and applies the "FrontEnd" subnet configuration.</p>
<p>→Creates a static public IP address named "challengepubdns52738772" with a 5-minute idle timeout.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3306.webp" style="width:7.6875in;height:4.80486in" /></p></td>

<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Creates a network security rule named "ChallengeRDP" allowing inbound TCP traffic on port 3389 (RDP) from any source to any destination.</p>
<p>→Creates a network security group named "ChallengeNSG" with the "ChallengeRDP" rule applied.</p>
<p>→Creates a network interface named "ChallengeNIC" and associates it with the first subnet of the VNet, the public IP, and the network security group.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Create a network security group Inbound rule named ChallengeRDP in a variable named $nsgRuleRDP that allows RDP access on TCP port 3389 with a priority of 500 by using the New-AzNetworkSecurityRuleConfig PowerShell cmdlet.</p>
<p>→Run the following command to create an inbound network security group rule for port 3389:</p>
<p>$nsgRuleRDP = New-AzNetworkSecurityRuleConfig -Name ChallengeRDP -Protocol TCP -Direction Inbound -Priority 500 -SourceAddressPrefix * -SourcePortRange * -DestinationAddressPrefix * -DestinationPortRange 3389 -Access Allow</p>
<p>Want to learn more? Review the documentation on <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/az.network/new-aznetworksecurityruleconfig">New-AzNetworkSecurityRuleConfig</a>.</p>
<p>→Create a new network security group named ChallengeNSG in a variable named $nsg and associate the network security group rule that you created in the previous step by using the New-AzNetworkSecurityGroup PowerShell cmdlet.</p>
<p>→ Run the following command to create a network security group named ChallengeNSG:</p>
<p>$nsg = New-AzNetworkSecurityGroup -ResourceGroupName $resourceGroup -Location $location -Name ChallengeNSG -SecurityRules $nsgRuleRDP</p>
<p>Want to learn more? Review the documentation on <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/az.network/new-aznetworksecurityruleconfig">New-AzNetworkSecurityGroup</a>.</p>
<p>→Create a new network interface named ChallengeNIC in a variable named $nic associated to the FrontEnd subnet, public IP address, and network security group you created in earlier steps by using the New-AzNetworkInterface PowerShell cmdlet.</p>
<p>→Run the following command to create a virtual network interface:</p>

<p>Want to learn more? Review the documentation on <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/az.network/new-aznetworkinterface">New-AzNetworkInterface</a>.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3307.webp" style="width:7.6875in;height:3.32639in" /></p></td>

#  Entra ID - App Registrations - Managed Identity 

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Azure App Registration in Microsoft Entra ID creates an <strong>identity</strong> for applications to securely integrate with the Microsoft identity platform.</p>
<p>→ It establishes a trust relationship, enabling apps to authenticate users and access protected resources using protocols like OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect.</p>
<p>→The process generates a unique Application ID and supports configuration of permissions, secrets, or certificates for secure access control.</p>
<p>→Azure App Registration in Microsoft Entra ID is commonly used for system-to-system communication.</p>
<p>→It enables access to APIs (Eg. Microsoft Graph) via client credentials.</p>
<p>→App registration DOES NOT store any users data.</p>
<p>→Entra ID is managed service, unlike other IdP like KeyCloak.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Typical user and their access 

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 46%" />
<col style="width: 53%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Assuming there is a user by name Bob, who has an account in Entra ID.</p>
<p>→That particualr user (or his account) has certain roles, which inturn can access certin resources on Azure.</p>
<p>→Eg. Bob can access an RG, which inturn has a VM, that has been enabled using IAM.</p>
<p>→Bob undergoines certain Authentication process to access the Entra ID viz., Username/Password or MFA or CA (Conditional Access etc)</p>
<p>→Simple Diagram as below.</p>
<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3330.webp" style="width:3.00486in;height:2.13472in" alt="{ED78BF21-E2CF-4CB3-BF0D-6E9A55E117E3}" /></p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3331.webp" style="width:3.92986in;height:2.46806in" alt="{D6CA92AF-24F7-4824-9F61-79A5DDC17CAE}" /></p>
<p>→If we observe closely Bob is access portal, who has to have permissions to view all the resources of azure.</p>
<p>→Upon logging in they will have basic view permissions, like EntraID/Subscriptions etc, but nothing more than that.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Managed Identity (or Service Principal) 

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Assuming we have an app, Eg. ‘<strong>Logic App’</strong> that wants to read some secrets from <strong>AKV</strong>.</p>
<p>→AKV is hosts typically, secrets, keys, certs and can be consumed by various other services.</p>
<p>→In order to do that the Logic App relies or has something called ‘<strong>managed identity’</strong> of Entra ID.</p>
<p>→Behind ‘managed identity’ is an Entra ID object called <strong>Service Principal,</strong> which is the actual account that Logic app will be using it a runtime.</p>
<p>→Here, Logic App is like a person ‘Bob’ which is access some resource.</p>
<p>→The Logi App itself is ‘authenticated’ to Managed Identity. (notice the green arrows)</p>
<p>→Resaons why it is called ‘maanged’, because it is AZURE that manages it.</p>
<p>→ This Managed ID is essentially sitting ‘on’ entra id.</p>
<p>→Once this is done, we give THIS managed identity, ‘ability’ to go to AKV and then read/write/etc.</p>
<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3332.webp" style="width:7.52639in;height:3.87708in" alt="{0375C476-2715-45CB-B597-5CD3A1E079E3}" /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→In sections ahead, there is a LOGIC APP, that is going to fetch data from KeyVault.</p>
<p>→We already have AKV created with a secret.</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## App Registration (Some background about this) 

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Before we ‘register an app’, it is important to understand the concept a bit more.</p>
<p>→Like mentioned above, a Logic App is accessing a resource on azure. Similarly assuming a WebApp wants to access a resource.</p>
<p>→Below is a high-level picture of understanding, where two DIFFERENT usecases are there.</p>
<p>→One on the left is typical Client Credentials Grant</p>
<p>→Second one on the right is Authorization Code Grant</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3359.webp" style="width:7.68611in;height:3.40069in" /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→With above picture on the left, in order for the WebApp to access resources, it must have an identity.</p>
<p>→ To create the identity, we will use the feature of ‘application registration’ option in Entra ID</p>
<p>→Once we create application (or register), it creates an APPLICATION OBJECT, which has Object ID</p>
<p>→The application registration is global level activity.</p>
<p>→From that APPLICATION OBJECT, there is a SERVICE PRINCIPAL gets created automatically.</p>
<p>→This Service Principal is nothing but ‘identity’.</p>
<p>→This Service Principal MUST BE now assigned with necessary permissions to access resources.</p>
<p>→Below diagram depicts what is mentioned above vs how to see them on Entra ID Sample Application.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3360.webp" style="width:6.45278in;height:4.27361in" /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Permissions given to the service principal.</p>
<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3361.webp" style="width:4.23056in;height:2.81597in" alt="{49EB2088-E27F-4024-87E8-B69B29CFDBE6}" /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→When we click the ‘service principal’ we get below which is same as previously seen details</p>
<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3362.webp" style="width:5.72014in;height:3.38264in" /></p>
<p>→Note that, though this is a Service Principal, however it is broadly called as ‘Enterprise Application’ which has ton of other configurations that gets carried.</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>→Here, we are not focussing on the ‘graph api’ but on the Azure Services.</p>

</tr>

<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>→Once we have the details click the Access Control (IAM) option.</p>

</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>→Notice we have various Roles that are mapped to various users.</p>

<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>→Click +Add →Add role assignment option</p>

</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>→Notice we get lots of power full permissions like owner etc, but we do not want the ‘service principal’ that we have to have that level of permissions.</p>

<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3410.webp" /><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3411.webp" style="width:5.80069in;height:3.43958in" alt="{3EB1B88F-A2EC-49D5-8B75-0AB3FA36E35C}" /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>→So choose a simple ‘Reader’ role and select ‘next’</p>
<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3412.webp" /><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3413.webp" /><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3414.webp" style="width:6.73819in;height:3.29306in" alt="{43AA7DB8-88CE-4114-8A31-40E4E9F9D9D2}" /></p></td>

<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>→We get below where we need to add members.</p>
<p>→Note that managed identity and ‘service principal’ are kind of same, however, the SERVICE PRINCIPAL, that we have is CREATED BY US.</p>
<p>→So we do not choose it as ‘managed identity’</p>
<p>→Click +Select members</p>
<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3415.webp" style="width:6.04167in;height:4.16667in" alt="{A6B42E0F-77E2-473A-99F8-C9CCE12A5810}" /></p></td>

<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>→Continue with ‘next’</p>

</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>→Continue with ‘permanent’. Based on the need we can make it time bound or PIM driven.</p>
<p>→Review + Assign</p>
<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3418.webp" style="width:5.53403in;height:3.69861in" alt="{7636AD66-9667-42A3-AF6D-A5EA39C0AECD}" /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>→ Now notice the service principal is listed here as ‘Reader’.</p>
<p>→Initially it was not there.</p>
<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3419.webp" style="width:7.67986in;height:3.53542in" alt="{951AC54A-9AA2-467C-82A2-D926EAD3D611}" /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>→Now use the curl commands ‘first’ to fetch the token and then use it to access the resources.</p>

<p>→ FETCH subscriptions :</p>

<p>→Fetch Resource groups under a subscription’</p>
<p>curl -X GET https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/{<mark>subscription-id</mark>}/resourcegroups?api-version=2021-04-01 -H "Authorization: Bearer <removed>

## Management APIs vs Graph APIs

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 60%" />
<col style="width: 39%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>→In azure there are two different sets of APIs to access various resources.</p>
<p>→Management APIs are meant to access the actual resources on Azure.</p>
<p>→Graph APIs are meant to access the M365 services like Sharepoint, Emails, etc</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3469.webp" style="width:4.24167in;height:3.86389in" /></p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>← Notice the boxed items in red for better understanding.</p>
<p>←Endpoints are as below.</p>
<p>←Azure Management APIs Endpoint:</p>
<p><a href="https://management.azure.com/">https://management.azure.com/</a></p>
<p>←Microsoft Graph APIs Endpoint:</p>
<p><a href="https://graph.microsoft.com/">https://graph.microsoft.com/</a></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><ul>
<li><p>Azure Management APIs Endpoint: https://management.azure.com/</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Virtual Machines</p></li>
<li><p>Resource Groups</p></li>
<li><p>Subscriptions</p></li>
<li><p>Storage Accounts</p></li>
<li><p>App Services</p></li>
<li><p>Azure Functions</p></li>
<li><p>Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)</p></li>
<li><p>Virtual Networks</p></li>
<li><p>Azure SQL Databases</p></li>
<li><p>Azure Cosmos DB</p></li>
</ul></li>
</ul>
<ul>
<li><p>Microsoft Graph APIs Endpoint: https://graph.microsoft.com/ SharePoint</p>
<ul>
<li><p>OneDrive</p></li>
<li><p>Outlook/Exchange (Emails, Calendars, Contacts)</p></li>
<li><p>Microsoft Teams</p></li>
<li><p>Azure Active Directory (Users, Groups, Permissions)</p></li>
<li><p>Planner</p></li>
<li><p>OneNote</p></li>
<li><p>Excel</p></li>
</ul></li>
</ul>
<ul>
<li><p>Azure Key Vault Endpoint: https://&lt;vault-name&gt;.vault.azure.net/ Secrets</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Keys</p></li>
<li><p>Certificates</p></li>
</ul></li>
</ul>
<ul>
<li><p>Other Azure Service-Specific Endpoints:</p></li>
<li><p>Azure Blob Storage: https://&lt;storage-account&gt;.blob.core.windows.net/</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Blobs</p></li>
<li><p>Containers</p></li>
</ul></li>
<li><p>Azure Table Storage: https://&lt;storage-account&gt;.table.core.windows.net/</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Tables</p></li>
</ul></li>
<li><p>Azure Queue Storage: https://&lt;storage-account&gt;.queue.core.windows.net/</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Queues</p></li>
</ul></li>
<li><p>Azure File Storage: https://&lt;storage-account&gt;.file.core.windows.net/</p>
<ul>
<li><p>File Shares</p></li>
</ul></li>
<li><p>Azure SQL Database: https://&lt;server-name&gt;.database.windows.net/</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Databases</p></li>
<li><p>SQL Instances</p></li>
</ul></li>
<li><p>Azure Cosmos DB: https://&lt;account-name&gt;.documents.azure.com/</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Databases</p></li>
<li><p>Collections</p></li>
</ul></li>
<li><p>Azure Event Hubs: https://&lt;namespace&gt;.servicebus.windows.net/</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Event Hubs</p></li>
</ul></li>
<li><p>Azure Service Bus: https://&lt;namespace&gt;.servicebus.windows.net/</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Queues</p></li>
<li><p>Topics</p></li>
<li><p>Subscriptions</p></li>
</ul></li>
<li><p>Azure Cognitive Services: https://&lt;resource-name&gt;.cognitiveservices.azure.com/</p>
<ul>
<li><p>Text Analytics</p></li>
<li><p>Computer Vision</p></li>
<li><p>Speech Services</p></li>
</ul></li>
<li><p>Azure API Management: https://&lt;service-name&gt;.azure-api.net/</p>
<ul>

</ul></li>
</ul></td>

<li><p>You learn to create a staging slot and swap with the production slot.</p></li>

<li><p>The hardware is nearing end-of-life and will soon need to be replaced.</p></li>
<li><p>Your organization wants to avoid new hardware costs by using Azure to host the websites.</p></li>
</ul></td>

## Create DNS Zone

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 53%" />
<col style="width: 46%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3566.webp" style="width:3.36597in;height:1.38472in" /></p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_613.webp" style="width:3.40903in;height:2.64097in" /></p>
<p>🡪Provide RG</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_614.webp" style="width:3.96319in;height:1.67778in" /></p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>🡨Provide the name as created in the domain registrar.</p>
<p>🡨Eg. cloudcognoscente.co.in</p>
<p>🡨Continue with ‘review + create’</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_615.webp" style="width:6.79167in;height:3.06042in" /></p>
<p>🡪When we create a DNS Zone it creates nameservers as shown.</p>
<p>→Azure DNS Zones is for <strong>hosting</strong> and <strong>managing</strong> DNS domains, providing reliable and secure domain name resolution.</p>
<p>→A <strong>record set</strong> is a collection of DNS records within a zone (e.g., A, CNAME, MX) that share the same name and type, defining how a domain or subdomain resolves to an IP or another resource.</p>
<p>→Nameservers are authoritative servers assigned to a DNS zone, responsible for responding to DNS queries and directing traffic to the correct resources.</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Check Record Sets – Copy the same to be used ahead. 

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>🡪Navigate to Record Sets</p>
<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3577.webp" /><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3578.webp" /><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3579.webp" /><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3580.webp" /><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3581.webp" style="width:7.12292in;height:2.09375in" /></p>
<p>🡪Here we can see two record sets viz., NS and SOA</p>
<p>🡪NS stands for Nameserver and SOA stands for <strong>Start of Authority</strong>.</p>
<p>🡪NS has all the values viz., primary + secondary.</p>
<p>🡪SOA has primary DNS server details that is responsible for domain name resolution.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>Note:</p>
<p>→When we create a DNS zone in Azure DNS, <strong>two</strong> record sets are automatically created.</p>
<p>→One: the SOA (Start of Authority) record set</p>
<p>→Two: the NS (Name Server) record set.</p>
<p>→These are essential for the DNS zone to function properly and are mandated by DNS standards.</p>
<p>→<strong>SOA</strong>: record is a key piece of information in a DNS zone that acts like a "control center" for the domain.</p>
<p>→ It tells the internet who is in charge of the domain, which server has the main DNS records, and how often those records should be checked or updated.</p>
<p>→Think of it as the ID card for your DNS zone, providing essential details to keep everything running smoothly.</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Add a record set – Type ‘a’

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 55%" />
<col style="width: 11%" />
<col style="width: 33%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td colspan="3" style="text-align: left;"><p>🡪Navigate to DNS Zone that is created, click ‘RecordSets’</p>
<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3624.webp" /><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3625.webp" style="width:5.58889in;height:3.13542in" /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3626.webp" /><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3627.webp" /><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3628.webp" style="width:4.79236in;height:2.78472in" /></p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>🡪Click Add.</p>
<p>🡪We will be adding ‘A’ record set which basically maps a ‘domain’ to ‘ip address’.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_629.webp" style="width:3.55972in;height:3.9625in" /></p></td>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>🡨Here we will be adding the IP address.</p>
<p>🡨Note that we can add a custom name like ‘jenkins’ / ‘gitlab’ / ‘jboss’ etc in the name.</p>
<p>🡨This way if our domain name is a ‘wild-card’ one, we can configure multiple record sets and map them to either same IP address or different public IP address on the backend.</p>
<p><strong>🡨'Name' field:</strong><br />
This sets the subdomain prefix. For example, if you enter app, it creates the record app.cloudcognoscente.co.in.</p>
<p><strong>🡨Multiple IPs:</strong><br />
We can enter multiple IP addresses. When the domain is queried, <strong>DNS round-robin</strong> is used—IP addresses are returned in a rotating order, distributing traffic across them.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="3" style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3633.webp" style="width:5.85278in;height:3.54931in" /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="3" style="text-align: left;"><p>🡪The record types are as below.</p>
<p>A – Maps a domain to an IPv4 address.</p>
<p>AAAA – Maps a domain to an IPv6 address.</p>
<p>CAA – Specifies which certificate authorities can issue SSL certs for the domain.</p>
<p>CNAME – Points a subdomain to another domain name, not an IP.</p>
<p>MX – Directs email to mail servers.</p>
<p>NS – Delegates a subdomain to name servers.</p>
<p>SRV – Defines location of specific services (e.g., SIP, LDAP).</p>
<p>TXT – Stores text-based data like SPF records or domain verification.</p>
<p>PTR – Maps an IP address to a domain name (reverse DNS).</p>
<p>DS – Used in DNSSEC to authenticate delegated zones.</p>
<p>TLSA – Associates TLS certificates with domain names via DNS.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="3" style="text-align: left;"><p>🡪After mapping the A Record, we can execute in the browser and check the result.</p>
<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3634.webp" style="width:7.60486in;height:1.98958in" /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="3" style="text-align: left;"><p>Important:</p>
<p>We can manage DNS directly at your <strong>domain registrar</strong> like <strong>GoDaddy</strong>, instead of using Azure DNS.</p>
<p>In GoDaddy:</p>
<ol type="1">
<li><p>Go to <strong>My Products &gt; Domains &gt; DNS</strong>.</p></li>
<li><p>Under <strong>DNS Management</strong>, add an <strong>A record</strong> pointing your domain (e.g., @ or www) to your server's IP address.</p></li>
</ol></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

#  Container Instances

## Introduction

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Your organization has a web application that runs on a virtual machine in your on-premises data center.</p>
<p>→The organization wants to move all applications to the cloud but doesn't want to have a large number of servers to manage.</p>
<p>→You decide to evaluate Azure Container Instances and Docker.</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

### Architecture

|  |
|:---|
| <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3641.webp" style="width:5.69792in;height:2.52986in" alt="Diagram of the tasks." /> |
|  |

### Comparision between Container Apps vs Container Instances

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>Comparision between</p>
<table style="width:79%;">
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 26%" />
<col style="width: 26%" />
<col style="width: 26%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th style="text-align: center;">Feature</th>
<th style="text-align: center;">Azure Container Apps</th>
<th style="text-align: center;">Azure Container Instances</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;">Orchestration</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Yes (uses KEDA, Envoy, Dapr)</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">No built-in orchestration</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;">Autoscaling</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Yes (HTTP scale, event-driven via KEDA)</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Limited (manual or scheduled restart)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;">Ingress Support</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Built-in with traffic splitting</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Basic IP/port exposure</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;">Microservices Support</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Yes, supports Dapr for service discovery</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">No native microservices support</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;">Startup Time</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Slower (cold start on scale-to-zero)</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Faster (always-on unless stopped)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;">Use Case</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Complex apps, microservices</td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><strong>Simple, short-lived or background jobs</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;">Pricing Model</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Consumption-based (vCPU, memory, exec)</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Per-second billing (vCPU, memory)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;">Managed Infrastructure</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Abstracts Kubernetes</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">No orchestration layer</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;">CI/CD &amp; DevOps Integration</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Strong (supports revisions, blue-green)</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Basic (manual deployment)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;">Best For</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Event-driven, scalable applications</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Quick tasks, isolated workloads</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Create ACR

<table>

#  Container Apps

## Intro

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Azure Container Apps is a serverless container service for running microservices and containerized applications.</p>
<p>→It supports features like autoscaling, traffic splitting, and Dapr for building event-driven apps.<br />
→It abstracts away Kubernetes infrastructure while still supporting cloud-native patterns.</p>
<p>→ Azure Container Apps take the concept of a managed Kubernetes cluster a step further and manages the cluster environment as well as provides other managed services on top of the cluster.</p>
<p>→Unlike an Azure Kubernetes cluster, where you must still manage the cluster, an Azure Container Apps instance removes some of the complexity to setting up a Kubernetes cluster.</p>
<p>→By default, the Azure container app that you create will accept traffic on port 80 using the sample Hello World application.</p>
<p>→Azure Container Apps will provide a DNS name for the application.</p>
<p>→Copy and navigate to this URL to ensure that the application is up and running.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>Lab scenario</p>
<p>Your organization has a web application that runs on a virtual machine in your on-premises data center. The organization wants to move all applications to the cloud but doesn't want to have a large number of servers to manage. You decide to evaluate Azure Container Apps.</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Comparision between Container Apps vs Container Instances

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>Comparision between</p>
<table style="width:79%;">
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 26%" />
<col style="width: 26%" />
<col style="width: 26%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th style="text-align: center;">Feature</th>
<th style="text-align: center;">Azure Container Apps</th>
<th style="text-align: center;">Azure Container Instances</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;">Orchestration</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Yes (uses KEDA, Envoy, Dapr)</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">No built-in orchestration</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;">Autoscaling</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Yes (HTTP scale, event-driven via KEDA)</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Limited (manual or scheduled restart)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;">Ingress Support</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Built-in with traffic splitting</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Basic IP/port exposure</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;">Microservices Support</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Yes, supports Dapr for service discovery</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">No native microservices support</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;">Startup Time</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Slower (cold start on scale-to-zero)</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Faster (always-on unless stopped)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><strong>Use Case</strong></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><strong>Complex apps, microservices</strong></td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Simple, short-lived or background jobs</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;">Pricing Model</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Consumption-based (vCPU, memory, exec)</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Per-second billing (vCPU, memory)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;">Managed Infrastructure</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Abstracts Kubernetes</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">No orchestration layer</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;">CI/CD &amp; DevOps Integration</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Strong (supports revisions, blue-green)</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Basic (manual deployment)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;">Best For</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Event-driven, scalable applications</td>
<td style="text-align: left;">Quick tasks, isolated workloads</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Deploy a POD to AKS using image on ACR. 

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>apiVersion: apps/v1</p>
<p>kind: Deployment</p>
<p>metadata:</p>
<p>  name: my-deployment1</p>
<p>spec:</p>
<p>  replicas: 3</p>
<p>  selector:</p>
<p>    matchLabels:</p>
<p>      app: myaksapp-pod1</p>
<p>  template:</p>
<p>    metadata:</p>
<p>      labels:</p>
<p>        app: myaksapp-pod1</p>
<p>    spec:</p>
<p>      nodeSelector:</p>
<p>        "beta.kubernetes.io/os": linux</p>
<p>      containers:</p>
<p>      - name: myaksapp-container</p>
<p>        image: myacr00009.azurecr.io/samples/nginx:latest</p>
<p>        ports:</p>
<p>        - containerPort: 80</p>
<p>---</p>
<p>apiVersion: v1</p>
<p>kind: Service</p>
<p>metadata:</p>
<p>  name: my-service1</p>
<p>spec:</p>
<p>  type: LoadBalancer</p>
<p>  ports:</p>
<p>  - port: 80</p>
<p>  selector:</p>
<p>    app: myaksapp-pod1</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Above is a sample deployment.yaml file using which we can deploy a pod to AKS.</p>
<p>→Note that the key component here is the image endpoint.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Save above file to a location and run below command</p>

</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

→Understand the scenario

→You are a Security Engineer for Hexelo, an organization that needs to deploy secure, containerized applications by using the Azure® Kubernetes Service (AKS).

→In this Challenge Lab, you will configure security by using the Kubernetes Service. First, you will create an AKS cluster, and then you will assign a role-based access control (RBAC) role to the cluster.

→Next, you will connect to the AKS cluster as the administrator by using Azure Cloud Shell. Finally, you will deploy an application as a developer in the AKS cluster, and then you will verify the security of the cluster.

→Create an Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster by using the values in the following table. For any property that is not specified, use the default value.

| **Property** | **Value** |
|:---|:---|
| Resource group | corp-datalod52832822 |
| Cluster preset configuration | Dev/Test |
| Kubernetes cluster name | aks |
| Availability zones | None |
| Authentication and Authorization | Local accounts with Kubernetes RBAC |
| Node size | Standard DS2_v2 - 2 vcpus, 8 GiB memory |
| Node count (Maximum node count) | 2 |
| Enable recommended alert rules checkbox | Cleared |

- On the Azure portal home page, in Azure services, select Create a resource to display the Azure Marketplace.

- In the Azure marketplace, search for and select Kubernetes Service, and then select the Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) tile.

- On the Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) blade, select Create.<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3777.webp" style="width:2.32153in;height:1.25139in" alt="IMG_256" />

- On the Create Kubernetes cluster blade, on the Basics page, in Project details, in Resource group, select corp-datalod52832822.

- In Cluster details, in Cluster preset configuration, select Dev/Test.

- In Kubernetes cluster name, enter aks.

- In Availability zones, ensure that the Zone 1, Zone 2, and Zone 3 check boxes are cleared, and then ensure that None is displayed.

- In Authentication and Authorization, select Local accounts with Kubernetes RBAC, and then select Next.

- On the Node pools page, in Node pools, select agentpool.

- On the Update node pool blade, in Node size, select Choose a size, search for and select DS2_v2, and then select Select.

- In Maximum node count, enter 2, and then select Update.

- On the Create Kubernetes cluster blade, select the Monitoring tab.

- On the Monitoring page, in Alerts, in Enable recommended alert rules, clear the checkbox.

- Select Review + create, review the specifications, and then select Create to create the Kubernetes cluster.

> It will take approximately 3-5 minutes to deploy the AKS cluster.
>
> Azure Kubernetes Service creates a fully managed hosting cluster for containerized applications. AKS supports the open-source Kubernetes platform.
>
> Want to learn more? Review the documentation on the [Azure Kubernetes Service](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/aks/intro-kubernetes).

- Assign the Azure Kubernetes Service Cluster User Role to the User1-52832822@cloudslice.onmicrosoft.com user at the resource scope.

<!-- -->

- On the Deployment blade, select Go to resource.

- On the aks service menu, select Access control (IAM).

- On the Access control (IAM) page, in Grant access to this resource, select Add role assignment.<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3778.jpeg" style="width:3.15in;height:1.57986in" alt="IMG_257" />

- On the Add role assignment blade, on the Role page, search for and select Azure Kubernetes Service Cluster User Role, and then select Next.

- On the Members page, select +Select members.

- On the Select members blade, search for and select User1-52832822@cloudslice.onmicrosoft.com, and then select Select.

- On the Add role assignment blade, select Review + assign twice to complete the assignment.

> Ignore any authorization errors when viewing the Kubernetes Service blade. This is expected as the AKS cluster will be used for testing only.
>

## Connect to AKS as Admin 

Launch an Azure Cloud Shell Bash session by using the values in the following table. For any property that is not specified, use the default value.

| **Property**       | **Value**            |
|:-------------------|:---------------------|
| Resource group     | corp-datalod52832822 |
| Cloud Shell region | (US) East US         |
| Storage account    | cs52832822           |
| File share         | cloudshell           |

- In the Azure portal, on the navigation bar, in the global controls, select the Cloud Shell icon.

- In the Welcome to Azure Cloud Shell dialog, select Bash.

- In the Getting started dialog, select Mount storage account, in Storage account subscription, select the existing Challenge Labs option, and then select Apply.

- In the Mount storage account dialog, select I want to create a storage account, and then select Next.

- In the Create storage account dialog, in Resource group, select corp-datalod52832822.

- In Region, select (US) East US.

- In Storage account name, enter cs52832822.

- In File share, enter cloudshell, and then select Create.

> It will take approximately 1-2 minutes to initialize the Cloud Shell.

- Connect to the aks cluster in the corp-datalod52832822 resource group as admin by using the az aks get-credentials Azure command-line interface (Azure CLI) command.

<!-- -->

- Run the following command to connect to the cluster:

> az aks get-credentials --resource-group corp-datalod52832822 --name aks --admin
>
> Cloud Shell does not support the keyboard shortcut Ctrl+V for paste. Instead, select the command prompt, and then use Ctrl+Shift+V to paste.
>
> Want to learn more? Review the documentation on using [az aks get-credentials](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cli/azure/aks?view=azure-cli-latest#az-aks-get-credentials).

- Verify that the current context of the connection to the cluster is aks-admin by using the kubectl config command.

<!-- -->

- Run the following command to verify that the current context of the connection to the cluster is aks-admin:

> kubectl config current-context
>
> Want to learn more? Review the documentation on using [kubectl config](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubectl/cheatsheet/#kubectl-context-and-configuration).

- Display a list of the cluster nodes by using the kubectl get command.

<!-- -->

- Run the following command to display a list of the cluster nodes:

> kubectl get nodes
>
> There should be two nodes in the cluster.

- Repeat the previous command and send the output to a file named ~/clouddrive/ListNodes.txt.

<!-- -->

- Run the following command to save output to a file:

> kubectl get nodes \> ~/clouddrive/ListNodes.txt
>

## Connect and Deploy to AKS - as Normal User

Open an InPrivate or incognito browser window, go to the Azure portal at https://portal.azure.com/, and then sign in as User1-52832822@cloudslice.onmicrosoft.com using Gp5Cp3@\*GcNn as the password.

Launch a Cloud Shell Bash session by using the values in the following table. For any property that is not specified, use the default value.

| **Property**       | **Value**            |
|:-------------------|:---------------------|
| Resource group     | corp-datalod52832822 |
| Cloud Shell region | (US) East US         |
| Storage account    | Existing: cs52832822 |
| File share         | Existing: cloudshell |

- 

> Ignore any file share mount warnings. This is expected because the user has read-only access in the Azure portal. You can access the AKS cluster as a non-administrative user.
>
> <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3828.jpeg" style="width:5.47292in;height:1.75347in" alt="IMG_256" />

- Connect to the aks cluster in the corp-datalod52832822 resource group by using the az aks get-credentials CLI command.

<!-- -->

- Run the following command to connect to the aks cluster:

> az aks get-credentials --resource-group corp-datalod52832822 --name aks

- Verify that the current context of the connection to the cluster is aks by using the kubectl config command.

<!-- -->

- Run the following command to verify that the current context of the connection to the cluster is aks:

> kubectl config current-context

- Attempt to stop the aks cluster in the corp-datalod52832822 resource group by using the az aks stop command.

<!-- -->

- Run the following command to attempt to stop the cluster:

> az aks stop --resource-group corp-datalod52832822 --name aks
>
> This operation should fail as you are not authorized to stop the AKS cluster as a non-admin user.
>
> <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3829.jpeg" style="width:7.67986in;height:1.05972in" alt="IMG_257" />
>
> Want to learn more? Review the documentation on using [az aks stop](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cli/azure/aks?view=azure-cli-latest#az-aks-stop).

- Deploy an application named nginx-52832822 that uses the nginx container image from Docker Hub by using the kubectl create deployment command.

<!-- -->

- Run the following command to deploy the application:

> kubectl create deployment nginx-52832822 --image=nginx
>
> Want to learn more? Review the documentation on using [kubectl create deployment](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubectl/cheatsheet/#creating-objects).

- Verify that an AKS pod was created for the application by using the kubectl get command.

<!-- -->

- Run the following command to verify that a pod was created:

> kubectl get pods
>
> There should be one pod running in the AKS cluster.

- Expose the pod in the nginx-52832822 deployment to the internet for testing by using the kubectl expose deployment command.

<!-- -->

- Run the following command to expose the nginx-52832822 deployment to the internet:

> kubectl expose deployment nginx-52832822 --port=80 --type=LoadBalancer

Run the following command to identify the public IP address of the application, and then re-run the command until the value in the EXTERNAL-IP column for nginx-52832822 changes from \<pending\> to a public IP address:

kubectl get services

Record the public IP address in the following Public IP Address text box:

Public IP Address\
Open a web browser, go to http://\<PublicIP\>, and then verify that the browser displays Welcome to nginx!

### Configure Recovery Service Vaults

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 51%" />
<col style="width: 48%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>→Azure Recovery Services Vault is a <strong>storage entity</strong> in Azure.</p>
<p>→This is used to manage backups and disaster recovery.<br />
→It stores <strong>recovery points</strong> for Azure VMs, on-premises servers, and workloads like SQL and SharePoint.<br />
→It enables centralized backup management, encryption, and retention policies.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_665.webp" style="width:2.39028in;height:1.19514in" alt="A screenshot of a computer AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p>
<p>Search for ‘Recovery Service Vaults’</p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_666.webp" style="width:2.45625in;height:1.42014in" alt="A computer screen shot of a computer AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p>
<p>Click Create</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_667.webp" style="width:2.73125in;height:2.42708in" alt="A screenshot of a computer AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p>
<p>Provide details and click ‘Review + Create’ and create</p>
<p><strong>Note</strong>: Make sure that you specify the <strong>same region</strong> into which you deployed virtual machines in the previous task.</p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3868.webp" style="width:3.16667in;height:2.16597in" alt="A computer screen shot of a computer AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p>
<p>→Once it is deployed, click ‘Go to resource’</p>
<p>→Important: Azure Availability Zones provide HA within a single region by distributing VMs across physically separate data centers.</p>
<p>→For cross-region HA and DR, Azure uses region pairs with geo-replication and services like Azure Site Recovery.</p>
<p>→Each region in a region pair requires its own Recovery Services Vault to manage backups and recovery points independently.</p>
<p>→Traffic Manager or Azure Front Door can be used to route traffic and enable failover between regions. →Availability Zones do not span multiple regions, so cross-region HA always involves multiple vaults and coordinated replication strategies.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3869.webp" style="width:3.82569in;height:2.33333in" alt="A computer screen shot of a computer AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

### Configure Backup policy

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 48%" />
<col style="width: 51%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_671.webp" style="width:3.39861in;height:1.55069in" alt="A computer screen shot of a computer AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p>
<p>→Navigate to the RSV.</p>
<p>→Click Overview and click +Backup</p></td>

<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>→The Disaster Recovery option in an Azure VM under Backup + DR enables replication to a secondary region using Azure Site Recovery.<br />
→It ensures business continuity by allowing VM failover in case the primary region becomes unavailable.<br />
→During setup, a cache storage account is used in the source region to temporarily store replication data before it's pushed to the target region.<br />

→This setup allows planned and unplanned failover, as well as regular testing without impacting production.</p></td>
