#  Backup - VMs

<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3982.webp" style="width:7.67431in;height:1.19167in" alt="{41F3BD5C-FD68-4635-818C-9B87C911362C}" />

→You are an Administrator for Hexelo, an organization that needs to implement Azure® backup for its Azure virtual machines.

In this Challenge Lab, you will implement Azure backup for your Azure virtual machines. First, you will back up an Azure virtual machine by using the Azure portal. Next, you will enable backups on an Azure virtual machine by using Azure PowerShell®. Finally, you will enable backups on an Azure virtual machine by using Azure CLI 2.0.

- Enable backups on the VM1 virtual machine by using an Azure recovery services vault named AZ300-RecoveryServicesVault-52853552.

<!-- -->

- On the Azure portal home page, in Azure services, select Virtual machines.

- On the Virtual machines blade, select VM1.

- On the VM1 service menu, in Backup + disaster recovery, select Backup.

- On the Backup page, in Recovery Services vault, ensure that Create new is selected.

- In Backup vault, enter AZ300-RecoveryServicesVault-52853552.

- In Policy sub type, select Standard.

- Review the remaining default values, and then select Enable backup.

→You should protect your virtual machine data by taking backups of virtual machines at regular intervals. You can enable backups for a virtual machine during or after the virtual machine deployment process. You will store the backup in a geo-redundant recovery services vault. Azure automatically uses geo-redundant storage to replicate your data to a secondary Azure region that is hundreds of miles away from the primary region where the backup is stored.

→You can use a backup policy to define when a backup should run and how long Azure should retain the backup. If you choose to use the default backup policy, a backup will be created once a day, and the backups will be retained for 30 days.

→The first virtual machine backup you run will create a full recovery point. Subsequent backups of the same virtual machine will create incremental backup points which only transfer changes made since the last backup.

Wait for backups on VM1 to be fully enabled before moving on to the next step.

- Back up the VM1 virtual machine.

<!-- -->

- On the Azure portal home page, in Resources, in Recent, select VM1.

- On the VM1 service menu, in Backup + disaster recovery, select Backup.

- On the command bar, select Backup now.

- On the Back up now blade, select OK to initiate the backup.

- Close the VM1 blade.

> Your first backup of a virtual machine will occur automatically according to the backup policy you set. However, you can initiate a backup of the virtual machine at any time.

## Portal - Configure Backup

→ Navigate to portal and see we have 3 VMs.

→For each VM we use different method to enable Backups viz., Portal, Powershell and AZ

<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image3983.webp" style="width:4.49792in;height:2.05833in" alt="{D92F6AAB-0456-45A0-9AB1-7E772AE87544}" />

→ Click VM1 and navigate to backup+dr→ backup→ click create new.

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 49%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→<strong>Backup</strong>: Uses a Recovery Services Vault in Azure which is a storage entity.</p>
<p>→This is for managing backups and disaster recovery data, primarily for Azure VMs, SQL databases, and on-premises workloads.</p>
<p>→It supports backup policies like the "Standard" policy, which schedules daily backups with a default 30-day retention for recovery points.</p>
<p>→The vault ensures data protection with features like geo-redundant storage (GRS) and soft delete for accidental deletion recovery.</p>
<p>→It simplifies backup management, offering centralized monitoring and secure data restoration</p></td>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→ <strong>Disaster Recovery</strong>: Uses a Recovery Services Vault in Azure to manage replication and failover for business continuity.<br />
→ It replicates Azure VMs or on-premises servers to a secondary Azure region using <strong>Azure Site Recovery</strong>.<br />
→ The "Standard" policy supports customizable replication settings for near-real-time data sync and automated failover.<br />
→ It ensures rapid system recovery with minimal downtime, enhancing resilience against regional outages.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>→Use <strong>Backup</strong> for scheduled data snapshots to restore files or databases after data loss, with longer recovery times.</p>
<p>→Use <strong>Disaster Recovery</strong> for near-real-time replication of entire systems to ensure rapid failover and minimal downtime during regional outages.</p>
<p>→Backup and Disaster Recovery can <strong>co-exist</strong> in the same Recovery Services Vault in Azure. They complement each other: Backup protects specific data with scheduled snapshots for restoration, while Disaster Recovery replicates entire systems for rapid failover during outages.</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Powershell - Configure Backup 

→ Using powershell

- Open an Azure Cloud Shell PowerShell® session without mounting a storage account-use the existing subscription.

> Maximize the Cloud Shell window to make it easier to see the commands.

- On the Azure portal toolbar, in the global controls, select the Cloud Shell icon.

- In the Welcome to Azure Cloud Shell dialog, select PowerShell.

- In the Getting started dialog, select No storage account required, in Subscription, select the existing Challenge Labs option, and then select Apply.

<!-- -->

- Set the vault context of the AZ300-RecoveryServicesVault-52853552 recovery vault by using the Get-AzRecoveryServicesVault and Set-AzRecoveryServicesVaultContext cmdlets.

<!-- -->

- Run the following command to set the recovery services vault context:

> PowerShell
>
> Get-AzRecoveryServicesVault -Name "AZ300-RecoveryServicesVault-52853552" \| Set-AzRecoveryServicesVaultContext

- Create a variable named \$policy to hold the Default Policy backup policy by using the Get-AzRecoveryServicesBackupProtectionPolicy cmdlet.

<!-- -->

- Run the following command to create a variable:

> PowerShell
>
> \$policy = Get-AzRecoveryServicesBackupProtectionPolicy -Name "DefaultPolicy"

- Enable backups on the VM2 virtual machine in the AZ300-RGlod52853552 resource group by using the \$policy variable and the Enable-AzRecoveryServicesBackupProtection cmdlet.

<!-- -->

- Run the following command to enable a virtual machine backup:

> PowerShell
>
> Enable-AzRecoveryServicesBackupProtection -ResourceGroupName "AZ300-RGlod52853552" -Name "VM2" -Policy \$policy
>
> Want to learn more? Review the documentation on the [Backup-AzRecoveryServicesBackupItem](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/az.recoveryservices/backup-azrecoveryservicesbackupitem?view=azps-3.6.1) cmdlet.

→ A backup of a VM in Azure is stored in the **Recovery Services Vault**, which uses geo-redundant storage (GRS) by default for data durability. The backup data, including VM snapshots and recovery points, resides in the Azure region specified in the vault, with a replicated copy in a paired region for redundancy.

#  Backup recovery 

<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4008.webp" style="width:7.67153in;height:0.65903in" alt="{9768DF6E-6C50-491C-A91A-35B92DE998D0}" />

→You are a Architect at Hexelo, an organization that is migrating its database services from its own datacenter to Azure®.

→In this Challenge Lab, you will enable virtual machine (VM) backup using a Recovery Services Vault.

→First, you will create an Azure VM that hosts Microsoft SQL Server.

→Next, you will create a Recovery Services vault, and then you will enable backup in the Azure VM.

→Finally, you will enable SQL Server backup in the Azure VM.

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→<strong>VM Backup</strong>: When you create a Recovery Services Vault and enable backup for the Azure VM, it captures the entire virtual machine, including its disks, operating system, and SQL Server installation. This ensures you can restore the entire VM to a previous state in case of failures like disk corruption or accidental deletion. However, this backup is at the VM level and doesn’t optimize for granular database recovery, meaning restoring specific SQL databases or performing point-in-time restores can be cumbersome and slow.</p>
<p>→SQL Server Backup: Enabling SQL Server backup explicitly within the Recovery Services Vault configures Azure Backup to manage SQL Server databases specifically. This process involves discovering SQL databases on the VM and setting up workload-aware backups. It provides granular control, allowing you to back up individual databases, perform point-in-time restores, and recover specific transactions, which is critical for database-driven applications. This is more efficient than restoring an entire VM to recover a single database.</p>
<p>→<strong>Why Both Are Needed</strong>: The VM backup ensures the entire machine’s integrity, while the SQL Server backup focuses on the database workload, offering faster, more precise recovery options for SQL data. Combining both provides comprehensive protection: VM backup for infrastructure-level recovery and SQL Server backup for application-level database recovery, aligning with best practices for critical systems in Azure.</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

→Create an Azure virtual machine (VM) named VM1 by using the values in the following table. For any property that is not specified, use the default values.

|:---|:---|

| Virtual machine name | VM1 |
| Region | (US) East US |
| Security type | Standard |
| Image | Free SQL Server License: SQL Server 2017 Developer on Windows Server 2019 - x64 Gen2 |
| Size | Standard B2ms |
| Username | testuser |
| Password | Pa55w.rd1234 |
| Public inbound ports | Allow selected ports |
| Select inbound ports | RDP (3389) |
| OS disk type | Standard HDD |
| Boot diagnostics | Disable |
| SQL Connectivity | Private |
| SQL Port | 1433 |
| SQL Authentication | Enable |

- On the Microsoft Azure home page, in Azure services, select Create a resource.

- On the Virtual machine blade, select Create.

- On the Create a virtual machine blade, in Project details, in Resource group, select corp-datalod52860620.

- In Instance details, in Virtual machine name, enter VM1.

- In Region, ensure that (US) East US is selected.

- In Image, select See all images.

- In Size, select See all sizes, search for and select B2ms, and then select Select.

- In Administrator account, in Username, enter testuser, and then in Password and Confirm password, enter Pa55w.rd1234.

- In Inbound port rules, in Public inbound ports, ensure that Allow selected ports is selected and in Select inbound ports, ensure RDP 3389 is selected.

- Select Next: Disks.

- On the Disks page, in OS disk, in OS disk type, select Standard HDD, and then select the Monitoring tab.

- On the Monitoring page, in Diagnostics, in Boot diagnostics, select Disable, and then select the SQL Server settings tab.

- On the SQL Server settings page, in Security & Networking, ensure that SQL connectivity is set to Private, and that the Port is set to 1433.

- In SQL Authentication, in SQL Authentication, select Enable.

### Configure SQL Server Settings

→ Navigate to SQL Server Settings and ensure the connectivity is private and port is 1433

→ Then enable the ‘SQL Authentication’

→SQL Server settings for an Azure VM allow you to configure SQL connectivity and authentication during provisioning. Choosing Private SQL connectivity restricts access to the SQL Server instance to within the virtual network, disabling public internet access by not opening the default SQL port (1433) in the network security group. Enabling SQL Authentication allows connections using SQL Server credentials (username and password) alongside Windows Authentication, which is required for public access but can also be used privately. This setup enhances security by limiting access and supports flexible authentication methods for database connections

##  Enable SQL Server Backup 

- Configure vault52860620 to backup MyDB SQL Server database on the VM1 virtual machine in the corp-datalod52860620 resource group by using the Start Discovery and Configure Backup options.

<!-- -->

- On the Azure portal menu, select All resources, and then select vault52860620.

- On the vault52860620 blade, on the command bar, select + Backup.

- On the Backup Goal blade, in Where is your workload running?, ensure that Azure is selected.

- In What do you want to backup?, select SQL Database in Azure VM, and then in Step 1: Discover DBs in VMs, select Start Discovery.

- If necessary, on the Select Virtual Machine pane, select the VM1 check box in the corp-datalod52860620 resource group, and then select Discover DB's.

- Wait until the Discovery process is complete - this can take 2-3 minutes; you can select Notifications in the Azure portal global toolbar to check the deployment status. You may have to select the ellipsis (…) to see the Notifications option.

- In Step 2: Configure Backup, select Configure Backup.

- In SQL Databases, select Add.

- On the Select items to backup blade, expand vm1\MSSQLSERVER.

- Select the check box for MyDB, and then select OK.

- On the Configure backup blade, select Enable backup.

→The *Start Discovery* operation should take 2-3 minutes and the *Configure Backup* operation should take 1-2 minutes to complete. You can select Notifications in the Azure portal global toolbar to check the deployment status. You may have to select the ellipsis (…) to see the Notifications option.

→If you refresh the browser during the Discovery process, you will have to reselect SQL Database in Azure VM in *What do you want to backup?* each time.

- Trigger an initial full backup of the MyDB database by using the Backup now option.

<!-- -->

- On the Deployment blade, select Go to resource.

- On the vault52860620 service menu, in Protected items, select Backup items.

- On the Backup items page, in BACKUP MANAGEMENT TYPE, select SQL Database in Azure VM.

- On the Backup Items (SQL Database in Azure VM) blade, to the right of mydb, select the ellipsis (…), and then select Backup now.

- On the Backup now blade, select OK.

→The Triggering backup for mydb operation should take 1-2 minutes to complete.

#  Backup - Attach Disks - Snaptshot - Recover

<p>You are an Administrator for Hexelo, an organization that needs to deploy workloads on an Azure® virtual machine.</p>
<p>→In this Challenge Lab, you will create an image of an Azure virtual machine that hosts Microsoft Visual Studio®.</p>
<p>→First, you will create a virtual machine with Visual Studio Image.</p>
<p>→Second you will add a data disk to the virtual machine.</p>
<p>→Third you will capture an image of a generalized version of the virtual machine in Azure.</p>
<p>→Fourth you will create a virtual machine from the image</p>

## Generalized Virtual Machine - making it ready for Image Capture

<table style="width:87%;">
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 87%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>→Open Powershell and execute below commands.</p>
<p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4178.webp" style="width:6.52431in;height:3.30972in" alt="{035188B2-9A06-4AB7-B873-526ED1064649}" /></p>
<p>→ This is done to create a <strong>generic image</strong> that can be deployed to multiple machines without conflicts, such as duplicate SIDs, and to prepare it for end-user setup.</p>
<p>What exactly happens with this command is as below.</p>
<blockquote>
<p>→Generalizes the system by removing unique identifiers (e.g., SID - Security Identifier) and resetting certain system settings, making the installation generic and reusable across multiple machines.</p>
<p>→Configures OOBE (Out-of-Box Experience), which sets up the system to prompt for initial user configuration (e.g., language, user account) when it restarts.</p>
<p>→Optimizes for VM with /mode:vm, ensuring the system is tailored for virtual machine deployment.</p>
<p>→Shuts down to freeze the state, allowing an imaging tool to capture the generalized installation without further changes.</p>
</blockquote></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>cd \windows\system32\sysprep</p>
<p>.\sysprep.exe /oobe /generalize /mode:vm /shutdown</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>After the sysprep process generalizes the virtual machine, the sysprep process should shut down the virtual machine, and the RDP session will close automatically.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4179.webp" style="width:6.52639in;height:2.27083in" alt="{C724C8E2-E611-48D4-8BBE-5BDF22D8BD62}" /></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

#  Monitor - Alerts - Actions - Rules - Logs 

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 100%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;">→Azure Monitoring provides a unified framework to observe, analyze, and respond to resource events and metrics.<br />
→Alerts are configured to notify you when specific conditions are met, such as a metric threshold or log event.<br />
→Triggers define the condition that causes an alert to fire, like CPU usage exceeding 80%.<br />
→Actions determine the response, such as sending an email, triggering an Azure Function, or running an automation runbook.<br />
→Processing rules help suppress or modify alerts based on defined logic to avoid alert noise.<br />
→Log queries allow deep analysis of diagnostic and activity logs using Kusto Query Language (KQL) for troubleshooting and insights.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

## Configure processing rule - Supress during maintenance. 

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 48%" />
<col style="width: 51%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p>→Configuring a processing rule in Azure Monitor lets you control how alerts behave without modifying the alert definitions themselves.<br />
→Below we are choosing a resource group as scope and selecting "Suppress notifications", we are preventing alerts from sending notifications during the specified schedule.<br />
→The start and end time under scheduling define the suppression window, useful for planned maintenance or testing.<br />
→This helps reduce alert noise and ensures only actionable alerts are surfaced during critical periods.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="2" style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_794.webp" style="width:5.07569in;height:2.23889in" alt="A computer screen shot of a computer AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p>

<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/flatten_795.webp" style="width:2.44931in;height:1.48611in" alt="A computer screen with a message AI-generated content may be incorrect." /></p></td>

#  Monitor - Diagnostic Settings on Azure Virtual Machines

<img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4351.webp" style="width:7.66597in;height:1.26667in" alt="{F3C2E0D3-C862-44FB-8057-5D48E24FF882}" />

→ You are an Architect with Hexelo.

→ You need to configure diagnostic settings on an Azure virtual machine.

→Step 1: you will create a Log Analytics Workspace

→Step 2: you will enable the Azure Monitor Agent on a virtual machine.

→Step 3: you will create a diagnostic setting for an Azure virtual machine by using the Azure portal.

→Step 4: you will manage virtual machine extensions by using Azure PowerShell®.

- Create a Log Analytics Workspace named AZ300-52865078-Workspace that uses the AZ300-RGlod52865078 resource group and the East US region.

<!-- -->

- In the Azure portal, select Create a resource to open the Azure Marketplace.

- In Search services and marketplace, search for and select Log Analytics Workspace.

- On the Log Analytics Workspace page, review the information, and then select Create.

- <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4352.jpeg" style="width:3.03264in;height:1.11597in" alt="IMG_256" />

- On the Create Log Analytics Workspace blade, in Resource group, select AZ300-RGlod52865078.

- In Name, enter AZ300-52865078-Workspace.

- In Region, ensure that East US is selected, and then select Review + Create.

- Review the configuration, and then select Create.

→ An [Azure Log Analytics Workspace](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/learn/quick-create-workspace) is important to your ability to manage Azure resources. It can be used to collect data from a variety of sources. Once data is collected, Log Analytics uses a query language and an analytics engine to give you insights into the operation of your applications and resources. You can either interact directly with Log Analytics data through log searches and views, or you can use analysis tools in other Azure services that store their data in Log Analytics-for example, Application Insights or Azure Security Center.

→There is little that you need to do to configure Azure to use Log Analytics to monitor your resources, as it is already integrated with other Azure services. You simply need to create a workspace to enable collection, and then you can install agents on your virtual machines. Adding agents to virtual machines will connect them to the workspace and enable you to implement a variety of management solutions.

→The Log Analytics Workspace should take a minute to deploy.

- Open the AZ300-52865078-Workspace in the AZ300-RGlod52865078 resource group.

<!-- -->

- In the Azure portal, on the portal menu, select Resource groups.

- <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4353.jpeg" style="width:2.21875in;height:2.69792in" alt="IMG_257" />

- Select AZ300-RGlod52865078.

- On the AZ300-RGlod52865078 Resource group page, select AZ300-52865078-Workspace.

<p>→This platform takes data from resources across subscriptions and services.</p>
<p>→ Within this ecosystem, <strong>Log Analytics Workspace</strong> serves as the <strong>foundational data store</strong> and <strong>query engine</strong> for</p>
<p>→ The LAW, particularly meant for logs and telemetry.</p></td>

<tr>
<td><p><strong>Azure Monitor </strong>is the core service for monitoring Azure resources. It collects performance metrics, activity logs, and diagnostics data. It provides insights into application health and performance. Metrics and logs are stored and analyzed here.</p>
<p><strong>Log Analytics Workspace </strong>is a centralized repository for log data. It stores logs from Azure Monitor, VMs, and other services. You query this data using Kusto Query Language (KQL). It integrates with other Azure monitoring tools.</p>
<p><strong>Application Insights </strong>monitors live web applications. It tracks requests, dependencies, and exceptions. Data is stored in a Log Analytics Workspace. It helps detect performance anomalies.</p>
<p><strong>Azure Diagnostics</strong> (Diagnostic Settings) collects resource-level logs and metrics. It sends data to Log Analytics, Storage, or Event Hubs. You enable it per Azure resource. It’s essential for troubleshooting.</p>
<p><strong>Activity Logs </strong>track subscription-level events. They include administrative actions and service health. You can route them to Log Analytics. They help audit Azure operations.</p>
<p><strong>Alerts and Action Groups </strong>notify you of critical conditions. Alerts trigger based on metrics or logs. Action Groups define who gets notified. They integrate with Log Analytics queries.</p>
<p><strong>Workbooks and Dashboards </strong>visualize monitoring data. Workbooks combine logs, metrics, and visuals. Dashboards display real-time metrics. Both pull data from Log Analytics.</p>
<p><strong>Azure Monitor Agent</strong> (AMA) replaces legacy agents. It collects logs and metrics from VMs. Data is sent to Log Analytics. It supports centralized monitoring.</p>
<p><strong>Network Watcher </strong>monitors network performance. It provides tools like Connection Monitor. Logs can be sent to Log Analytics. It helps diagnose networking issues.</p>
<p><strong>Security Center &amp; Sentinel </strong>use Log Analytics for threat detection. They analyze security logs stored there. Alerts and incidents are generated. They enhance Azure’s security posture.</p>
<p>All these components feed into or rely on Log Analytics Workspace, making it the backbone of Azure monitoring. Data correlation happens here, enabling unified insights.</p></td>
</tr>

## VM1: Enable Azure Monitor Agent (AMA) using Azure Portal 

→ Enable the Azure Monitor Agent by creating a Data Collection Rule named WindowsVM-Rule1 for the WindowsVM virtual machine by using the AZ300-52865078-Workspace Log Analytics Workspace and the values in the following table.

| **Data source type**                           | **Destination**    |
|:-----------------------------------------------|:-------------------|
| Windows Event Logs (all event logs and levels) | Azure Monitor Logs |
| Performance Counters (all Basic counters)      | Azure Monitor Logs |

- On the Azure portal menu, select All resources, and then select AZ300-52865078-Workspace.

- On the AZ300-52865078-Workspace Overview page, in Get started with Log Analytics, in Connect a data source, select Azure virtual machines (VMs).

- <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4361.jpeg" style="width:4.45in;height:3.69583in" alt="IMG_256" />

- On the Create Data Collection Rule blade, on the Basics page, in Rule Name, enter WindowsVM-Rule1, in Platform Type, ensure that Windows is selected, and then select Next : Resources.

- On the Resources page, select Add resources.

- <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4362.jpeg" style="width:2.57292in;height:0.75in" alt="IMG_257" />

- On the Select a scope pane, expand the AZ300-RGlod52865078 resource group, select the check box for the WindowsVM virtual machine, and then select Apply.

- <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4363.jpeg" style="width:4.20764in;height:2.05833in" alt="IMG_258" />

- On the Resources page, select Next : Collect and deliver.

- On the Collect and deliver page, select Add data source.

- <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4364.jpeg" style="width:3.5in;height:0.84375in" alt="IMG_259" />

- On the Add data source blade, on the Data source page, in Data source type, select Windows Event Logs, and then select all of the check boxes for the event logs and levels to collect.

- <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4365.jpeg" style="width:4.78958in;height:3.62153in" alt="IMG_260" />

- On the Data source page, select Next : Destination.

- On the Destination page, select Add destination.

- <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4366.jpeg" style="width:3.53125in;height:0.64583in" alt="IMG_261" />

- On the Destination page, in Destination type, select Azure Monitor Logs, in Destination Details, select AZ300-52865078-Workspace (AZ300-RGlod52865078), and then select Add data source.

- On the Collect and deliver page, select Add data source again to add a second data source.

- On the Add data source blade, on the Data source page, in Data source type, select Performance Counters, and then ensure that all Basic Performance counters are selected.

- <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4367.jpeg" style="width:4.08056in;height:2.37222in" alt="IMG_262" />

- On the Data source page, select Next : Destination.

- On the Destination page, select Add destination.

- On the Destination page, in Destination type, select Azure Monitor Logs, in Destination Details, select AZ300-52865078-Workspace (AZ300-RGlod52865078), and then select Add data source.

- On the Collect and deliver page, ensure that both data sources are listed.

- <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4368.jpeg" style="width:4.94444in;height:2.25556in" alt="IMG_263" />

- On the Create Data Collection Rule, select Review + create, and then select Create to create the Data Collection Rule.

> If the WindowsVM virtual machine is not available, it may be still deploying in the background. Wait a minute and then try again.
>
> When you create a Data Collection Rule (DCR) in the Azure portal, the [Azure Monitor Agent](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/agents/azure-monitor-agent-manage?tabs=azure-portal) is installed on any machine that's added as a resource for the DCR. The agent immediately begins to collect data as defined in the DCR.

- Enable the Azure Monitor Agent for the WindowsVM2 virtual machine by adding WindowsVM2 as an additional resource in the WindowsVM-Rule1 Data Collection Rule.

> Expand this hint for guidance on enabling the Azure Monitor Agent by updating a Data Collection Rule.

- On the Azure portal menu, select All resources, and then select WindowsVM-Rule1.

- On the WindowsVM-Rule1 resource menu, expand Configuration, and then select Resources.

- <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4369.jpeg" style="width:2.79167in;height:1.29653in" alt="IMG_264" />

- On the Resources page, on the command bar, select Add.

## Create Diagnostic Settings for VMs 

- Enable guest-level monitoring on the WindowsVM virtual machine by using the Diagnostics storage account that begins with standard.

- <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4427.jpeg" style="width:1.23194in;height:1.35764in" alt="IMG_256" />

- <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4428.jpeg" style="width:3.42292in;height:3.63125in" alt="IMG_257" />

> To turn on diagnostic settings, you need to enable guest-level monitoring first.
>
> Wait for guest-level monitoring to be enabled. It may take a minute.
>
> <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4429.jpeg" style="width:3.8625in;height:1.30139in" alt="IMG_258" />
>
> You should then see the Diagnostic settings page change to resemble the following screenshot:
>
> <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4430.jpeg" style="width:4.52847in;height:3.22014in" alt="IMG_259" />

- Enable the collection of the CPU, Disk, and Memory performance counters on WindowsVM.

<!-- -->

- On the WindowsVM Diagnostic settings page, select Performance counters.

- On the Performance counters page, select Clear all counters.

- <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4431.jpeg" style="width:3.10417in;height:0.76042in" alt="IMG_260" />

- On the Performance counters page, select Select basic counters.

- <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4432.jpeg" style="width:3.42708in;height:0.63542in" alt="IMG_261" />

- On the Select basic counter groups pane, in Select basic counters, select the check boxes for CPU, Disk, and Memory performance counters, and then select Select.

- <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4433.jpeg" style="width:4.22708in;height:2.69097in" alt="IMG_262" />

- On the WindowsVM Diagnostic settings page, select the Apply to save your changes.

> Wait for your changes to be applied. It may take a minute.
>
> <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4434.jpeg" style="width:3.87431in;height:1.41042in" alt="IMG_263" />

- Enable Failed request logs storing the logs in wad-failedrequest-logs, enable IIS logs, storing the logs in wad-iis-logs, and enable application logs for Critical events on WindowsVM.

<!-- -->

- On the WindowsVM Diagnostic settings page, select Logs.

- On the Logs page, in Failed requests, select the check box for Collect failed request logs, and then in Storage container name, ensure that wad-failedrequest-logs is entered.

- On the Logs page, scroll down, in IIS Logs, select the check box for Collect IIS logs, and then in Storage container name, ensure that wad-iis-logs is entered.

- In Application Logs, select the check box for Collect application logs, and then in Log level to collect, select Critical.

- <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4435.jpeg" style="width:2.57153in;height:2.03681in" alt="IMG_264" />

- On the WindowsVM Diagnostic settings page, select the Apply to save your changes.

> Wait for your changes to be applied. It may take a minute.
>
> <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4434.jpeg" style="width:3.63472in;height:1.32292in" alt="IMG_265" />
>
> To create a diagnostic setting for a virtual machine, you can use the Azure portal, the [Set-AzDiagnosticSetting](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/az.monitor/set-azdiagnosticsetting?view=azps-3.6.1) PowerShell command, or the [az vm diagnostics set](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/cli/azure/vm/diagnostics?view=azure-cli-latest#az-vm-diagnostics-set) CLI 2.0 command.

Enable guest-level monitoring on WindowsVM2 by using the Diagnostics storage account that begins with standard.

Enable the collection of the CPU, Disk, and Memory performance counters on WindowsVM2.

Enable Failed request logs storing the logs in wad-failedrequest-logs, enable IIS logs, storing the logs in wad-iis-logs, and enable application logs for Critical events on WindowsVM2.

##  Manage VM Extensions using Powershell 

- Configure an Azure Cloud Shell PowerShell session by using the Challenge Labs subscription and No storage account required setting.

> Expand this hint for guidance on configuring Azure Cloud Shell.

- <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4479.jpeg" style="width:2.76111in;height:0.76528in" alt="IMG_256" />

- <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4480.jpeg" style="width:4.78056in;height:1.13819in" alt="IMG_257" />

- <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4481.jpeg" style="width:5.20694in;height:1.65417in" alt="IMG_258" />

> →You would need to configure a storage account if you wish to persist files from one session to another. In this case, we do not need that feature.
>
> [Azure Cloud Shell](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cloud-shell/overview) is a shell for managing Azure resources. Azure Cloud Shell supports Bash or PowerShell. You can access [Azure Cloud Shell](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cloud-shell/quickstart-powershell) on the Azure portal toolbar or by entering https://shell.azure.com in a browser.
>
> Maximize the Azure Cloud Shell window to make it easier to see the commands.
>
> <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4482.jpeg" style="width:2.16667in;height:1.95833in" alt="IMG_259" />

View properties for all extensions installed on WindowsVM2 by using the [Get-AzVMExtension](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/az.compute/get-azvmextension?view=azps-3.6.1) PowerShell cmdlet.

- Run the following command to display the properties of all extensions installed on WindowsVM2:

> Get-AzVMExtension -ResourceGroupName "AZ300-RGlod52865078" -VMName "WindowsVM2"
>
> To paste text into the Azure Cloud Shell window use Ctrl+Shift+V.

Enter the name of the ExtensionType for the Diagnostic settings extension in the following text box.

ExtensionType: 

Remove the Diagnostic settings extension on WindowsVM2 by using the [Remove-AzVMDiagnosticsExtension](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/az.compute/remove-azvmdiagnosticsextension?view=azps-3.6.1) cmdlet.

- Run the following command to remove the Log Analytics extension on WindowsVM2:

> Remove-AzVMDiagnosticsExtension -ResourceGroupName "AZ300-RGlod52865078" -VMName "WindowsVM2"
>
> The Remove-AzVMDiagnosticsExtension may take a few minutes to run to completion.
>
> <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4483.jpeg" style="width:5.15in;height:0.87222in" alt="IMG_260" />
>
> To clear the screen in Cloud Shell you can use the cls command.

- Verify that the Azure Monitor Agent has been removed on WindowsVM2 by using the Azure portal.

> You may need to refresh the WindowsVM2 Diagnostic settings page by using Ctrl+R.
>
> <img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4484.jpeg" style="width:4.75in;height:4.49722in" alt="IMG_261" />

## Enable Guest Level Monitoring

<p>→Refer previous sections where Diagnostics is enabled.</p>

#  Monitor - Gues Level - Snapshot impl 

<table style="width:87%;">
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 87%" />
</colgroup>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p><img src="subjects/tech/azure/az-104-and-305-labs/img/media/image4619.webp" style="width:6.52153in;height:0.95972in" alt="{FBA4445D-1360-4F05-81D6-3FC871997B94}" /></p>
<p>You are an Administrator for Hexelo, an organization that needs to <strong>migrate</strong> its primary web app from its on-premises datacenter to Azure®.</p>
<p>→will deploy an Azure virtual machine and configure <strong>storage</strong>.</p>
<p>→First, you will create a virtual machine that has boot <strong>diagnostics enabled</strong>.</p>
<p>→ Next, you will add a <strong>data disk</strong> to the virtual machine,</p>
<p>→Next, you will create a <strong>snapshot</strong>.</p>
<p>→Finally, you will enable <strong>guest-level</strong> monitoring.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: left;"><p>We are migrating Hexelo's web app from an on-premises datacenter to Azure by setting up a virtual machine with boot diagnostics, adding a data disk for storage, creating a snapshot for backup, and enabling guest-level monitoring for performance tracking. This ensures a secure, scalable, and monitored cloud environment for the app. The process involves configuring Azure resources to support the app’s deployment and management.</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
